gancho: Em Yap, na Micronésia, discos de pedra de até 4 toneladas mudavam de dono sem sair do lugar. Uma pedra que afundou no mar continuou sendo negociada.
explicacao: As pedras rai são discos de calcário com um furo no meio, feitos pelos habitantes das ilhas Yap, na Micronésia. As menores têm 3,5 centímetros; a maior que ainda existe tem 3,6 metros de diâmetro e pesa cerca de 4 toneladas. Elas eram extraídas sobretudo em Palau, outra ilha, e levadas de canoa ou, as maiores, em jangadas de bambu. Serviam para transações sociais importantes e raras, como casamentos, heranças e acordos políticos. Como as grandes eram pesadas demais e raramente eram movidas, a posse não dependia de onde a pedra estava, mas da sua história, guardada na memória coletiva: cada pedra tinha uma tradição oral com os nomes dos donos anteriores, e acrescentar uma transferência a essa história bastava para mudar o dono. Numa ocasião, uma pedra grande caiu de uma canoa e afundou. Ninguém nunca mais a viu, mas todos concordaram que ela continuava lá, e ela seguiu sendo negociada como qualquer outra. Alguns economistas usam as pedras rai para mostrar que o valor do dinheiro pode depender só do acordo entre as pessoas.

fontes.trecho: The typical rai stone is carved out of crystalline limestone and shaped like a disk with a hole in the center. The smallest may be 3.5 centimetres (1.4 in) in diameter. The largest extant stone is located on Rumung island, near the Riy village; it is 3.6 metres (12 ft) in diameter and 50 centimetres (20 in) thick, and weighs 4,000 kilograms (8,800 lb). Rai stones were quarried on several of the Micronesian islands, mainly Palau, but briefly on Guam as well. [...] The ownership of a large stone, which would be too difficult to move, was established by its history as recorded in oral tradition rather than by its location. Appending a transfer to the oral history of the stone thus effected a change of ownership. Some modern economists have viewed Rai stones as a form of money, and the stones are often used as a demonstration of the fact that the value of some forms of money can be assigned purely through a shared belief in said value. [...] Each large stone had an oral history that included the names of previous owners. In one instance, a large rai being transported by canoe and outrigger was accidentally dropped and sank to the sea floor. Although it was never seen again, everyone agreed that the rai must still be there, so it continued to be transacted as any other stone. [...] On the return, the stones could be carried by canoe or (for the larger specimens) on bamboo rafts. [...] Rai stones were, and still are, used in rare important social transactions, such as marriage, inheritance, political deals

gancho: Na Hungria de 1946, os preços chegaram a dobrar a cada 15 horas. Foi a maior hiperinflação já registrada, e o banco central imprimiu uma nota de 100 quintilhões.
explicacao: O pengő foi a moeda da Hungria de 1927 a 1946. Depois da Segunda Guerra Mundial, ele perdeu valor de forma vertiginosa, na maior hiperinflação já registrada na história, muito pior que a da Alemanha em 1923. Num certo momento, os preços dobravam em cerca de 15 horas, e em uns quatro dias a moeda perdia 90% do valor. O governo tentou de tudo, até criar uma moeda paralela para impostos, o adópengő. Não adiantou. Em julho de 1946, o banco central lançou a última cédula: 100 milhões de "B-pengős", ou seja, 100 quintilhões de pengős, um 1 seguido de 20 zeros. Uma nota de 1 sextilhão chegou a ser impressa, mas nunca circulou. No fim daquele mês, o pengő foi substituído pelo forint.

fontes.trecho: was the currency of Hungary between 1 January 1927, when it replaced the korona, and 31 July 1946, when it was replaced by the forint. [...] The pengő lost value dramatically after World War II, suffering the highest rate of hyperinflation ever recorded in human history. This far exceeded the hyperinflation that affected the German mark in 1923. [...] The hyperinflation was so out of control that at one stage it took only about 15 hours for prices to double and about four days for the pengő to lose 90% of its prior value. [...] The Hungarian government introduced the adópengő (lit. 'tax pengő') on 1 January 1946 [...] On 11 July 1946, the Hungarian National Bank released the last pengő banknotes, for 100 million B-pengős (1020 = 100 quintillion); the Bank also printed banknotes for one billion B-pengős (1021 = one sextillion), but they never entered circulation.

gancho: Para acabar com a hiperinflação, o Brasil passou quatro meses de 1994 com uma moeda que não se podia gastar: a URV, que só servia para marcar preços e salários.
explicacao: No começo de 1994, a inflação brasileira passava de 1.200% ao ano. Parte dela era inercial: os preços subiam porque todos esperavam que subissem e reajustavam por precaução. O Plano Real atacou essa psicologia com uma ideia que vinha de 1984, dos economistas Pérsio Arida e André Lara Resende. Em março de 1994 foi criada a Unidade Real de Valor, a URV, uma unidade de conta que não era dinheiro. Seu valor acompanhava índices de preços e o dólar, e a cotação em cruzeiros reais era publicada todo dia. Preços eram anunciados nas duas unidades, contratos e salários foram reescritos em URV, mas os pagamentos continuavam em cruzeiros reais. A moeda velha absorvia a inflação, enquanto a URV ficava estável. Em 1º de julho de 1994, a URV virou dinheiro: 1 real passou a valer 1 URV, ou 2.750 cruzeiros reais. Em cerca de 45 dias, quase todo o dinheiro do país foi trocado.

fontes.trecho: was a unit of account (a non-monetary reference currency) used in Brazil. It was created in March 1994, as part of the Plano Real. URV was based on the "Larida Plan", published in 1984 by Pérsio Arida and André Lara Resende. Its main purpose was to establish a parallel currency to the cruzeiro real, free from the effects of inertial inflation on the latter, which exceeded 1,200% per year prior to the implementation of the new currency, the real. [...] The idea was to let the old currency (the cruzeiro real) fully absorb the effects of hyperinflation while having a new currency to be stable (in nominal terms) by adjusting its exchange rate against the old one. URVs were quoted in cruzeiros reais and its intrinsic value was pegged to three price indices and had a fixed parity of 1-to-1 to the daily U.S. dollar exchange rate. The exchange rate of URVs to cruzeiros reais was recalculated and published daily by the government. Prices were quoted both in URVs and cruzeiros reais, but payments had to be made exclusively in cruzeiros reais, since the URV would not become legal tender until July 1, 1994. [...] The URV was extinguished on July 1, 1994, when it was converted to a new currency, the real, at parity (i.e., 1 real = 1 URV = CR$2,750) [...] with almost the entirety of the country's legal tender replaced in about 45 days.

gancho: Somando todas as trocas de moeda do Brasil desde os réis, 1 real de hoje equivale a 2,75 quintilhões dos réis antigos. Foram oito moedas entre 1942 e 1994.
explicacao: Até 1942, o Brasil usava o real antigo, cujo plural, réis, aparecia em expressões como mil-réis. Daí em diante, a inflação foi obrigando a cortar zeros e trocar de nome repetidas vezes. Veio o cruzeiro, em 1942, valendo mil réis; o cruzeiro novo, em 1967, valendo mil cruzeiros; o cruzeiro de novo, em 1970, só uma troca de nome; o cruzado, em 1986, valendo mil cruzeiros; o cruzado novo, em 1989, valendo mil cruzados; outra vez o cruzeiro, em 1990, com o Plano Collor, de novo só no nome; o cruzeiro real, em 1993, valendo mil cruzeiros; e, finalmente, o real, em 1994, valendo 2.750 cruzeiros reais. Juntando todas as conversões, um real atual equivale a 2,75 quintilhões dos réis antigos, um número com 19 algarismos. Quando foi lançado, o real valia exatamente um dólar americano.

fontes.trecho: The old Brazilian real from 1747 to 1942, with 1,000 réis also called the milréis. The first cruzeiro from 1942 to 1967, at 1 cruzeiro = 1 milréis or 1,000 réis. The cruzeiro novo from 1967 to 1970, at 1 cruzeiro novo = 1,000 first cruzeiros. From 1970 it was simply called the (second) cruzeiro and was used until 1986. The cruzado from 1986 to 1989, at 1 cruzado = 1,000 second cruzeiros. The cruzado novo from 1989 to 1990, at 1 cruzado novo = 1,000 cruzados. From 1990, because of the Plano Collor it was renamed the (third) cruzeiro and was used until 1993. The cruzeiro real (CR$) from 1993 to 1994, at 1 cruzeiro real = 1,000 third cruzeiros. The current real was introduced in 1994 at 1 real = 2,750 cruzeiros reais. [...] As a consequence, the real was worth exactly one U.S. dollar when it was introduced [...] Combined with all previous currency changes in the country's history, this reform made the new real equal to 2.75×1018 (2.75 quintillion) of Brazil's original réis.

gancho: Nos campos de prisioneiros da Segunda Guerra, cigarros viraram moeda, com inflação e deflação. Em muitas prisões dos EUA, depois da proibição do fumo, o dinheiro passou a ser lata de cavala.
explicacao: Em 1945, o economista R. A. Radford descreveu como surgiu uma moeda dentro de um campo de prisioneiros. Os presos deixavam roupas, artigos de higiene e comida numa espécie de loja, e tudo era vendido a preço fixo em cigarros. Só se aceitava pagamento em cigarros, sem troca direta de mercadorias. A loja tinha até capital inicial, emprestado do estoque de cigarros da Cruz Vermelha. Radford mostrou que essa "moeda de cigarro" seguia as leis da economia: tinha inflação, deflação e a lei de Gresham, em que a moeda pior expulsa a melhor. Décadas depois, a mesma lógica reapareceu. Quando o fumo foi proibido nas prisões dos Estados Unidos, por volta de 2003, em muitas delas o dinheiro informal passou a ser lata de filé de cavala: custa em geral 1 dólar, dura muito, é fácil de guardar e é popular como comida rica em proteína.

fontes.trecho: Radford (1945) described the establishment of commodity money in POW camps. People left their surplus clothing, toilet requisites and food there until they were sold at a fixed price in cigarettes. Only sales in cigarettes were accepted – there was no barter [...] the capital was provided by a loan from the bulk store of Red Cross cigarettes and repaid by a small commission taken on the first transactions. Thus the cigarette attained its fullest currency status, and the market was almost completely unified. Radford documented the way that this "cigarette currency" was subject to Gresham's law, inflation, and especially deflation. In another example, in US prisons after smoking was banned circa 2003, commodity money has switched in many places to containers of mackerel fish fillets, which have a fairly standard cost (typically $1 per tin), have a long shelf-life, are easy to store and are popular as food for their high protein content.

gancho: "Dólar" vem do nome de um vale: as moedas de prata cunhadas a partir de 1518 em Joachimsthal, na Boêmia, eram os "Joachimsthaler", que viraram "thaler" e depois "dollar".
explicacao: Em 1516 abriram-se minas de prata em Joachimsthal, o "vale de São Joaquim", na Boêmia, hoje parte da República Tcheca. Em 1518 começaram a ser cunhadas ali grandes moedas de prata, chamadas Joachimsthaler. O nome encurtou para "taler" ou "thaler", e o sufixo quer dizer "do vale", o mesmo de Neanderthaler, o homem do vale de Neander. Moedas de prata desse tamanho, com cerca de 40 milímetros e 25 a 30 gramas, se espalharam pela Europa por séculos, e o nome ganhou formas regionais, como o "daler" do baixo-alemão. O inglês adotou a forma baixo-alemã "daler" por volta de 1550, e ela virou "dollar" por volta de 1600. Hoje o nome batiza várias moedas do mundo. O padrão do thaler durou muito: o dólar de prata americano foi cunhado até 1935.

fontes.trecho: A thaler size silver coin has a diameter of about 40 mm (1+1⁄2 in) and a weight of about 25 to 30 grams (roughly 1 ounce). The word is shortened from Joachimsthaler, the original thaler coin minted in Joachimsthal, Bohemia, from 1520. [...] The thaler silver coin type continued to be minted until the 20th century in the form of the Mexican peso until 1914, the five Swiss franc coin until 1928, the US silver dollar until 1935, and the Austrian Maria Theresa thaler. [...] The current derivative of the name, dollar (first Spanish and now mostly English), also survives as the name of several modern currencies. [...] The silver mines at Joachimstal had opened in 1516, and the first such coins were minted there in 1518. [...] German -taler means "of the valley" (cf. Neanderthaler) [...] Low German daler, dahler. [...] The Low German word was adopted in English as daler by 1550, modified to dollar by about 1600.

gancho: Isaac Newton passou as últimas três décadas da vida cuidando da Casa da Moeda inglesa. Interrogou suspeitos pessoalmente e levou à forca o falsificador mais habilidoso do reino.
explicacao: Em 1696, Newton foi nomeado guarda da Casa da Moeda Real, em Londres, e em 1699 virou seu diretor, cargo que manteve até morrer, em 1727. Os postos eram pensados como sinecuras, empregos quase sem trabalho, mas Newton os levou a sério. Ele estimou que 20% das moedas recolhidas na grande reforma monetária de 1696 eram falsas. Falsificar moeda era crime de alta traição, punido com morte, mas as condenações eram difíceis. Entre junho de 1698 e o Natal de 1699, Newton conduziu mais de 100 interrogatórios de testemunhas, informantes e suspeitos e conseguiu condenar 28 falsificadores. O mais famoso foi William Chaloner, descrito por um historiador como o falsificador mais habilidoso do reino, que já tinha passado várias vezes pela prisão. Newton provou sua culpa, e Chaloner foi enforcado em março de 1699. Além disso, Newton melhorou a técnica de cunhagem e deixou as moedas mais uniformes.

fontes.trecho: spent the last three decades of his life in London, serving as Warden (1696–1699) and Master (1699–1727) of the Royal Mint, in which he increased the accuracy and security of British coinage. [...] These appointments were intended as sinecures, but Newton took them seriously. [...] Newton estimated that 20 per cent of the coins taken in during the Great Recoinage of 1696 were counterfeit. Counterfeiting was high treason, punishable by the felon being hanged, drawn and quartered. [...] Then he conducted more than 100 cross-examinations of witnesses, informers, and suspects between June 1698 and Christmas 1699. He successfully prosecuted 28 coiners, including the serial counterfeiter William Chaloner, whom historian John Craig described as "the most accomplished counterfeiter in the kingdom". Chaloner was hanged in 1699. Beyond prosecuting counterfeiters, he improved minting technology and reduced the standard deviation of the weight

William Chaloner (1650 – 22 March 1699) was a serial counterfeit coiner and confidence trickster, who was imprisoned in Newgate Prison several times and eventually proven guilty of high treason by Sir Isaac Newton, Warden of the Royal Mint. He was hanged on the gallows at Tyburn on 22 March 1699.

gancho: Na Suécia dos séculos XVII e XVIII, a maior moeda era uma placa de cobre de quase 20 quilos. Carregar esse dinheiro era tão difícil que o país lançou as primeiras cédulas da Europa, em 1661.
explicacao: A prata andava escassa na Suécia. A partir de 1624, sua moeda, o daler, passou a ser emitida também em cobre. Como o cobre valia pouco, a moeda tinha de conter muito metal, e surgiram as moedas-placa: chapas retangulares de cobre que chegavam a pesar vários quilos. A maior, de 10 dalers, pesava quase 20 quilos. Elas circularam até 1776. O tamanho e o peso desse dinheiro acabaram levando a Suécia a ser o primeiro país da Europa a emitir cédulas de papel. Quem fez isso foi o Stockholms Banco, fundado em 1657 por Johan Palmstruch, que começou a imprimir notas em 1661. O banco emitiu notas demais, elas perderam valor, e ele foi liquidado em 1667. Mas dele nasceu, em 1668, o banco central da Suécia, o Riksbank.

fontes.trecho: From 1624, daler was issued in copper as well as silver. Because of the low value of copper, large plate money (plåtmynt) was issued. These were rectangular pieces of copper weighing in some cases several kilograms, with the largest one worth 10 daler and weighing almost 20 kilograms (44 lb). They circulated until 1776. [...] The cumbersome size and weight of plate money eventually prompted Sweden to become the first country in Europe to issue banknotes. These were issued by Stockholms Banco in 1661. The notes lost much of their value due to overproduction [...] As silver became scarce, the silver daler rose in value relative to the copper daler

was the first European bank to print banknotes. It was founded in 1657 by Johan Palmstruch in Stockholm, began printing banknotes in 1661, but ran into financial difficulties and was liquidated in 1667. Stockholms Banco was the immediate precursor to the central bank of Sweden, founded in 1668 as Riksens Ständers Bank and renamed in 1866 as Sveriges Riksbank

gancho: Fabricar uma moeda de 1 centavo nos EUA chegou a custar 3,69 centavos em 2024. Em novembro de 2025, a Casa da Moeda parou de produzi-las para circulação.
explicacao: O centavo americano, o "penny", é feito desde 1982 de zinco com uma camada de cobre e pesa 2,5 gramas. Desde 2006, fabricar cada moeda custa mais do que ela vale. Em 2024, o custo chegou a 3,69 centavos, quase quatro vezes o valor de face. É o que os economistas chamam de senhoriagem negativa: o governo perde dinheiro a cada moeda que emite. Ao mesmo tempo, a inflação tirou quase todo o poder de compra do centavo, e uma pesquisa encontrou 2% dos americanos que jogavam as moedas no lixo. Em novembro de 2025, sobretudo por causa do custo, a Casa da Moeda suspendeu a produção para circulação, mantendo só conjuntos para colecionadores. O centavo, porém, continua valendo e circulando.

fontes.trecho: The current copper-plated zinc cent issued since 1982 weighs 2.5 grams, while the previous 95% copper cent still found in circulation weighed 3.11 g. In the early 2010s, the price of metal used to make pennies rose to a noticeable cost to the mint which peaked at more than 2¢, a negative seigniorage, for the 1¢ face-value coin. [...] Due to inflation, a single penny has lost virtually all its purchasing power. [...] one survey found that 2 percent of Americans throw pennies in the trash. [...] In November 2025, the mint suspended the production of pennies for circulation while continuing to mint annual sets of pennies for collectors. The decision was largely due to cost, and would be codified into law by the Common Cents Act, passed by Congress in September 2026. The Common Cents Act permits, but does not require, businesses to round cash payments to the nearest five cents (nickel) if exact change is unavailable. The penny remains legal tender and in circulation. [...] Since 2006, the mint's costs for cents have exceeded the face value of the coin. [...] The cost to mint a cent in 2024 was 3.69 cents.

gancho: A tulipomania de 1637 é contada como a bolha que arruinou a Holanda. Nos contratos da época, uma historiadora achou menos de meia dúzia de pessoas em apuros, e nem nesses casos a culpa é clara.
explicacao: No auge, em fevereiro de 1637, certos bulbos chegaram a valer mais de dez vezes o que um artesão qualificado ganhava num ano. As flores mais disputadas tinham pétalas com chamas e listras, e hoje se sabe que esse desenho era obra de um vírus do mosaico que infectava os bulbos. A famosa Semper Augustus nem era uma variedade, e sim uma tulipa doente. A imagem de um país inteiro arruinado vem de um livro de 1841, do jornalista escocês Charles Mackay, segundo o qual até limpadores de chaminé e criadas especulavam com tulipas. As fontes dele, porém, bebiam de diálogos satíricos escritos para zombar dos especuladores, e os panfletos contra a febre tinham motivação sobretudo religiosa, não vinham de vítimas. Ao estudar os contratos arquivados, a historiadora Anne Goldgar viu que o negócio ficou quase só entre comerciantes e artesãos ricos, e que o impacto econômico foi muito limitado. Há uma razão simples: quase não houve troca de bulbos nem de dinheiro. Os holandeses chamavam aquilo de "comércio de vento", e no fim a maioria dos contratos simplesmente nunca foi cumprida.

fontes.trecho: At the peak of tulip mania in February 1637, certain tulip bulbs sold for more than 10 times the annual income of a skilled artisan. [...] It is now known that this effect is produced when the bulbs are infected with a type of tulip-specific mosaic virus known as the "tulip breaking virus" [...] The multicolour effects of intricate lines and flame-like streaks on the petals were vivid and spectacular, making the bulbs that produced these even more exotic-looking plants highly sought after. [...] Semper Augustus was actually not a tulip variety but rather a tulip affected by the tulip mosaic virus. [...] The Dutch described tulip contract trading as windhandel ('air trade'), because no bulbs were actually changing hands. [...] In the end, most contracts were simply never honoured. [...] The modern discussion of tulip mania began with the book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds, published in 1841 by the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay. [...] but all of them drew heavily from the satirical Dialogues that were written to mock the speculators. [...] Nobles, citizens, farmers, mechanics, seamen, footmen, maidservants, even chimney sweeps and old clotheswomen, dabbled in tulips. [...] Goldgar's study of archived contracts finds that even at its peak the trade in tulips was conducted almost exclusively by merchants and skilled craftsmen who were wealthy, but not members of the nobility. Any economic fallout from the bubble was very limited. Goldgar, who identifies many prominent buyers and sellers in the market, finds fewer than half a dozen who experienced financial troubles in the time period, and even of these cases it is not clear that tulips were to blame. [...] Although prices had risen, money had not changed hands between buyers and sellers. [...] These pamphlets were not written by victims of a bubble but were primarily religiously motivated.

gancho: O escocês John Law matou um homem em duelo, foi condenado à morte, fugiu e acabou no comando das finanças da França. A bolha que ele inflou, e que estourou em 1720, deu origem à palavra "milionário".
explicacao: Law era um jogador habilidoso, interessado nas regras da probabilidade. Em 1694, em Londres, matou Edward Wilson num duelo de espada e foi condenado à morte por homicídio. A pena virou multa, mas o irmão da vítima recorreu, Law voltou à prisão e conseguiu escapar para Amsterdã. Na França, ficou próximo do regente Filipe de Orléans, que em 1716 aprovou o banco dele, emissor de cédulas. Em 1717 veio a Companhia do Mississippi, criada para explorar a Louisiana, e em 1718 a fundação de Nova Orleans. As ações, que valiam 500 libras francesas, chegaram a 10 mil. A oferta de dinheiro dobrou, e a inflação mensal bateu 23% em janeiro de 1720, mês em que Law foi nomeado controlador-geral das finanças. Ele chegou a ser o homem mais rico da Europa. A bolha estourou no fim daquele ano, Law teve de deixar o país e morreu pobre em Veneza, em 1729. Em setembro de 1721, as ações tinham voltado aos 500 do começo. Do episódio ficou uma palavra: "millionaire", criada para quem enriqueceu com o esquema.

fontes.trecho: Born in Scotland, Law was an accomplished gambler with an interest in the rules of probability. After killing a man in a duel and being sentenced to death, he fled to mainland Europe. He read economics and made the acquaintance of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who became regent for the juvenile Louis XV in 1715. In 1716 Philippe approved Law's plan to create a private bank which would take gold deposits in return for bank notes [...] In 1717 Law founded another joint-stock company, the Mississippi company, whose purpose was the economic exploitation of Louisiana as well as other French colonies. Law became Controller General of Finances in 1720 and was the richest man in Europe. He had to leave France that same year, as a stock boom turned into a bust. He then lived in various European cities and died in Venice, impoverished. [...] On 9 April 1694, John Law fought a duel with another British dandy, Edward "Beau" Wilson, in Bloomsbury Square, London. [...] Law killed Wilson with a single pass and thrust of his sword. [...] was found guilty of murder and sentenced to death. [...] His sentence was later commuted to a fine, on the grounds that the killing only amounted to manslaughter. Wilson's brother appealed and had Law imprisoned, but he managed to escape to Amsterdam. [...] started an unprecedented colonization of its own in Louisiana with the foundation of New Orleans in 1718. [...] The Regent then appointed Law as Controller-General of Finances on 5 January 1720 [...] contracted pneumonia and died poor in 1729. [...] The term "millionaire" was coined for beneficiaries of Law's scheme.

which until then had stayed around their par level of 500 livres. [...] The market price of company shares eventually reached the peak of 10,000 livres. As the shareholders were selling their shares, the money supply in France suddenly doubled, and inflation burgeoned. Inflation reached a monthly rate of 23% in January 1720. [...] The "bubble" burst at the end of 1720. [...] By September 1721 share prices had dropped to 500 livres, where they had been at the beginning.

gancho: Em 1902, Hanói pagava a quem entregasse rabos de rato. Logo surgiram ratos vivos sem rabo: os caçadores cortavam o rabo e soltavam o bicho para ele procriar. Apareceram até criações de ratos.
explicacao: A colônia francesa tinha acabado de construir uma grande rede de esgotos, e os ratos se espalharam por ela, com relatos de bichos saindo até dos vasos sanitários das casas francesas. Era a época da terceira pandemia de peste, poucos anos depois de se descobrir que os roedores ajudavam a espalhar a doença. Primeiro, o governo contratou caçadores profissionais, pagos por rato morto. Como a população de ratos não diminuía, passou a oferecer 1 centavo por rato a qualquer morador, bastando entregar o rabo. No começo choveram rabos. Depois, as autoridades notaram ratos sem rabo correndo pela cidade, ouviram relatos de ratos trazidos de fora e acharam fazendas nos arredores criando os bichos só pelo rabo. O programa foi cancelado, e os ratos ficaram mais numerosos do que nunca. O caso, redescoberto nos arquivos coloniais pelo historiador Michael Vann, virou exemplo clássico de incentivo perverso, o "efeito cobra". Esse nome vem de uma história da Índia britânica, de gente criando cobras para ganhar recompensa, mas não há registro documental que a comprove. Vann sugere trocar o nome para "efeito rato", porque o de Hanói está nos documentos.

fontes.trecho: occurred in 1902, in Hanoi, Tonkin, French Indochina [...] To collect the bounty, people would need to provide the severed tail of a rat. Colonial officials, however, began noticing rats in Hanoi with no tails. The Vietnamese rat catchers would capture rats, sever their tails, then release them back into the sewers so that they could produce more rats. [...] Today, the events are often used as an example of a perverse incentive, commonly referred to as the cobra effect. The modern discoverer of this event, American historian Michael G. Vann argues that the cobra example from the British Raj cannot be proven, but that the rats in the Vietnam case can be proven, so the term should be changed to the Rat Effect. [...] Among the large projects, ordered by Paul Doumer, was the construction of a massive underground sewage system [...] with reports coming out that people had spotted rats climbing up the outflow pipes and later even out of the toilets in French houses. [...] the Government-General of French Indochina hired professional Vietnamese rat-catchers, these would descend into the sewers to hunt the rats down, and be paid for each rat that they had eliminated. [...] the French realised that the professional pest control services weren't making a dent in the rat population [...] To incentivise this, the French set a bounty of 1 cent per rat. To not be overrun with rat corpses, the civilians only had to submit a rat's tail to the municipal offices. [...] Initially, the new plan appeared to be working as devised as large numbers of tails were being brought in. [...] The French soon started noticing living and healthy rats running around without their tails. [...] Furthermore, there were also reports that some Vietnamese people were deliberately smuggling in rats from outside Hanoi into the city. The final straw for this plan was when French health inspectors discovered rat farming operations popping up in the countryside on the outskirts of Hanoi, that were breeding rats solely for their tails [...] they cancelled the bounty programme. [...] After the failed campaign ended, the rats, now more numerous than ever, continued frolicking underneath the city [...] The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre happened in the middle of a global plague pandemic only a few years after Swiss-French physician and bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin linked the spread of the pandemic to rodents.

According to the story, the British government, concerned about the number of venomous cobras in Delhi, offered a bounty for every dead cobra. [...] Eventually, however, people began to breed cobras for the income. [...] The investigation found no contemporary records of cobra breeding operations or prosecutions in British India

gancho: Num experimento na China, famílias pobres que ganharam desconto no arroz passaram a comprar menos arroz. É o raro "bem de Giffen", que contraria a lei da procura.
explicacao: Pela lei da procura, quando um produto encarece, as pessoas compram menos dele. O bem de Giffen é a exceção: um alimento básico e barato, consumido por quem é muito pobre. Se ele fica mais caro, a família deixa de ter dinheiro para os alimentos melhores e acaba comprando ainda mais do básico. Se ele fica mais barato, sobra dinheiro para variar a dieta, e o consumo do básico cai. O exemplo clássico, do economista Alfred Marshall, é o pão, mas a ideia já aparecia num livro de Simon Gray em 1815. Por muito tempo, as batatas da Grande Fome irlandesa foram citadas como exemplo, até que um artigo de 1984 mostrou que a evidência histórica não sustentava essa lenda. Provas concretas sempre foram escassas. Em 2007, os economistas Robert Jensen e Nolan Miller fizeram um experimento de campo nas províncias de Hunan e Gansu, oferecendo a famílias sorteadas o alimento básico local com subsídio. Em Hunan, onde a base é o arroz, as famílias que receberam o desconto passaram a comprar menos arroz. Em Gansu, onde a base é o trigo, a evidência foi fraca.

fontes.trecho: a Giffen good is a product that people consume more of as the price rises and vice versa, violating the law of demand. [...] The classic example given by Marshall is of inferior quality staple foods, whose demand is driven by poverty that prevents their purchasers from affording superior foodstuffs. As the price of the cheap staple rises, they can no longer afford to supplement their diet with better foods, and must consume more of the staple food. As Mr. Giffen has pointed out, a rise in the price of bread makes so large a drain on the resources of the poorer labouring families [...] Simon Gray described "Gray goods" in his 1815 text [...] Evidence for the existence of Giffen goods has generally been limited. [...] Another 2008 paper by the same authors experimentally demonstrated the existence of Giffen goods among people at the household level by directly subsidizing purchases of rice and wheat flour for extremely poor families. In this paper, a 2007 field experiment was conducted in the provinces of Hunan and Gansu, where the staples were rice and wheat respectively. In both provinces, randomly selected households were offered their dietary staples at subsidized rates. After the completion of the project, it could be found that the demands from Hunan households who were offered the rice fell drastically. Meanwhile, the demands of wheat in Gansu implies weak evidence of the Giffen paradox. [...] Potatoes during the Irish Great Famine were once considered an example of a Giffen good. [...] However, Gerald P. Dwyer and Cotton M. Lindsey challenged this idea in their 1984 article Robert Giffen and the Irish Potato, where they showed the contradicting nature of the Giffen "legend" with respect to historical evidence. [...] Jensen, Robert; Miller, Nolan (2008).

gancho: Na virada do Império para a República, o Brasil viveu uma bolha em que as empresas listadas saltaram de pouco mais de 90 para cerca de 450 entre 1888 e 1891. O nome, "encilhamento", veio do turfe.
explicacao: A febre começou com uma lei bancária de 1888, ainda no Império, e explodiu quando Rui Barbosa, ministro da Fazenda do novo governo republicano, adotou crédito livre para a indústria, sustentado por emissão farta de papel-moeda. O decreto de 17 de janeiro de 1890 abriu as comportas. Vieram especulação em todos os mercados, inflação forte e ações sem lastro: pela nova lei, até uma empresa sem capital podia lançar ações. Em 1888 havia pouco mais de 90 empresas listadas no país, e em 1891 já eram cerca de 450. O apelido vem das corridas de cavalos, onde encilhar é arrear o animal para a largada, e se apoia no ditado "cavalo encilhado não passa duas vezes": a oportunidade de enriquecer não podia ser perdida. A palavra apareceu primeiro no Jornal do Commercio, em 1890, que a considerava pejorativa, e depois outros jornais a adotaram. A bolha estourou de forma lenta até 1892, deixando falências em série e uma das piores inflações da história do país. O Visconde de Taunay transformou o período no romance "O Encilhamento".

fontes.trecho: A crise do encilhamento foi uma crise econômica que ocorreu no Brasil, entre o final da Monarquia e início da República. [...] Seu início é considerado quando, o então Ministro da Fazenda Ruy Barbosa, sob a justificativa de estimular a industrialização no país, adotou uma política baseada em créditos livres aos investimentos industriais garantidos pelo aumento da emissão de papel-moeda. O novo plano econômico, transformado em lei pelo decreto de 17 de janeiro de 1890 [...] vieram desenfreada especulação financeira em todos os mercados e forte alta inflacionária [...] Em 1888, havia pouco mais de 90 empresas listadas no país. Em 1891, esse número já tinha saltado para cerca de 450 empresas. [...] O termo "encilhamento" foi inspirado no procedimento adotado no hipismo de arrear (equipar com arreios) o cavalo, preparando-o para a corrida. [...] Esta analogia é reforçada no ditado popular "cavalo encilhado não passa duas vezes". O uso da palavra encilhamento como apelido da situação econômica na praça do Rio de Janeiro à época, foi feito pela primeira vez em Retrospecto Commercial, no Jornal do Commercio, em 1890. Nesse jornal, o termo por ser considerado pejorativo, só era usado em matéria paga, mas outros periódicos passaram a repeti-lo [...] Este período conturbado da história do Rio de Janeiro e do Brasil é retratado em forma de romance pelo Visconde de Taunay no livro “O Encilhamento”.

The first step that led to the Encilhamento took place during the final years of the Empire of Brazil under the command of Viscount of Ouro Preto, the last finance minister of the imperial era, when a new Banking Act was enacted in November 1888. [...] For example, a company without any capital could launch an IPO [...] the process led to one of the worst inflation outbreaks in the country's history [...] and although the burst has been initiated then, it occurred in a slow way, until 1892. [...] widespread bankruptcy

gancho: Na crise bancária de 1907, J. P. Morgan reuniu cerca de 120 banqueiros na sua biblioteca, trancou a porta e pôs a chave no bolso. Só os deixou ir para casa depois que assinaram um resgate.
explicacao: Em outubro de 1907, uma tentativa fracassada de dominar as ações de uma companhia de cobre provocou corridas aos bancos que tinham emprestado para a manobra, e o pânico se espalhou por Nova York e pelo país. Os Estados Unidos não tinham banco central desde 1836, e Morgan, o banqueiro mais rico e mais bem relacionado da cidade, virou o socorro informal. Num dos episódios, avisou que até 50 corretoras quebrariam se 25 milhões de dólares não aparecessem em dez minutos, e às 14h16 já havia 14 presidentes de bancos prometendo 23,6 milhões. Mais tarde, duas companhias fiduciárias ainda corriam risco. Às 3 da manhã, cerca de 120 executivos ouviam o relatório na biblioteca de Morgan quando perceberam que estavam trancados lá dentro, uma tática de força que ele já tinha usado antes. Morgan exigiu que as fiduciárias juntassem 25 milhões para salvar as mais fracas. Por volta das 4h45, o líder delas assinou, os outros o seguiram, e só então os banqueiros puderam sair. A crise aumentou a preocupação com o poder de Morgan e reacendeu o debate sobre reformas, que acabou na criação do Federal Reserve, em 1913.

fontes.trecho: The panic was triggered by the failed attempt in October 1907 to corner the market on stock of the United Copper Company. When the bid failed, banks that had lent money to the cornering scheme suffered runs that later spread to affiliated banks and trusts [...] The panic then extended across the nation as vast numbers of people withdrew deposits from their regional banks [...] When United States President Andrew Jackson allowed the charter of the Second Bank of the United States to expire in 1836, the U.S. was without any sort of central bank [...] Morgan was not only the city's wealthiest and most well-connected banker [...] Morgan informed them that as many as 50 stock exchange houses would fail unless $25 million was raised in 10 minutes. By 2:16 p.m., 14 bank presidents had pledged $23.6 million to keep the stock exchange afloat. [...] There was deep concern that the Trust Company of America and the Lincoln Trust might fail to open on Monday due to continuing runs by depositors. [...] At 3 a.m. about 120 bank and trust company officials assembled to hear a full report on the status of the failing trust companies. [...] As discussion ensued, the bankers realized that Morgan had locked them in the library and pocketed the key to force a solution, the sort of strong-arm tactic he had been known to use in the past. Morgan then entered the talks and advised the trust companies that they must provide a loan of $25 million to save the weaker institutions. [...] at about 4:45 a.m. he persuaded the unofficial leader of the trust companies to sign the agreement, and the remainder of the bankers followed. Having received these commitments, Morgan allowed the bankers to go home. [...] The frequency of crises and the severity of the 1907 panic added to concern about the outsized role of J.P. Morgan and renewed impetus toward a national debate on reform. [...] it was not until December 23, 1913, that Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act.

gancho: No início da Guerra dos Trinta Anos, estados alemães cunhavam imitações baratas das moedas de outros territórios e iam gastá-las o mais longe possível de casa. A crise levou o nome das balanças do golpe.
explicacao: A guerra fez os gastos militares dispararem. Para arrecadar, cidades e principados do Sacro Império passaram a piorar o dinheiro, com o auge entre 1620 e 1623. O método começava na balança: as moedas boas, mais pesadas, eram separadas, derretidas, misturadas com chumbo, cobre ou estanho e cunhadas de novo, enquanto as leves voltavam a circular. Daí o nome alemão "Kipper und Wipper", tirado do vocabulário das balanças de pesar moedas, que pendiam diante da moeda boa. Muitas vezes, o truque era não estragar a própria moeda, e sim fabricar cópias de pouco valor das moedas de outros territórios e gastá-las bem longe, para que o prejuízo caísse sobre a economia alheia. Os vizinhos responderam fazendo o mesmo, e a inflação se espalhou de estado em estado. O público acabou percebendo: vieram panfletos, revoltas e soldados que só lutavam se recebessem em moeda boa, e os governos passaram a receber de volta, nos impostos, o próprio dinheiro ruim. Houve punições como banimento e confisco de bens para quem importasse moeda ruim ou exportasse a boa. Por volta de 1623 a prática parou, e as moedas ruins foram declaradas ilegais e recolhidas.

fontes.trecho: was a financial crisis at the start of the Thirty Years' War. While debasement of coinage was observed earlier, with the onset of the war, military expenditures rose drastically and the city-states in the Holy Roman Empire began to heavily debase currency in order to raise revenue. The most severe debasing occurred around 1620–1623. After that time the authorities attempted to curb inflation and debased coins were declared illegal and withdrawn from circulation. [...] The name refers to the use of  balance scales (Wippen) which quickly tilted (kippen) on good coins. [...] The not-yet-debased coins were then taken out of circulation, melted, mixed with baser metals such as lead, copper or tin, and re-issued. Often the states did not debase their own currency, but instead manufactured low-value imitations of coins from other territories and then spent them in yet other territories as far as possible from their own lands, hoping that the resulting damage would then occur to the economy of those other regions rather than their own. Weighing and sorting formed the core of the operation: heavier coins were set aside for melting, while lighter or debased money went back into circulation. [...] This worked for a while; but after a time, the general public caught on to the manipulation, resulting in pamphlets denouncing the practice, local riots and the refusal of soldiers and mercenaries to fight unless paid in real, non-debased money. Also, the states began to get back their own debased coins in taxes and customs fees. [...] Due to these problems the practice largely stopped around 1623 [...] However, the neighboring states also debased their coins to prevent a loss of money. This resulted in hyperinflation, the rapid increase of prices in a short period of time, which eventually became a crisis throughout many states in Europe as debased coins spread rapidly from state to state. [...] In Europe, the import of bad coins and the export of good coins were punished by measures such as banishment, burning, or the confiscation of goods.

gancho: Em 1949, um estudante neozelandês montou numa garagem um computador que simulava a economia britânica com água colorida correndo por tanques e canos. Calibrado, chegava a 2% de precisão.
explicacao: O inventor foi Bill Phillips, então aluno da London School of Economics, com a ajuda do economista Walter Newlyn. O protótipo saiu da garagem da senhoria de Phillips em Croydon, ao custo de 400 libras, e usou até sobras de bombardeiros Lancaster da guerra. A máquina, chamada MONIAC, tem cerca de 2 metros de altura e é feita de tanques e tubos de plástico transparente presos a uma placa de madeira. A água faz o papel do dinheiro. No alto fica o tanque do Tesouro, de onde torneiras liberam água para os tanques de gastos, como saúde e educação. Bombas devolvem parte dela ao topo, como impostos, e a velocidade das bombas representa as alíquotas. A poupança drena água do fluxo, e importações e exportações tiram ou põem água no circuito. Boias, contrapesos e eletrodos controlam tudo sozinhos. Feita para dar aula, numa época em que os poucos computadores digitais estavam restritos a governos e militares, ela se mostrou também um simulador eficaz. Foram construídas pelo menos doze, e várias ainda funcionavam em 2023.

fontes.trecho: is an analogue computer which uses fluidic logic to model the workings of an economy. [...] It was created in 1949 by the New Zealand economist Bill Phillips to model the national economic processes of the United Kingdom, while Phillips was a student at the London School of Economics (LSE). Phillips built the prototype with Walter Newlyn [...] While designed as a teaching tool, it was discovered to be quite accurate, and thus an effective economic simulator. At least twelve machines were built, donated to or purchased by various organisations around the world. As of 2023, several are in working order. [...] including bits and pieces of war surplus parts from old Lancaster bombers. The first MONIAC was created in his landlady's garage in Croydon at a cost of £400 [...] In 1949, the few computers in existence were restricted to government and military use [...] The machine is approximately 2 m (6 ft 7 in) high [...] consisted of a series of transparent plastic tanks and pipes which were fastened to a wooden board. [...] the flow of money around the economy was illustrated by coloured water. At the top of the board was a large tank called the treasury. [...] For example, there were tanks for health and education. [...] Water could be pumped back to the treasury from some of the tanks to represent taxation. Changes in tax rates were modeled by increasing or decreasing pumping speeds. [...] The machine showed it by draining water (savings) from the expenditure stream [...] Import and export were represented by water draining from the model and by additional water being poured into the model. The flow of the water was automatically controlled through a series of floats, counterweights, electrodes, and cords. [...] To their surprise, Phillips and his associate Walter Newlyn found that the machine could be calibrated to an accuracy of 2%.

gancho: Na Grande Depressão, a cidadezinha austríaca de Wörgl lançou um dinheiro feito para perder valor se ficasse parado. O emprego cresceu, outras cidades quiseram copiar, e o banco central mandou parar.
explicacao: A ideia vinha do economista Silvio Gesell, que defendia um dinheiro com "demurrage": uma taxa que corrói aos poucos o valor de quem o guarda. Num formato típico, era preciso comprar todo mês um selo de cerca de 1% do valor da cédula e registrá-lo nela, senão ela perdia todo o valor. O objetivo era fazer o dinheiro circular em vez de ser entesourado. Em 31 de julho de 1932, o prefeito Michael Unterguggenberger pôs a ideia em prática em Wörgl, e a taxa era recolhida em benefício dos desempregados. Enquanto o resto da Áustria sofria com o desemprego alto, a cidade ganhou casas novas, um reservatório, uma rampa de salto de esqui e uma ponte. Pelo menos 200 cidades austríacas fizeram planos para imitar o sistema, e o caso atraiu o primeiro-ministro francês Édouard Daladier e o economista Irving Fisher. O banco central da Áustria encerrou o experimento para manter o monopólio do governo sobre a moeda. Keynes escreveu que a ideia do dinheiro carimbado era sólida, embora a criticasse, e até hoje se discute se o efeito teria durado.

fontes.trecho: Wörgl was the site of the "Miracle of Wörgl", beginning on 31 July 1932 during the Great Depression. Beginning with the issuing of "Certified Compensation Bills", a form of local currency commonly known as Stamp Scrip or Freigeld. This was an application of the monetary theories of the economist Silvio Gesell by the town's then-mayor, Michael Unterguggenberger. The experiment resulted in a growth of employment and meant that local projects such as new houses, a reservoir, a ski jump and a bridge could all be completed, contrasting with high unemployment in the rest of Austria (although the extent of its long-term sustainability and effectiveness has been under question). Despite attracting great interest at the time, including from French Premier Edouard Daladier and economist Irving Fisher, the "experiment" was ended by Austria's central bank Oesterreichische Nationalbank on 1 September 1933, so that the federal government would maintain a monopoly on the country's legal tender.

The German-Argentine economist Silvio Gesell advocated for demurrage currency [...] Demurrage currency, also known as depreciating money or stamp scrip in its paper money form, is a type of money that is designed to gradually lose purchasing power at a constant rate. [...] He referred to demurrage as Freigeld ("free money")—"free" because it would be freed from hoarding and interest. [...] One type of stamp scrip worked this way. [...] Every month a stamp costing a certain amount (in a typical case, 1% of the face value) had to be purchased and recorded in a box, otherwise the scrip lost all its value. [...] British economist John Maynard Keynes wrote "the idea behind stamped money is sound", but he also contended [...] Demurrage-charged local currency was tested in the Austrian town of Wörgl between 1932 and 1934, as a tax collected for the benefit of the unemployed. Due to the local currency's success in reducing unemployment and increasing economic activity, at least 200 cities across Austria formed plans to mimic the currency system in Wörgl.

gancho: Em 1979, dois irmãos texanos acumularam uma montanha de prata, boa parte em contratos alavancados, enquanto a onça saltava de menos de US$ 10 para mais de US$ 50. Em 27 de março de 1980, ela fechou a US$ 10,80.
explicacao: Nelson Bunker Hunt e William Herbert Hunt, filhos do petroleiro H. L. Hunt, compravam prata desde o começo dos anos 1970. Em 1979 aceleraram, e no fim do ano eles e uma empresa ligada à família controlavam cerca de 195 milhões de onças troy. A prata, que valia menos de 10 dólares a onça antes de agosto de 1979, passou de 50 dólares em janeiro de 1980. A joalheria Tiffany publicou um anúncio no New York Times com o título "Inescrupuloso", criticando o entesouramento. O ponto fraco era a alavancagem: cerca de metade da posição estava em contratos futuros, que exigem só um depósito de margem e podem gerar cobranças enormes se o preço cair. As bolsas reagiram com limites de posição e, depois, permitindo apenas ordens de liquidação. O preço virou. Em 25 e 26 de março, Herbert avisou aos credores que a família não tinha mais dinheiro nem garantias para cobrir as margens. No dia 27, a corretora Bache liquidou as posições dos Hunt, e a SEC suspendeu a negociação das ações da própria Bache: o saldo devedor sem garantia das contas dos Hunt na corretora, de cerca de 122 milhões de dólares, teria reduzido muito o patrimônio da Bache.

fontes.trecho: By the end of 1979, Bunker Hunt, Herbert Hunt and the Hunt-related International Metals Investment Company controlled approximately 195 million troy ounces of silver. Silver, which had traded below $10 per troy ounce before August 1979, rose to $34.45 by December 31 and to more than $50 in January 1980. [...] On March 27, 1980, silver closed at $10.80 per ounce, Hunt-related positions were liquidated, and major brokers and lenders faced potential losses. [...] Nelson Bunker Hunt and William Herbert Hunt, sons of oilman H. L. Hunt, began acquiring silver in the early 1970s. [...] The Hunts expanded their position substantially in 1979. [...] About half of the Hunt-related position at the end of 1979 was held in silver futures rather than physical silver. Because futures contracts required only a margin deposit rather than full payment for the metal, a rapid fall in prices could produce very large margin calls. [...] On March 26, 1980, Tiffany & Co. ran an advertisement in The New York Times headed "Unconscionable", criticizing the hoarding [...] On January 7, 1980, COMEX imposed position limits on silver futures. On January 21, it limited trading in silver futures to liquidation orders and bona fide hedging transactions [...] The restrictions coincided with a reversal in prices. [...] On March 25 and 26, 1980, Herbert Hunt told major creditors and brokers that the Hunts no longer had sufficient cash or collateral to meet margin calls. [...] When silver fell sharply on March 27, Bache liquidated Hunt-related silver futures positions. At March 27 prices, the unsecured debit balance in Hunt accounts at Bache was about $122 million, an amount that would have severely reduced Bache's net worth. The SEC suspended trading in Bache common stock on March 27

gancho: Charles Ponzi dizia lucrar com cupons postais internacionais. Para cobrir o dinheiro que ele captou em 1920, seriam precisos 160 milhões de cupons em circulação. Havia cerca de 27 mil.
explicacao: O cupom-resposta internacional servia para pagar o selo da resposta de uma carta enviada a outro país. Era vendido pelo preço da postagem no país de compra e trocado por selos no país de destino. Com a inflação do pós-guerra, a postagem na Itália ficou baratíssima em dólares, então em tese dava para comprar cupons lá e trocá-los por selos americanos mais valiosos, uma arbitragem legal. Ponzi prometia 50% de lucro em 45 dias, numa época em que os bancos pagavam 5% ao ano. Na prática, pagava os primeiros investidores com o dinheiro dos seguintes, sem tentar lucrar de verdade. Em julho de 1920, entrava quase um milhão de dólares por dia, e perto de 75% da polícia de Boston tinha aplicado no esquema. Quando um jornalista financeiro disse que aqueles retornos eram impossíveis, Ponzi o processou e ganhou. A conta dos cupons foi feita por Clarence Barron, chefe da Dow Jones. O golpe durou mais de um ano e custou 20 milhões de dólares aos investidores. Ponzi não inventou a fraude, mas o nome dela ficou com ele.

fontes.trecho: He promised clients a 50% profit within 45 days or 100% profit within 90 days, by buying discounted postal reply coupons in other countries and redeeming them at face value in the U.S. as a form of arbitrage. In reality, Ponzi was paying earlier investors using the investments of later investors. While this type of fraudulent investment scheme was not invented by Ponzi, it became so identified with him that it now is referred to as a "Ponzi scheme". His scheme ran for over a year before it collapsed, costing his "investors" $20 million [...] Postal reply coupons allowed a person in one country to pay for the postage of a reply to a correspondent in another country. IRCs were priced at the cost of postage in the country of purchase, but could be exchanged for stamps to cover the cost of postage in the country where redeemed [...] Inflation after World War I had greatly decreased the cost of postage in Italy expressed in U.S. dollars, so that an IRC could be bought cheaply in Italy and exchanged for U.S. stamps of higher value, which could then be sold. [...] This was a form of arbitrage, or profiting by buying an asset at a lower price in one market and immediately selling it in a market where the price is higher, which is legal. [...] in an environment when banks were paying only 5% annual interest. [...] In January 1920, Ponzi started his own company, the "Securities Exchange Company", to promote the scheme. [...] By July, he was approaching a million dollars per day. [...] as he made no effort to generate legitimate profits. [...] In its heyday, nearly 75% of Boston's police force had invested in the scheme. [...] When a Boston financial writer suggested there was no way Ponzi could legally deliver such high returns in a short period of time, Ponzi sued for libel and won [...] The paper contacted Clarence W. Barron, the financial journalist who headed Dow Jones & Company, to examine Ponzi's scheme. [...] Barron then noted that to cover the investments made with the Securities Exchange Company, 160 million postal reply coupons would have to be in circulation. However, only about 27,000 actually were.

gancho: Entre as duas guerras mundiais, o sueco Ivar Kreuger emprestava dinheiro a governos em troca do monopólio dos fósforos no país. O "Rei dos Fósforos" chegou a controlar de dois terços a três quartos da produção mundial.
explicacao: Kreuger era engenheiro civil, filho de um industrial do ramo de fósforos, e montou um império que ia de bancos e imóveis a uma mina de ouro e fábricas de celulose. O negócio central se apoiava num detalhe econômico: fósforo era indispensável para fumar e acender fogões, então a procura quase não caía mesmo com preço alto, e um monopolista podia lucrar muito. Entre 1925 e 1930, com a Europa se reconstruindo da Primeira Guerra, as empresas dele emprestaram a vários governos, e como garantia recebiam o monopólio dos fósforos. Ao assinar o primeiro empréstimo a um país, a Polônia, ele não sabia de onde sairia o dinheiro. À Alemanha emprestou 125 milhões de dólares. Em 1930, os empréstimos a estados somavam cerca de 387 milhões de dólares. Para pagar dividendos altos, porém, ele precisava de dinheiro novo e inflava lucros que não existiam. O império desabou na Grande Depressão, e em março de 1932 Kreuger foi encontrado morto em Paris; a polícia concluiu que foi suicídio. A auditoria da Price Waterhouse disse que as fraudes nos livros eram tão infantis que qualquer noção de contabilidade as revelaria.

fontes.trecho: was a Swedish civil engineer, financier, entrepreneur and industrialist. [...] Between the two world wars, he negotiated match monopolies with European, Central American and South American governments, and finally controlled between two thirds and three quarters of worldwide match production, becoming known as the "Match King". [...] He owned banks, real estate, a gold mine, and pulp industrial companies. [...] Kreuger's financial empire collapsed during the Great Depression. The Price Waterhouse autopsy of his financial empire stated: "The manipulations were so childish that anyone with but a rudimentary knowledge of bookkeeping could see the books were falsified." In March 1932, he was found dead in the bedroom of his flat in Paris. The police concluded that he had committed suicide [...] Kreuger was born in Kalmar, the eldest son of Ernst August Kreuger, an industrialist in the match industry in that city [...] matches were a necessity for smoking and the lighting of stoves and gas appliances among other uses, and therefore demand for them was highly inelastic, meaning that a monopolist could raise prices (and hence profits) significantly without much affecting the quantity sold. [...] From 1925 to 1930, years when many countries in Europe were suffering after the First World War, Kreuger's companies gave loans to governments to speed up reconstruction. As a security, the governments would grant him the match monopoly in their country. [...] which reported profits when there were none and paid out ever increasing dividends by attracting new investment [...] His first sovereign loan went to Poland, and when Kreuger signed the agreement he had no idea where the funds would come from. He made a deal with Germany for a $125 million-dollar loan [...] The total loans by Kreuger to foreign states have been estimated to US$387m in 1930

gancho: A bolha das ferrovias britânicas dos anos 1840 arruinou famílias, mas deixou trilhos de verdade: os projetos de 1844 a 1846 renderam cerca de 10 mil km, extensão equivalente a mais da metade da malha atual.
explicacao: Depois do sucesso da linha Liverpool–Manchester, inaugurada em 1830, e com juros em queda, investir em ferrovias virou febre. O governo quase não regulava: qualquer um podia abrir uma companhia, captar dinheiro e pedir ao Parlamento a aprovação do traçado, sem nenhuma checagem de viabilidade, e muitos deputados eram grandes investidores. Ações podiam ser compradas com um depósito de 10%. No auge, em 1846, o Parlamento aprovou 263 leis criando companhias, com rotas que somavam 15.300 km. Quando o Banco da Inglaterra subiu os juros no fim de 1845, o dinheiro fugiu, os preços caíram e o investimento parou quase da noite para o dia. Muitas famílias de classe média tinham posto ali todas as economias e perderam tudo. Cerca de um terço das linhas autorizadas nunca saiu do papel, e algumas companhias eram fraudes. Ainda assim, a bolha teve um saldo concreto: foram construídos 10.010 km de linhas a partir dos projetos de 1844 a 1846. Para comparar, a rede ferroviária britânica inteira de hoje tem perto de 18 mil km. Muitas linhas que quebraram se tornaram viáveis nas mãos de companhias maiores.

fontes.trecho: Railway Mania was a stock market bubble in the railway industry of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in the 1840s. [...] The mania reached its zenith in 1846, when 263 Acts of Parliament for setting up new railway companies were passed, with the proposed routes totalling 9,500 miles (15,300 km). About a third of the railways authorised were never built—the companies either collapsed because of poor financial planning, were bought out by larger competitors before they could build their line, or turned out to be fraudulent enterprises [...] the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (the L&M), opened in 1830 and proved to be successful [...] The Bank of England cut interest rates, making government bonds less attractive investments [...] Shares were promoted and could be purchased for a 10% deposit. [...] but there were no limits on the number of companies and no real checks on the financial viability of a line. Anyone could form a company, gain investment and submit a bill to Parliament. Many Members of Parliament were heavy investors in such schemes. [...] Coupled to this, in late 1845 the Bank of England increased interest rates. As banks began to re-invest in bonds, the money began to flow out of railways, undercutting the boom. [...] As they began to fall, investment stopped virtually overnight [...] Many middle-class families on modest incomes had sunk their entire savings into new companies during the mania, and they lost everything when the speculation collapsed. [...] Even many of the routes that failed when the mania collapsed became viable (if not lucrative) when each was in the hands of the larger company that had purchased it. A total of 6,220 miles (10,010 km) of railway line were built as a result of projects authorised between 1844 and 1846—by comparison, the total route mileage of the modern UK railway network is around 11,000 miles (18,000 km).

gancho: A Coca-Cola custou 5 centavos de dólar de 1886 a 1959. Parte da culpa era das máquinas automáticas, na maioria feitas só para essa moeda, e o chefe da empresa pediu ao presidente dos EUA uma moeda de 7,5 centavos.
explicacao: Os economistas Daniel Levy e Andrew Young documentaram que a garrafa de 6,5 onças custou 5 centavos por mais de 70 anos, atravessando duas guerras mundiais e a Grande Depressão. Eles apontam três motivos. Até 1921, um contrato que fixava o preço do xarope vendido aos engarrafadores favorecia manter o preço final. Por volta de 1950, havia cerca de 400 mil máquinas automáticas de Coca-Cola, e provavelmente a grande maioria das já instaladas só aceitava a moeda de 5 centavos. E pagar com uma moeda só era cômodo para o cliente: o menor aumento que mantinha isso era dobrar o preço para 10 centavos, e qualquer valor intermediário exigiria várias moedas. Robert Woodruff, presidente da empresa a partir de 1923 e figura decisiva na manutenção do preço, levou o assunto tão a sério que em 1953 pediu ao amigo e companheiro de caçadas Dwight Eisenhower, recém-eleito, que o Tesouro cunhasse uma moeda de 7,5 centavos. O Tesouro não gostou da ideia. Antes disso, em 1951, a equipe de preços da empresa já tinha bolado o "Plano da Moeda Única": a máquina entregaria uma garrafa vazia, ou nenhuma, a cada nove moedas depositadas, cobrando na prática 5,625 centavos por Coca, sempre com moedas de 5. A última Coca de 5 centavos sumiu em 1959.

fontes.titulo: "The Real Thing": Nominal Price Rigidity of the Nickel Coke, 1886-1959 (Levy e Young, Journal of Money, Credit and Banking, 2004)
fontes.trecho: We report that the price of a 6.5-oz Coca-Cola was 5¢ from 1886 until 1959. Thus, we are documenting a nominal price rigidity that lasted more than 70 years! [...] two World Wars, the Great Depression, and numerous regulatory interventions and lawsuits [...] a contract between the Company and its parent bottlers that encouraged retail price maintenance [...] 1923: Robert Woodruff becomes the President of Coca-Cola; plays a decisive role in maintaining the nickel price policy. [...] 1953: Woodruff asks the Treasury Department to issue a 7.5¢ coin. [...] 1959: The last of the nickel Cokes is gone. [...] an installed base of vending machines with nickel-only capability [...] at the 5¢ price per serving, the smallest price increase compatible with the consumer still using a single coin was a 100% jump to 10¢. [...] by 1950 there were about 400,000 Coca-Cola vending machines [...] However, a less than 100% increase in the price would require the public to use anywhere between two and [...] Woodruff submitted a request in 1953 to the newly elected President Dwight Eisenhower (his hunting companion and friend) to get the U.S. Department of Treasury to mint a new 7.5¢ coin. [...] who did not like the idea. [...] the development of an ingenious plan called the “Single Coin Plan,” by the Coca-Cola Company’s pricing team. [...] Under the plan, the vending machines’ customers would pay a higher price (for example, 5.625¢, or 6¢, or 7¢, etc), but still use only nickels. [...] coin cooler [delivers] either an empty bottle or no bottle at all for one nickel in every nine deposited. [...] The contract guarantees the right to buy syrup from the Coca-Cola Company at the nominal price of $0.92 per gallon in perpetuity. [...] We argue that the model can help explain the Coca-Cola price rigidity, but only until 1921, the year a new contract was signed with bottlers [...] It is likely, therefore, that a considerable majority of the 400,000 machines were nickel-only machines in 1950. [...] 1951: The “Single Coin Plan” is developed.

gancho: Uma lei americana de 1856, ainda em vigor, deixa cidadãos dos EUA tomarem posse, em nome do país, de ilhas sem dono que tenham guano, o excremento acumulado de aves marinhas. O último pedido foi em 1997.
explicacao: Rico em nitrogênio, fosfato e potássio, o guano era um adubo muito eficaz, e na década de 1840 virou mercadoria cobiçada, usada também para fazer pólvora. Os povos andinos já o recolhiam nas ilhas da costa do Peru para adubar a terra, e documentos coloniais espanhóis dizem que os incas puniam com a morte quem perturbasse as aves. A "mania do guano" dos anos 1850 trouxe preços altos num mercado dominado por poucos e o medo de que o produto acabasse. A resposta americana foi a Lei das Ilhas de Guano: qualquer cidadão podia reivindicar para os EUA uma ilha com guano em qualquer lugar do mundo, desde que não fosse ocupada por cidadãos de outro país nem estivesse sob outro governo. A lei ainda autoriza o presidente a usar os militares para proteger essas posses. Empreendedores saíram à caça de ilhotas e recifes no Caribe e no Pacífico. A lei continua valendo, e o último pedido, de 1997, foi para a ilha de Navassa. Foi negado porque um tribunal decidiu que a ilha já estava sob jurisdição americana, algo que o Haiti contesta.

fontes.trecho: is a United States federal law passed by the Congress that enables citizens of the United States to take possession of unclaimed islands containing guano deposits in the name of the United States. The islands can be located anywhere, so long as they are not occupied by citizens of another country and not within the jurisdiction of another government. It also empowers the president  to use the military to protect such interests [...] In the 1840s, guano became a prized agricultural fertilizer and source of saltpeter for gunpowder. [...] The "guano mania" of the 1850s led to high prices in an oligopolistic market, government attempts to control prices, fear of resource exhaustion, and eventually the enactment of the Guano Islands Act of 1856 in August 1856. [...] This encouraged American entrepreneurs to search for and exploit new deposits on tiny islands and reefs in the Caribbean and Pacific. [...] The Act continues to be part of the law of the United States. The most recent Guano Islands Act claim was made in 1997 to Navassa Island. However, the claim was denied because an American court ruled the island was already under American jurisdiction (a claim Haiti disputes).

is the accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats. Guano is a highly effective fertiliser due to the high content of nitrogen, phosphate, and potassium, all key nutrients essential for plant growth. [...] Archaeological evidence suggests that Andean people collected seabird guano from small islands and points off the desert coast of Peru for use as a soil amendment [...] Spanish colonial documents suggest that the rulers of the Inca Empire greatly valued guano, restricted access to it, and punished any disturbance of the birds with death.

gancho: Em ilhas da Papua-Nova Guiné, colares de concha circulam de ilha em ilha no sentido horário e braceletes no anti-horário. Não servem para nada prático, e o prestígio vem de passá-los adiante.
explicacao: O sistema se chama kula e liga 18 comunidades do arquipélago Massim, entre elas as ilhas Trobriand, com milhares de participantes. Há dois tipos de objeto: colares vermelhos de discos de concha, que seguem rumo ao norte, girando no sentido horário, e braceletes brancos de concha, que vão para o sul, no sentido contrário. Quem abre uma troca com um bracelete recebe de volta um colar, e vice-versa. As pessoas chegam a viajar centenas de milhas de canoa para isso. Os objetos não têm uso: não ficam muito tempo nas mãos de ninguém e precisam ser repassados a outro parceiro dentro de certo prazo. Ainda assim, até a posse temporária dá status, e as parcerias, idealmente para a vida toda, trazem deveres de hospitalidade e proteção. Num livro de 1922, o antropólogo Bronisław Malinowski tornou o kula famoso com uma pergunta: por que homens arriscariam a vida no mar para dar o que parecem bugigangas sem valor? A resposta ligava as trocas à autoridade política. Em 1925, Marcel Mauss retomou o caso no "Ensaio sobre a dádiva", e o kula virou peça central do debate sobre as economias baseadas em presentes. Nas mesmas viagens, porém, também se faz escambo comum, com regateio duro.

fontes.trecho: Kula, also known as the Kula exchange or Kula ring, is a ceremonial exchange system conducted in the Milne Bay Province of Papua New Guinea. [...] His seminal work on the topic, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), directly confronted the question, "Why would men risk life and limb to travel across huge expanses of dangerous ocean to give away what appear to be worthless trinkets?" Malinowski carefully traced the network of exchanges of bracelets and necklaces across the Trobriand Islands and established that they were part of a system of exchange (the Kula ring) and that the exchange system was clearly linked to political authority. Malinowski's study became the subject of debate with the French anthropologist Marcel Mauss, the author of The Gift ("Essai sur le don," 1925). Since then, the Kula ring has been central to the continuing anthropological debate on the nature of gift-giving and the existence of gift economies. [...] The Kula ring spans 18 island communities of the Massim archipelago, including the Trobriand Islands, and involves thousands of individuals. Participants travel at times hundreds of miles by canoe to exchange Kula valuables, which consist of red shell-disc necklaces (veigun or soulava) that are traded to the north (circling the ring in clockwise direction) and white shell armbands (mwali) that are traded in the southern direction (circling counterclockwise). If the opening gift was an armband, the closing gift must be a necklace and vice versa. The exchange of Kula valuables is also accompanied by the trade in other items known as gimwali (barter). [...] All Kula valuables are non-use items traded purely for purposes of enhancing one's social status and prestige. [...] relationships between the exchange parties (karayta'u, "partners"). [...] Such a partnership involves strong mutual obligations such as hospitality, protection and assistance. [...] Kula valuables never remain for long in the hands of the recipients; rather, they must be passed on to other partners within a certain amount of time and thus constantly circle around the ring. However, even temporary possession brings prestige and status. [...] the latter, in contrast, often done as part of Kula exchange journeys, involves hard bargaining and serves purely economic purposes.

gancho: Do fim do século XIX até 1951, o Canadá proibiu por lei uma festa indígena: o potlatch, em que um anfitrião ganha prestígio dando, e às vezes destruindo, riquezas. A pena prevista ia de dois a seis meses de prisão.
explicacao: O potlatch é praticado por povos indígenas da costa noroeste do Pacífico, como os haida, os tlingit e os kwakwaka'wakw. Mais que uma festa, é tradicionalmente a principal instituição de governo e o sistema econômico desses povos. Acontece em nascimentos, mortes, casamentos e outros marcos, e nele se transmitem títulos que dão direito a territórios de caça, pesca e coleta. O status de uma família não sobe com o que ela acumula, mas com o que ela distribui. O nome vem do jargão chinook e quer dizer "dar". Missionários e agentes do governo viam o costume como desperdício, contrário aos valores "civilizados" de acumulação, e uma emenda de 1884 à Lei dos Índios o tornou crime, com pena de dois a seis meses de prisão. Em 1888, o antropólogo Franz Boas já chamava a proibição de fracasso: as aldeias eram numerosas demais e o governo não conseguia fiscalizá-las. O potlatch continuou às escondidas até a lei ser revogada, em 1951. Hoje voltou a ser feito abertamente em várias comunidades, e a nação haida baseia a sua democracia na lei do potlatch.

fontes.trecho: Potlatch is the gift-giving feast practiced by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast of Canada and the United States, among whom it is traditionally the primary governmental institution, legislative body, and economic system. This includes the Heiltsuk, Haida, Nuxalk, Tlingit, Makah, Tsimshian, Nuu-chah-nulth, Kwakwaka'wakw, and Coast Salish cultures. [...] A potlatch involves giving away or destroying wealth or valuable items in order to demonstrate a leader's wealth and power. [...] From 1885 to 1951, the Government of Canada criminalized potlatches. However, the practice persisted underground despite the risk of government reprisals including mandatory jail sentences of at least two months; [...] Since the practice was decriminalized in 1951, the potlatch has re-emerged in some communities. In many it is still the bedrock of Indigenous governance, as in the Haida Nation, which has rooted its democracy in potlatch law. The word comes from the Chinook Jargon, meaning "to give away" or "a gift"; [...] A potlatch was held on the occasion of births, deaths, adoptions, weddings, and other major events. [...] These ranked titles granted rights to hunting, fishing and berrying territories. [...] The status of any given family is raised not by who has the most resources, but by who distributes the most resources. [...] Potlatching was made illegal in Canada in 1884 in an amendment to the Indian Act. To some extent, this was at the urging of missionaries and government agents who considered it "a worse than useless custom" that was seen as wasteful, unproductive, and contrary to 'civilized values' of accumulation. [...] shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not more than six nor less than two months in any gaol or other place of confinement; [...] In 1888, the anthropologist Franz Boas described the potlatch ban as a failure: [...] Besides, the Government is unable to enforce it. The settlements are so numerous, and the Indian agencies so large, that there is nobody to prevent the Indians doing whatsoever they like. [...] The potlatch ban was repealed in 1951. [...] Indigenous people now openly hold potlatches to commit to the restoring of their ancestors' ways.

gancho: O Ratoncito Pérez, o ratinho que troca dentes de leite por presentes na Espanha e na América hispânica, tem autor e data: virou o "ratinho dos dentes" num conto de 1894 escrito para o rei Afonso XIII, aos 8 anos.
explicacao: Um rato chamado Pérez já aparecia em contos populares espanhóis, como marido de uma formiguinha, em histórias publicadas em 1877. Quem o transformou num negociante de dentes foi o escritor Luis Coloma. Em 1894, a rainha Maria Cristina encomendou a ele uma história para o filho, o rei Afonso XIII, que tinha perdido um dente aos oito anos. No conto, o rato mora com a família numa caixa de biscoitos no porão de uma confeitaria de Madri, a Prast, e foge pelos canos da cidade até os quartos das crianças que perderam dentes, sempre enganando os gatos pelo caminho. O pequeno rei aparece na história com o apelido que a mãe lhe dava, "Buby". O texto só foi publicado em 1902, e o manuscrito original, com dedicatória ao rei, está guardado no Palácio Real de Madri. Hoje a tradição é quase universal no mundo hispânico: a criança põe o dente debaixo do travesseiro, e o ratinho o troca por um pequeno pagamento ou presente. Em 2003, Madri pôs uma placa no endereço onde o rato "morava", e ele se tornou o primeiro personagem de ficção homenageado assim pela prefeitura da cidade.

fontes.trecho: El Ratoncito Pérez or Ratón Pérez (lit. transl. Perez the Little Mouse or Perez Mouse) is a fantasy figure of early childhood in Spanish and Hispanic American cultures. The folklore states that when children lose one of their milk teeth, they should place it underneath their pillow or on their bedside table and he will visit while they sleep, replacing the lost tooth with a small payment or gift, as does the Tooth Fairy in other cultures. Although he first appeared in oral tradition folktales such as The Vain Little Mouse, it was Luis Coloma who in 1894 turned him into a tooth dealer in a tale written for an eight-year-old King Alfonso XIII. The tradition is almost universal in Spanish cultures, with some slight differences. [...] first appeared in the oral tradition folktales La hormiguita (transl. The Little Ant), as her gentle and timid husband, and in The Vain Little Mouse, also as her husband. These tales were first published in Cuentos, oraciones, adivinanzas y refranes populares (1877) by Fernán Caballero. [...] In 1894, Queen Maria Christina commissioned Coloma to write a tale for King Alfonso XIII, who had just lost a tooth at the age of eight. Coloma's story follows Ratón Pérez, who lived with his family in a box of cookies at the basement of Prast confectionery store in Madrid, but frequently ran away from home through the pipes of the city, and into the bedrooms of children who had lost their teeth. The story details how he cunningly misleads any cats in the vicinity who may be lurking, and includes his interaction with King Buby (Queen Maria Christina's nickname for Alfonso XIII). The tale was first published in 1902 together with other stories in Nuevas lecturas. [...] Coloma's original manuscript, with his signature and a dedication to King Alfonso XIII, is now kept in the vault of the Royal Library at Royal Palace of Madrid. In 2003, the City Council of Madrid paid tribute to Ratón Pérez with a commemorative plaque at the façade of Number 8 Calle del Arenal, where the mouse was said to have lived. [...] He thus became the first fictional character honored with a plaque by the City Council.

gancho: No folclore de Natal da Islândia, um gato gigante devora quem não ganhou roupa nova. Segundo a tradição, a ameaça era usada nas fazendas para os trabalhadores terminarem de processar a lã do outono antes do Natal.
explicacao: O Jólakötturinn, o "gato de Natal", seria enorme e cruel e rondaria o campo nevado nessa época do ano.
