[...] Four scrolls found their way into his hands: the Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa), the Community Rule, the Habakkuk Pesher (a commentary on the book of Habakkuk), and the Genesis Apocryphon. [...] Four of the Dead Sea Scrolls eventually went up for sale in an advertisement on 1 June 1954, The Wall Street Journal. On 1 July 1954, the scrolls, after delicate negotiations and accompanied by three people including Mar Samuel, arrived at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York. They were purchased by Professor Mazar and the son of Professor Sukenik, Yigael Yadin, for $250,000 (approximately $3,000,000 in 2025 dollars), and brought to Jerusalem.

gancho: O Museu da Bíblia, em Washington, abriu em 2017 exibindo fragmentos dos Manuscritos do Mar Morto. Em 2020, análises concluíram que os 16 fragmentos do acervo eram falsificações modernas.
explicacao: Os fragmentos de pergaminho foram doados pelo fundador do museu, Steve Green, para a inauguração. Assim que o catálogo foi divulgado, especialistas de fora estranharam que a procedência das peças não estivesse bem documentada, e Årstein Justnes, professor de estudos bíblicos da Universidade de Agder, na Noruega, afirmou que eram falsificações. O museu encomendou análises a um instituto federal alemão de pesquisa e teste de materiais, mas manteve os fragmentos em destaque na abertura, com testes ainda incompletos e uma placa dizendo que os estudiosos continuavam a debater a autenticidade. Em 2018, anunciou que 5 dos 16 eram falsos e os tirou da exposição: segundo os pesquisadores alemães, tinham características incompatíveis com uma origem antiga. Em 2020, o museu informou que todos os 16 fragmentos que havia comprado entre 2009 e 2014 eram falsificações modernas. Eles pertencem a um grupo de cerca de 70 fragmentos que apareceram no mercado a partir de 2002, provavelmente todos falsos. A história mostra quanto pesa a procedência: desde 2002, muitos falsos manuscritos do mar Morto surgiram no mercado negro.

fontes.trecho: Founder Steve Green donated purported Dead Sea Scrolls parchment fragments to the museum collection for its opening. When the museum catalog was released to the public, however, several outside experts expressed concern that the museum had not adequately accounted for the fragments' provenance. Arstein Justnes, a professor of biblical studies at the University of Agder in Norway, declared they were outright forgeries. The museum subsequently enlisted the German Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und Prüfung) to analyze the scrolls. The museum kept the fragments prominently on display for its official opening, while testing was still incomplete. The text of display stated that "scholars continue to debate the authenticity of this fragment". In 2018 the museum announced that expert examination had led it to conclude that five of the sixteen fragments of the Dead Sea Scrolls were forgeries and that the museum had removed them from display. According to the German researchers, those five showed "characteristics inconsistent with ancient origin". By March 2020, all 16 fragments displayed at the museum were confirmed to be modern forgeries. The forgeries are part of a group of about 70 fragments of the Dead Sea Scrolls which came onto the market in 2002, all of which are likely forgeries [...] The Museum of the Bible is a museum in Washington, D.C., United States [...] The museum, which opened on November 17, 2017

Since 2002, many forgeries of Dead Sea Scrolls have appeared on black markets. [...] the Museum of the Bible in the United States (also known as Green Collection) reported that all 16 purported "Dead Sea Scroll fragments" they had acquired between 2009 and 2014 were in fact modern forgeries.

gancho: O "Arquivo Secreto do Vaticano" não tinha esse nome por esconder segredos: "secreto" estava no sentido antigo de "particular", pois o acervo pertence ao papa. Em 2019, Francisco o rebatizou de Arquivo Apostólico.
explicacao: O arquivo guarda os atos promulgados pela Santa Sé, e o papa, como soberano do Vaticano, é dono do material até morrer ou renunciar. A palavra "secreto" do nome antigo não indicava confidencialidade no sentido moderno: uma tradução mais fiel seria algo como "arquivo apostólico particular", sinal de que o acervo é propriedade pessoal do papa, e não de algum departamento da Cúria Romana. Em inglês, esse sentido antigo sobrevive em palavras como "secretary", secretário, que indicavam um posto de honra e de confiança. Há, sim, partes fechadas a quem é de fora, sobretudo o que trata de pessoas e assuntos recentes, como tudo o que é posterior a 1958. Durante séculos o arquivo ficou fechado a estranhos, até que o papa Leão XIII o abriu aos pesquisadores no fim do século XIX; a sala de leitura foi inaugurada em 1º de janeiro de 1881. Hoje, mais de mil estudiosos consultam documentos ali a cada ano. Estima-se que haja 85 quilômetros de estantes. Entre as peças conhecidas estão o pedido de Henrique VIII da Inglaterra para anular o casamento, uma transcrição manuscrita do julgamento de Galileu por heresia e cartas em que Michelangelo reclama de não ter sido pago pelo trabalho na Capela Sistina. A troca de nome foi feita pelo papa Francisco em outubro de 2019.

fontes.trecho: The Vatican Apostolic Archive (Latin: Archivum Apostolicum Vaticanum; Italian: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano), formerly known as the Vatican Secret Archive (Latin: Archivum Secretum Vaticanum; Italian: Archivio Segreto Vaticano), is the central repository in the Vatican City of all acts promulgated by the Holy See. The Pope, as the sovereign of Vatican City, owns the material held in the archive until his death or resi [...] the archive remained closed altogether to outsiders until the late 19th century, when Pope Leo XIII opened the archive to researchers, more than a thousand of whom now examine some of its documents each year. [...] The use of the word secret in the former title, "Vatican Secret Archive", does not denote the modern meaning of confidentiality. A fuller and perhaps better translation of the archive's former Latin name may be the "private Vatican Apostolic archive", indicating that its holdings are the pope's personal property, not those of any particular department of the Roman Curia or the Holy See. [...] most of these classified materials, which are actively denied to outsiders, relate to contemporary personalities and activities, including everything dated after 1958 [...] On 28 October 2019, Pope Francis issued an Apostolic Letter motu proprio dated 22 October, renaming the archives from the Vatican Secret Archive to the Vatican Apostolic Archive. [...] Pope Leo ordering a reading room constructed for researchers; it opened on 1 January 1881. [...] The Vatican Apostolic Archive has been estimated to contain 85 kilometres (53 mi) of shelving [...] Notable documents include Henry VIII of England's request for a marriage annulment, a handwritten transcript of the trial of Galileo for heresy, and letters from Michelangelo complaining he had not been paid for work on the Sistine Chapel. [...] The word secret continues to be used in this older, original sense in the English language, in phrases such as secret servants, secret cupbearer, or secretary, much like an esteemed position of honour and regard comparable to a VIP.

gancho: No século V, o monge sírio Simeão viveu cerca de 36 anos no alto de colunas, perto de Aleppo. Subiu para fugir das multidões, mas atraiu ainda mais gente, e até um imperador ouvia seus conselhos.
explicacao: Filho de um pastor, Simeão levou a vida ascética a tal extremo que os colegas do mosteiro julgaram que ele não servia para a vida em comunidade e lhe pediram que fosse embora. Passou então a viver numa encosta rochosa, mas os peregrinos não paravam de procurá-lo em busca de conselhos e orações, e lhe sobrava pouco tempo para as devoções. A saída foi subir numa coluna que restava entre ruínas. A primeira tinha pouco mais de 3 metros; ele trocou de plataforma algumas vezes, e a última, segundo os relatos, passava de 15 metros. No topo havia uma plataforma que, acredita-se, tinha cerca de um metro quadrado e uma grade em volta. Os relatos divergem sobre quanto tempo ele ficou lá em cima: as estimativas vão de 35 a 42 anos. O efeito foi o contrário do planejado: chegavam ainda mais peregrinos e curiosos. Todas as tardes ele conversava com visitantes, que subiam uma escada até ficar ao alcance da voz. Escrevia cartas, orientava discípulos e pregava contra a usura. O imperador Teodósio II e a esposa o tinham em alta conta. Outros ascetas imitaram seu modelo e ficaram conhecidos como estilitas, da palavra grega para coluna. As ruínas do enorme conjunto erguido em sua honra, quatro basílicas em forma de cruz em torno da base da coluna, ainda podem ser vistas a cerca de 30 km de Aleppo.

fontes.trecho: c. 390 – 2 September 459) was a Syrian Christian ascetic who achieved notability by living 36 years on top of a pillar near Aleppo (in modern Syria). Several other stylites later followed his model (the Greek word style means "pillar"). [...] The son of a shepherd, Simeon was born and raised in Sis [...] From the first day, he gave himself up to the practice of an austerity so extreme that his brethren judged him to be unsuited to any form of community life. They asked Simeon to leave the monastery. [...] Simeon sought a rocky eminence on the slopes of what is now the Sheik Barakat Mountain [...] But crowds of pilgrims invaded the area to seek him out, asking his counsel or his prayers, and leaving him insufficient time for his own devotions. [...] Simeon discovered a pillar which had survived among ruins in nearby Telanissa [...] The first pillar that Simeon occupied was little more than 3 meters (10 ft). He later moved his platform to others, the last in the series reportedly more than 15 meters (50 ft) from the ground. At the top of the pillar was a platform, which is believed to have been about one square meter and surrounded by a baluster. [...] If anything, the new pillar attracted even more people, both pilgrims who had earlier visited him and sightseers as well. Simeon was available each afternoon to talk with visitors. By means of a ladder, visitors were able to ascend within speaking distance. It is known that he wrote letters, the text of some of which have survived to this day, that he instructed disciples, and that he also lectured to those assembled beneath. He especially preached against profanity and usury. [...] The Emperor Theodosius II and his wife Aelia Eudocia greatly respected Simeon and listened to his counsels [...] The ruins of the vast edifice erected in his honour and known in Arabic as the Qalaat Semaan ("the Fortress of Simeon") can still be seen. They are located about 30 km northwest of Aleppo [...] consist of four basilicas built out from an octagonal court towards the four points of the compass to form a large cross. In the centre of the court stands the base of the style or column on which Simeon stood. [...] Accounts differ with regard to how long Simeon lived upon the pillar, with estimates ranging from 35 to 42 years.

gancho: Na ilha de Tanna, em Vanuatu, seguidores de John Frum, figura retratada como um militar americano da Segunda Guerra, desfilam todo 15 de fevereiro com armas de bambu, à espera da volta dele.
explicacao: O movimento surgiu no máximo no fim dos anos 1930, quando Vanuatu ainda se chamava Novas Hébridas. Ganhou força no começo dos anos 1940, quando 50 mil soldados americanos se instalaram no arquipélago, com uma quantidade enorme de suprimentos, a "carga". Cerca de 10 mil homens locais trabalharam num batalhão de mão de obra dos EUA. É um dos chamados cultos da carga: John Frum traria riqueza e prosperidade a quem o seguisse. Uma interpretação lê o nome como "John from (America)", embora possa indicar alguém vindo de qualquer lugar fora dali. Em 1957, líderes do movimento criaram o "Exército de Tanna", uma tropa não violenta com bonés que imitavam os americanos, as letras "T-A USA" no peito e fuzis de bambu com baionetas entalhadas. O desfile anual acontece na data em que os fiéis acreditam que John Frum voltará. Em 1959, o naturalista David Attenborough perguntou a um seguidor por que ele ainda esperava a carga, prometida 19 anos antes. A resposta: quem espera 2 mil anos pela volta de Jesus pode esperar mais de 19 por John. A crença está em declínio: segundo relatos, eram mais de 5 mil membros nos anos 1990, e menos de 500 em 2022.

fontes.trecho: John Frum (also called Jon Frum, John Brum, and John Prum) is a figure associated with cargo cults on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu (formerly the New Hebrides). He is often depicted as an American World War II serviceman who will bring wealth and prosperity to the people if they follow him. [...] In the 1990s, there were reportedly over 5,000 members of the John Frum movement. However, belief in John Frum is in decline; as of 2022, there are fewer than 500 practitioners. [...] The religion centering on John Frum arose no later than the late 1930s, when Vanuatu was known as the New Hebrides. [...] the movement gained popularity in the early 1940s after 50,000 American troops were stationed in Vanuatu during World War II, bringing with them an enormous amount of supplies (or "cargo"). During the war, approximately 10,000 Ni-Vanuatu men served in the Vanuatu Labor Corps, a labor battalion of the United Stat [...] Versions of the cult emphasizing the American connection interpret "John Frum" as a corruption of  "John from (America)" (although it could mean "John from" anywhere outside Vanuatu). In 1957, leaders of the John Frum movement created the "Tanna Army", a non-violent faux army that organized military-style parades with men wearing imitation American caps, long trousers, singlets across their chests with the letters "T-A USA" (Tanna Army USA), and carried imitation bamboo guns with carved bayonets. [...] A Tanna Army parade takes place every year on February 15, the date on which followers believe John Frum will return [...] In 1959, when David Attenborough asked one of the followers why he was still waiting for the cargo after it had been 19 years since it was promised and had not arrived, the man said "If you can wait two thousand years for Jesus Christ to come 'an 'e no come, then I can wait more than nineteen years for John."

gancho: Os samaritanos, os da parábola do bom samaritano, ainda existem: são cerca de 900. Como a comunidade é minúscula, todo casamento passa antes pelo aval de um geneticista, para evitar doenças hereditárias.
explicacao: Eles seguem uma religião aparentada ao judaísmo, mas aceitam como escritura sagrada só a Torá samaritana e creem que o santuário escolhido por Deus é o monte Gerizim, e não o Monte do Templo, em Jerusalém. A peregrinação ao Gerizim inclui o sacrifício da Páscoa, o rito mais famoso do grupo. Na Antiguidade, os samaritanos eram a principal população da Samaria, mas revoltas fracassadas, a repressão bizantina e, mais tarde, conversões forçadas ao islã reduziram drasticamente seu número: em 1919, eram 141. Desde então, a população voltou a crescer. Em 2024, os cerca de 900 se dividiam entre Holon, perto de Tel Aviv, e Kiryat Luza, no próprio monte Gerizim, perto de Nablus. Com só quatro famílias e a recusa geral de aceitar convertidos, é comum casar dentro da família ampliada, até entre primos, e há histórico de doenças genéticas no grupo. Por isso, todos os casamentos são aprovados antes por um geneticista do Hospital Tel HaShomer. Para ampliar a variedade genética, a comunidade também passou a admitir noivas de fora, como judias israelenses e algumas mulheres da Rússia e da Ucrânia, desde que sigam as práticas samaritanas.

fontes.trecho: Samaritans recognize only the Samaritan Torah as sacred scripture, rejecting most of the later Jewish canon as well as rabbinic tradition, and their central theological distinction from Judaism is the belief that Mount Gerizim, not the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, is God's chosen sanctuary. Their religion is centered on the hereditary high priesthood, strict observance of biblical law and festivals, and pilgrimages to Mount Gerizim, most famously the Passover sacrifice. In classical antiquity, the Samaritans were the principal population of Samaria, but their numbers were drastically reduced following a series of failed revolts and severe Byzantine repression [...] but their population has grown since, reaching around 900 people as of 2024; they are one of the world's smallest surviving ethnoreligious groups, concentrated mainly in Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus (ancient Shechem) and in the neighborhood of Neve Pinchas in Holon near Tel Aviv. [...] many Samaritan families were forced to convert to Islam during that time. [...] There were 100 in 1786 and 141 in 1919, then 150 in 1967. [...] the parable of the Good Samaritan. [...] With such a small population, divided into only four families or houses (Cohen, Tsedakah, Danafi, and Marhiv, with the Matar family dying out in 1968), and a general refusal to accept converts, it is common for Samaritans to marry within their extended families, even first cousins. There has been a history of genetic disorders within the group due to the small gene pool. To counter this, the Holon Samaritan community has allowed men from the community to marry non-Samaritan (primarily Israeli Jewish) women, provided that the women agree to follow Samaritan religious practices. [...] all marriages within the Samaritan community are first approved by a geneticist at Tel HaShomer Hospital, in order to prevent the spread of genetic disorders. In meetings arranged by "international marriage agencies", a small number of women from Russia and Ukraine who agree to observe Samaritan religious practices have been allowed to marry into the Qiryat Luza Samaritan community in an effort to expand the gene pool.

gancho: Na arte bizantina, são Cristóvão às vezes aparece com cabeça de cachorro. As lendas mais antigas o descrevem como um cinocéfalo, um "homem-cão" de uma tribo que comia carne humana, antes da conversão.
explicacao: No Ocidente, a imagem mais comum é a de um gigante com um cajado, atravessando um rio com o menino Jesus no ombro. Não há, porém, nenhuma prova de que o santo tenha existido, e as lendas variam. A tradição oriental, mais antiga, dá ao Cristóvão de antes da conversão uma natureza feroz e traços de animal, em especial a cabeça de cão. A ocidental, mais recente, insiste menos nisso e destaca o tamanho, a falta de cultura e a feiura. Numa versão antiga, um certo Reprebos, capturado pelos romanos e obrigado a servir numa unidade militar, é um cinocéfalo de uma tribo de canibais que não sabe falar a língua deles; depois de rezar, recebe o dom da fala. O bispo e poeta alemão Walter de Speyer o retratou como um gigante dessa espécie, que comia carne humana e latia. Ao encontrar o menino Jesus, ele se arrepende, é batizado e ganha aparência humana. Não se sabe quando essas imagens começaram, porque boa parte da arte cristã antiga foi destruída nas ondas de iconoclastia bizantina dos séculos VIII e IX. Na liturgia católica, a comemoração dele saiu do calendário geral em 1970 e ficou restrita a calendários particulares.

fontes.trecho: the older Eastern tradition describes the pre-conversion Christopher as having a ferocious nature and animal features (in particular, the head of a dog) while the younger Western tradition does not dwell as much on these animal-like mental and physical features but rather emphasizes the lack of culture, the giant size and the ugliness of the saint. [...] In the iconography of Western Christianity, the saint is often depicted as a giant with a staff crossing a river with the infant Jesus on his shoulder. In Byzantine art, the saint is depicted in various guises including as a young man, a martyr in a red himation with a cross in his hand, a warrior on horseback or a man with the head of a dog in line with the early legendary tradition. [...] There is no evidence for the historicity of the saint. [...] A certain Reprebos is captured by the Romans in battle and then forced to join the Roman numerus Marmaritarum, i.e. a military unit made up by Marmaritae people. Reprebos is a physically repulsive Cynocephalus (i.e. a man with a dog's head) from a tribe of cannibals who is incapable of speaking "our language". After praying to his God he is granted the gift of language. [...] The German bishop and poet Walter of Speyer portrayed St. Christopher in his Vita et passio sancti Christopher martyris as a giant of a cynocephalic species in the land of the Chananeans who ate human flesh and barked. Eventually, Christopher meets the infant Jesus, regrets his former behavior and receives baptism. He is further rewarded with a human appearan [...] It is not clear when this type of representation started as most early Christian artworks were destroyed during the 8th and 9th century Byzantine Iconoclasms. [...] it was dropped in 1970 from the general calendar and restricted to particular calendars of the Roman rite.

gancho: Em 1659, comemorar o Natal virou infração em Boston, com multa de cinco xelins. Os puritanos viam a festa como sem base na Bíblia. A proibição caiu em 1686, e o Congresso dos EUA só a fez feriado em 1870.
explicacao: A aversão veio da Inglaterra. Calvinistas, os puritanos queriam tirar do cristianismo o que consideravam sem base bíblica, incluindo as festas estabelecidas pela Igreja Anglicana. Em 1647, o Parlamento inglês, controlado por eles, proibiu a celebração do Natal e pôs no lugar um dia de jejum, tratando a data como uma "festa papista" e uma época de desperdício e mau comportamento. Na América, os peregrinos de Plymouth mostraram o desprezo pela data em 1620: passaram o primeiro Natal no Novo Mundo construindo a primeira casa. Em Boston, a proibição de 1659 também valeu para New Hampshire e o Maine, então controlados por Massachusetts. Ela foi revogada em New Hampshire em 1683 e em Massachusetts em 1686, por Edmund Andros, governador nomeado pela Inglaterra. Mesmo assim, o Natal só virou moda na região de Boston em meados do século XIX, e antes da independência, em 1776, ele não era muito comemorado nas colônias americanas. Quem não era puritano lamentava a perda dos feriados de que os trabalhadores desfrutavam na Inglaterra.

fontes.trecho: The Puritans as Calvinists objected to the Christian feast of Christmas. [...] Puritans sought to remove elements they viewed as unbiblical, from their practice of Christianity, including those feasts established by the Anglican Church. In 1647, the Puritan-led English Parliament banned the celebration of Christmas, replacing it with a day of fasting and considering it "a popish festival with no biblical justification", and a time of wasteful and immoral behavi [...] The Plymouth Pilgrims put their loathing for the day into practice in 1620 when they spent their first Christmas Day in the New World building their first structure in the New World—thus demonstrating their complete contempt for the day. Non-Puritans in New England deplored the loss of the holidays enjoyed by the laboring classes in England. Christmas observance was outlawed in Boston in 1659 in light of the impending Restoration with a fine of five shillings. It was also banned in the Province of New Hampshire and Maine, which were controlled by Massachusetts. The ban by the Puritans was revoked in New Hampshire in 1683 by Edward Cranfield and in Massachusetts in 1686 by an English appointed governor, Edmund Andros; however, it was not until the mid-19th century that celebrating Christmas became fashionable in the Boston region. Before the Declaration of Independence in 1776, it was not widely celebrated in the American Colonies. [...] Christmas was not proclaimed a holiday by the United States Congress until 1870.

gancho: O verde vivo da moda no século XIX costumava vir do arsênico. Em 1861, uma jovem de 19 anos que polvilhava esse pó em flores artificiais para enfeitar roupas morreu envenenada, com as unhas e o branco dos olhos verdes.
explicacao: O pigmento era o verde de Scheele, um arsenito de cobre inventado em 1775 pelo químico Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Mais brilhante e durável que os verdes de carbonato de cobre usados antes, ele coloriu papéis de parede, tintas, velas e tecidos de roupa. Por dar um verde vivo, o arsênico foi parar em vestidos, luvas, sapatos e nas coroas de flores artificiais que as mulheres punham no cabelo e na roupa. Quem mais sofria, porém, era quem fabricava. O trabalho de Matilda Scheurer era espalhar o pó verde nas flores falsas. Ela teve convulsões e vômitos, e a autópsia achou arsênico no estômago, no fígado e nos pulmões. As reportagens sobre a morte dela e sobre as condições das floristas ajudaram a virar a opinião pública. O British Medical Journal chegou a escrever que a mulher vestida de arsênico levava nas saias veneno bastante para matar todos os admiradores que encontrasse em meia dúzia de bailes. Países escandinavos, a França e a Alemanha proibiram o pigmento; a Grã-Bretanha, não. A invenção dos corantes sintéticos facilitou o abandono, e no começo do século XX o verde de Scheele já não era usado como pigmento.

fontes.titulo: Killer Clothing Was All the Rage In the 19th Century (National Geographic)
fontes.trecho: Because it dyed fabric bright green, arsenic also ended up in dresses, gloves, shoes, and artificial flower wreaths that women used to decorate their hair and clothes. [...] But like mercury hats, arsenic fashions were most dangerous for the people who manufactured them, says Matthews David. For example, in 1861, a 19-year-old artificial flower maker named Matilda Scheurer—whose job involved dusting flowers with green, arsenic-laced powder—died a violent and colorful death. She convulsed, vomited, and foamed at the mouth. Her bile was green, and so were her fingernails and the whites of her eye. An autopsy found arsenic in her stomach, liver, and lungs. Articles about Scheurer’s death and the plight of artificial flower makers raised public awareness about arsenic in fashion. The British Medical Journal wrote that the arsenic-wearing woman “carries in her skirts poison enough to slay the whole of the admirers she may meet with in half a dozen ball-rooms.” [...] Scandinavia, France, and Germany banned the pigment (Britain did not). The move away from arsenic was hastened by the invention of synthetic dyes

Scheele's green, also called Schloss green, is chemically a cupric hydrogen arsenite (also called copper arsenite or acidic copper arsenite), CuHAsO3. [...] Scheele's green was invented in 1775 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele. [...] By the dawn of the 20th century, Scheele's green had completely fallen out of use as a pigment [...] Scheele's green was used to color wallpapers, paper furniture linings, and textiles used in clothing and bookbindings, along with paints, wax candles, and even some children's toys. [...] Scheele's green is more brilliant and durable than the then-used copper carbonate pigments.

gancho: Chapeleiros usavam mercúrio para fazer feltro com pelo de coelho, e muitos ficavam trêmulos e irritadiços. Nos EUA, o método só foi largado em 1941, quando a guerra precisou do metal para detonadores.
explicacao: Na etapa chamada em inglês de "carroting", os pelos de coelhos, lebres ou castores eram tratados com uma solução alaranjada de nitrato de mercúrio, que ajudava as fibras a se embolarem em feltro. Depois, o feltro liberava aos poucos vapor de mercúrio, e os chapeleiros, muitas vezes em oficinas apertadas, o respiravam. O envenenamento crônico, chamado eretismo, trazia tremores, timidez doentia e irritabilidade forte. Na cidade chapeleira de Danbury, nos EUA, os tremores ganharam apelido: "Danbury shakes". O risco não era segredo. Em 1869, a Academia de Medicina da França o demonstrou, e desde 1874 havia alternativas ao mercúrio. Ainda assim, nos EUA o processo seguiu até 1941. E a expressão inglesa "mad as a hatter", louco como um chapeleiro? A ligação com o mercúrio é a explicação mais popular, mas estudiosos a contestam, e a origem da frase é incerta. Ela já aparece impressa em 1829, décadas antes do Chapeleiro Maluco de Lewis Carroll. E o personagem, ao que tudo indica, foi inspirado num vendedor de móveis excêntrico conhecido do autor, Theophilus Carter.

fontes.trecho: Erethism, also known as erethismus mercurialis, mad hatter disease, or mad hatter syndrome, is a neurological disorder which affects the whole central nervous system, as well as a symptom complex, derived from mercury poisoning. [...] The character was almost certainly based on Theophilus Carter, an eccentric furniture dealer who was well known to Carroll. [...] After chronic exposure to the mercury vapours, hatters tended to develop characteristic psychological traits, such as pathological shyness and marked irritability [...] During the carroting process in which furs from small animals such as rabbits, hares or beavers were separated from their skins and matted together, an orange-colored solution containing mercuric nitrate was used as a smoothing agent. [...] In treated felts, a slow reaction released volatile free mercury. Hatters (or milliners) who came into contact with vapours from the impregnated felt often worked in confined areas. [...] In 1869, the French Academy of Medicine demonstrated the health hazards posed to hatmakers. Alternatives to mercury use in hatmaking became available by 1874. [...] In the United States, the mercury-based process continued to be adopted until as late as 1941, when it was abandoned mainly due to the wartime need for the heavy metal in the manufacture of detonators. Thus, for much of the 20th century mercury poisoning remained common in the U.S. hatmaking industries, including those located in Danbury, Connecticut (giving rise to the expression the "Danbury shakes").

The etymology of the phrase is uncertain, with explanations both connected and unconnected to the trade of hatmaking. The earliest known appearance of the phrase in print is in an 1829 issue of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, predating the Mad Hatter from Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by several decades.

fontes.titulo: Killer Clothing Was All the Rage In the 19th Century (National Geographic)
fontes.trecho: Many people think that “mad as a hatter” refers to the mental and physical side effects hatmakers endured from using mercury in their craft. Though scholars dispute whether this is actually the origin of the phrase, many hatters did develop mercury poisoning. [...] In order to make this fur stick together to form felt, hatters brushed it with mercury.

gancho: O salto alto nasceu para homens a cavalo: na Pérsia, ele firmava o pé do cavaleiro no estribo na hora de atirar com o arco. Na Europa do século XVII, era sinal de masculinidade, e Luís XIV o usava vermelho.
explicacao: Segundo Elizabeth Semmelhack, do Museu do Calçado Bata, em Toronto, o salto foi por séculos um calçado de montaria no Oriente Próximo: quando o soldado persa se erguia nos estribos, ele ajudava a firmar a postura para disparar flechas. Em 1599, o xá Abbas I, dono da maior cavalaria do mundo e em busca de aliados europeus contra os otomanos, mandou sua primeira missão diplomática à Europa. A moda persa pegou, e aristocratas adotaram o salto para parecer mais viris. Quando gente de classes mais baixas passou a imitá-los, a nobreza subiu a altura: inútil nas ruas enlameadas, o salto mostrava que quem o usava não precisava trabalhar no campo. Luís XIV, com 1,63 m, ganhava 10 cm com saltos, sempre com sola e salto vermelhos, e, nos anos 1670, decretou que só membros da corte podiam usá-los. As mulheres aderiram nos anos 1630, numa onda de masculinizar o visual. No fim do século, o salto masculino ficou mais baixo e robusto, e o feminino, mais fino. Com o Iluminismo, a roupa dos homens ficou mais prática, o salto passou a ser visto como tolo e efeminado, e, segundo Semmelhack, por volta de 1740 os homens tinham deixado o salto alto de lado; ficaram só saltos baixos e robustos, como os das botas de montaria.

fontes.titulo: Why did men stop wearing high heels? (BBC News)
fontes.trecho: "The high heel was worn for centuries throughout the near east as a form of riding footwear," says Elizabeth Semmelhack of the Bata Shoe Museum in Toronto. [...] "When the soldier stood up in his stirrups, the heel helped him to secure his stance so that he could shoot his bow and arrow more effectively," says Semmelhack. At the end of the 16th Century, Persia's Shah Abbas I had the largest cavalry in the world. He was keen to forge links with rulers in Western Europe to help him defeat his great enemy, the Ottoman Empire. [...] So in 1599, Abbas sent the first Persian diplomatic mission to Europe [...] Persian style shoes were enthusiastically adopted by aristocrats, who sought to give their appearance a virile, masculine edge [...] As the wearing of heels filtered into the lower ranks of society, the aristocracy responded by dramatically increasing the height of their shoes [...] In the muddy, rutted streets of 17th Century Europe, these new shoes had no utility value whatsoever - but that was the point. [...] "They aren't in the fields working and they don't have to walk far." [...] For a great king, he was rather diminutively proportioned at only 5ft 4in (1.63m). He supplemented his stature by a further 4in (10cm) with heels [...] The heels and soles were always red [...] In the 1670s, Louis XIV issued an edict that only members of his court were allowed to wear red heels. [...] "In the 1630s you had women cutting their hair, adding epaulettes to their outfits," says Semmelhack. [...] And this is why women adopted the heel - it was in an effort to masculinise their outfits." [...] "Men started to have a squarer, more robust, lower, stacky heel, while women's heels became more slender, more curvaceous." [...] Men's fashion shifted towards more practical clothing. [...] High heels were seen as foolish and effeminate. By 1740 men had stopped wearing them altogether.

In early 17th-century Europe, high heels were a sign of masculinity and high social status. [...] Starting in the 10th century, the Persian cavalry wore galesh, a kind of boot with heels, to ensure their feet stayed in the stirrups. [...] By this time, heels for men were chunky squares attached to riding boots or tall formal dress boots [...] Over the course of the Enlightenment, men's heels began to concentrate on either practical riding boots or tall leather boots worn for status.

gancho: Em 1918, uma revista do comércio de roupa infantil dos EUA dizia que a regra era rosa para meninos e azul para meninas. Mas a história de que as cores simplesmente se inverteram depois é exagero.
explicacao: O texto de junho de 1918 explicava que o rosa, cor mais decidida e forte, combinava com meninos, e o azul, mais delicado, com meninas. Em 1927, a revista Time publicou uma tabela com a opinião de grandes lojas americanas: a Filene's, de Boston, e outras recomendavam rosa para meninos, e quatro lojas diziam o contrário. Outras fontes ligavam as cores ao cabelo ou aos olhos do bebê. Antes, crianças pequenas dos dois sexos usavam quase sempre branco, que podia ser lavado com frequência; os corantes químicos, que aguentavam água quente sem desbotar, ajudaram a espalhar as cores. Dessas citações nasceu a ideia, muito repetida, de que rosa e azul trocaram de lado em meados do século XX. Mas o psicólogo Marco Del Giudice vasculhou um banco de mais de 5 milhões de livros publicados nos EUA de 1880 a 1980 e achou muitos exemplos de "azul para meninos" e praticamente nenhum do inverso. Em jornais e revistas de 1881 a 1930, contou 34 casos da regra atual e 28 da contrária. A conclusão dele: houve inconsistência, não inversão. A própria historiadora Jo Paoletti, cuja pesquisa deu origem à ideia, falava em inconsistência; a "inversão total" foi uma leitura distorcida.

fontes.titulo: Unraveling the Colorful History of Why Girls Wear Pink and Boys Wear Blue (Smithsonian Magazine)
fontes.trecho: In June 1918, for example, a trade publication called the Infant’s Department reported, “The generally accepted rule is pink for the boy and blue for the girl. The reason is that pink, being a more decided and stronger color, is more suitable for the boy, while blue, which is more delicate and dainty, is prettier for the girl.” According to Paoletti, other sources said blue was flattering for blondes and pink for brunettes, or blue was for blue-eyed babies and pink for brown-eyed babies. In 1927, Time magazine printed a chart showing appropriate colors for girls and boys, in the view of leading U.S. department stores. In Boston, Filene’s told parents to dress boys in pink. [...] Four other stores across the country advised the exact opposite. [...] Based in large part on Paoletti’s research, scholars, book authors and the media have argued that blue’s connection with boys and pink’s with girls wasn’t solidified until the mid-20th century. Prior to that point, many sources state, the gendered nature of the colors was either reversed or at best inconsistent (Paoletti’s original argument, which has since been misconstrued as a total reversal). [...] In 2012, Del Giudice published a paper refuting the “pink-blue reversal,” as he called it. After searching a database of more than five million books published in the U.S. between 1880 and 1980, he found many examples of the standard “blue for boys” and “pink for girls” association, but virtually none for the reverse. [...] Interestingly, Del Giudice’s follow-up analysis of U.S. newspapers and magazines published between 1881 and 1930 yielded results more in line with Paoletti’s findings. He recorded 34 instances of the standard color coding and 28 instances of the reverse [...] “Pink-blue gender coding showed a certain degree of inconsistency (though not a reversal) between the late 19th and early 20th centuries,”

One reason for the increased use of pink for girls and blue for boys was the invention of new chemical dyes, which meant that children's clothing could be mass-produced and washed in hot water without fading. Prior to this time, most small children of both sexes wore white, which could be frequently washed.

gancho: Por séculos, o bolso das mulheres era uma bolsinha à parte, amarrada na cintura sob a saia. Com os vestidos retos e finos do fim do século XVIII, ele ficou inútil, e elas passaram a levar a bolsa no braço.
explicacao: No século XVII, as roupas masculinas já tinham bolsos costurados, enquanto os das mulheres seguiam como bolsinhas soltas, presas à cintura por baixo das saias. Do século XVII ao XIX, elas levavam tesoura, alfinetes, agulhas e chaves. A ideia tinha raízes medievais: a partir do século XIII, fendas verticais na túnica davam acesso a uma bolsa ou a chaves penduradas no cinto, por baixo. A palavra inglesa "pocket" vem justamente de um diminutivo normando para bolsa. A mudança veio com a moda da Regência, no fim do século XVIII: saias em forma de coluna e tecidos finos tornaram os bolsos amarrados praticamente inúteis. A saída foi a retícula, uma bolsinha com cordão levada no braço, parecida com as bolsas de festa de hoje e usada sobretudo de 1795 a 1820. O nome vem do latim "reticulum", redinha, porque as primeiras eram de rede, e ela também era chamada de "ridicule" e de "indispensable". A diferença entre os sexos persiste: um estudo de 2018 do site The Pudding constatou que menos da metade dos bolsos da frente de roupas femininas comportava uma carteira fina.

fontes.trecho: In medieval Europe, early pocket-like openings called fitchets appeared in the 13th century. These vertical slits, cut into the outer tunic, allowed access to a purse or keys suspended from the girdle beneath. [...] By the 17th century, pockets were sewn into men's clothing, while women's remained as separate tie-on pouches hidden beneath skirts. The word pocket entered Middle English from a Norman diminutive of the Old French poke or pouque [...] In the 17th to 19th centuries, women's tie-on pockets—mentioned in the rhyme Lucy Locket—often carried everyday tools like scissors, pins, needles, and keys. [...] A 2018 study by the Pudding found that fewer than half of women's front pockets could fit a thin wallet

A reticule, also known as a ridicule or indispensable, was a type of small handbag or purse, similar to a modern evening bag, used mainly from 1795 to 1820. The reticule became popular with the advent of Regency fashions in the late 18th century. Previously, women had carried personal belongings in pockets tied around the waist, but the columnar skirts and thin fabrics that had come into style made pockets essentially unusable. When the reticule first appeared, it was made of netting. [...] A reticule usually had a drawstring closure at the top and was carried over the arm on a cord or chain. [...] the Latin reticulum, a diminutive of rete, or "net".

gancho: As saias armadas com arcos de aço do século XIX eram um risco de fogo. Florence Nightingale estimou que ao menos 630 mulheres morreram em 1863 e 1864 porque a roupa pegou fogo.
explicacao: A crinolina começou como um tecido duro de crina de cavalo ("crin", em francês) com algodão ou linho, usado em anáguas. Em 1856 veio a gaiola de arcos de aço, patenteada em Paris e, meses depois, na Grã-Bretanha. Feita em fábricas aos montes, ela permitia saias cuja circunferência chegava a seis jardas. Só a fábrica de Nova York consumia, em 1859, 300 mil jardas de arame de aço por semana. Numa época em que velas, lampiões e lareiras iluminavam e aqueciam as casas, as saias largas eram um perigo. Em 1863, o jornal The Times noticiou a morte de uma ajudante de cozinha de 14 anos: a saia, armada pela crinolina, pegou fogo quando ela subiu no guarda-fogo da lareira para alcançar umas colheres. No fim daquele ano, um incêndio numa igreja de Santiago, no Chile, matou de 2 mil a 3 mil pessoas, e parte da gravidade é atribuída ao tecido inflamável dos vestidos com crinolina. Em 1871, Emily e Mary, filhas ilegítimas do médico William Wilde, pai de Oscar Wilde, morreram queimadas depois que seus vestidos pegaram fogo. Já existiam tecidos antichama, mas eram vistos como feios e quase ninguém os queria.

fontes.trecho: Originally, crinoline described a stiff fabric made of horsehair ("crin") and cotton or linen which was used to make underskirts and as a dress lining. [...] The steel-hooped cage crinoline, first patented in April 1856 by R.C. Milliet in Paris, and by their agent in Britain a few months later, became extremely popular. Steel cage crinolines were mass-produced in huge quantity [...] At its widest point, the crinoline could reach a circumference of up to six yards [...] In 1859, the New York factory, which employed about a thousand girls, used 300,000 yards (270,000 m) of steel wire every week [...] Although trustworthy statistics on crinoline-related fatalities are rare, Florence Nightingale estimated that at least 630 women died from their clothes catching fire in 1863–1864. One such incident, the death of a 14-year-old kitchenmaid called Margaret Davey was reported in The Times on 13 February 1863. Her dress, "distended by a crinoline," ignited as she stood on the fender of the fireplace to reach some spoons on the mantelpiece, and she died as a result of extensive burns. [...] A month later, on 8 December 1863, a serious fire at the Church of the Company of Jesus in Santiago, Chile, killed between two and three thousand people. The severity of the death toll is credited in part to the large amounts of flammable fabric that made up the women's crinoline dresses. Two notable victims of crinoline fires were William Wilde's illegitimate daughters, Emily and Mary, who died in November 1871 of burns sustained after their gowns caught fire. Although flame-retardant fabrics were available, these were thought unattractive and were unpopular.

fontes.titulo: Killer Clothing Was All the Rage In the 19th Century (National Geographic)
fontes.trecho: In the days when candles, oil lamps, and fireplaces lit and heated American and European homes, women’s wide hoop skirts and flowing cotton and tulle dresses were a fire hazard

was an Irish oto-ophthalmologic surgeon and the author of significant works on medicine, archaeology and folklore, particularly concerning his native Ireland. He was the father of Oscar Wilde. [...] Emily and Mary both died in 1871 following a Halloween party at which their dresses accidentally caught fire.

gancho: O jeans com rebites não foi ideia de Levi Strauss, e sim de Jacob Davis, um alfaiate nascido em Riga. Davis comprava tecido de Strauss e pediu a ele apoio financeiro para patentear a invenção.
explicacao: Davis emigrou para os EUA em 1854 e, depois de muitas andanças, abriu uma alfaiataria em Reno, no Nevada, em 1869. Fazia barracas, mantas de cavalo e lonas de carroça para os operários da ferrovia e reforçava os pontos de tensão com rebites de cobre. Em dezembro de 1870, uma cliente pediu calças resistentes para o marido, lenhador. Davis pôs rebites nos cantos dos bolsos e nas costuras frágeis, a fama correu entre os trabalhadores da ferrovia, e logo ele não dava conta dos pedidos. Em 1872, escreveu a Strauss, seu fornecedor de tecido, propondo a parceria. A patente americana 139.121 saiu em 20 de maio de 1873, em nome de Davis e da Levi Strauss & Co. Davis passou o resto da vida em San Francisco, gerindo a fábrica das calças para Strauss. Uma lenda popular diz que Strauss já vendia calças de lona a mineiros e só pôs rebites depois da carta, o que é falso. Outra diz que o denim usado nas primeiras calças vinha de Nîmes, na França; era de um fabricante americano. Mas os nomes vieram mesmo da Europa: "jeans" deriva de Gênes, Gênova em francês, e "denim" quer dizer "de Nîmes", cidade cujos tecelões tentaram imitar o tecido genovês.

fontes.trecho: Jacob William Davis (Russian: Якоб Яковлевич Юфес , May 14, 1831 – January 20, 1908) was a Russian-American tailor who is credited with inventing modern jeans. [...] Jacob Youphes was born to a Jewish family in the city of Riga, in 1831. [...] In 1854, at the age of 23, he emigrated to the United States [...] 1869 saw Davis revert to his original trade, opening a tailor shop in the main street of the town. In his tailor shop, Davis made functional items such as tents, horse blankets and wagon covers for the railway workers on the Central Pacific Railroad. [...] To strengthen the stress points of the sewn items he was making, Davis used copper rivets to reinforce the stitching. In December 1870, Davis was asked by a customer to make a pair of strong working pants for her husband who was a woodcutter. To create suitably robust pants for working, he used duck cloth and reinforced the weak points in the seams and pockets with the copper rivets. Such was the success of these pants that word spread throughout the labourers along the railroad. [...] Before long, he found he could not keep up with demand. [...] in 1872, he approached Levi Strauss, who was still his supplier of fabric, and asked for his financial backing in the filing of a patent application. Strauss agreed, and on May 20, 1873, US Patent No. 139,121 for "Improvements in fastening pocket openings" was issued in the name of Jacob W. Davis and Levi Strauss and Company. [...] As demand continued to grow, the shop was superseded by a manufacturing plant which Davis managed for Strauss. Davis continued to work there for the remainder of his life [...] Davis died in San Francisco in 1908. [...] By 1868, the family had moved, this time to Reno, Nevada

Gênes, the French word for Genoa, is the origin of the word "jeans". In Nîmes, weavers tried to reproduce jean fabric but instead developed a similar twill fabric that became known as denim, "de Nîmes", meaning "from Nîmes". [...] The denim used was produced by an American manufacturer. Popular legend incorrectly states that it was imported from Nîmes. A popular myth is that Strauss initially sold brown canvas pants to miners, later dyed them blue, turned to using denim, and only after Davis wrote to him, added rivets.

gancho: O zíper demorou décadas para se firmar nas roupas. Nasceu para fechar botas, e o nome veio de galochas de borracha da B. F. Goodrich, de 1923, que se fechavam com um só "zip" da mão.
explicacao: Em 1893, o americano Whitcomb Judson patenteou um fecho para substituir os cadarços de botas, uma espécie de colchete complicado. Exibido na Feira Mundial de Chicago naquele ano, chamou pouca atenção e emperrava. Quem o tornou prático foi o engenheiro sueco-americano Gideon Sundbäck: ele passou de quatro para dez ou onze dentes por polegada, criou duas fileiras opostas que o cursor junta numa peça só e inventou a máquina que fabricava a corrente de dentes. O fecho foi à venda em 1913, e por anos seus usos principais foram botas e bolsas de fumo. Em 1923, a B. F. Goodrich o usou numa nova galocha e o chamou de "zipper", palavra que imita o som do fecho, e o nome pegou. Em 1925, a marca Schott NYC passou a usá-lo em jaquetas de couro. Nos anos 1930, foi anunciado aos pais como um jeito de as crianças se vestirem sozinhas. Em 1937, venceu o botão na chamada "Batalha da Braguilha", depois que estilistas franceses elogiaram o zíper nas calças masculinas. Um anúncio prometia livrar os homens de um "desalinho involuntário e constrangedor".

fontes.trecho: The zipper gets its name from a brand of rubber boots (or galoshes) it was used on in 1923. The galoshes could be fastened with a single zip of the hand, and soon the hookless fasteners came to be called "Zippers". [...] The word zipper is onomatopoetic, as the device makes a high-pitched zip when used. [...] Forty-two years later, in 1893, Whitcomb L. Judson patented a "Shoe-Fastening". Judson decided to develop a new shoelace alternative which replaced the standard boot laces for men and women. [...] The initial prototype functioned despite having mechanical problems that resulted in jamming occurrences. [...] The device served as a (more complicated) hook-and-eye shoe fastener. [...] He exhibited his clasp-locker at the World's Fair in Chicago of 1893 but the invention received minimal public attention. [...] Gideon Sundbäck, a Swedish-American electrical engineer, was hired to work for the company in 1906. [...] the zipper first went on sale in 1913. [...] Sundbäck increased the number of fastening elements from four per inch (about one every 6.4 mm) to ten or eleven (around every 2.5 mm), introduced two facing rows of teeth that pulled into a single piece by the slider [...] Gideon Sundbäck also created the manufacturing machine for the new device. [...] The popular North American term zipper (UK zip, or occasionally zip-fastener) came from the B. F. Goodrich Company in 1923. The company used Gideon Sundbäck's fastener on a new type of rubber boots (or galoshes) and referred to it as the zipper, and the name stuck. The two chief uses of the zipper in its early years were for closing boots and tobacco pouches. Zippers began being used for clothing in 1925 by Schott NYC on leather jackets. In the 1930s, a sales campaign began for children's clothing featuring zippers. The campaign praised zippers for promoting self-reliance in young children by making it possible for them to dress themselves. The zipper beat the button in 1937 in the "Battle of the Fly", after French fashion designers raved over zippers in men's trousers. A Talon advertisement in the first Esquire magazine declared the zipper the "Newest Tailoring Idea for Men", and that among the zippered fly's many virtues was that it would exclude "The Possibility of Unintentional and Embarrassing Disarray."

gancho: Uma febre da moda nasceu de um fracasso: em 1856, um estudante de 18 anos tentava fabricar quinina contra a malária e obteve um sólido preto. Ao limpar o frasco com álcool, apareceu um roxo intenso.
explicacao: William Henry Perkin era assistente do químico August Wilhelm von Hofmann, que lhe propôs o desafio de sintetizar a quinina, remédio natural caro e muito procurado contra a malária. Nas férias de Páscoa de 1856, no laboratório improvisado de casa, em Londres, ele oxidou anilina com dicromato de potássio. Impurezas reagiram e deixaram um sólido preto, cara de experimento perdido, mas a limpeza com álcool revelou o roxo. Perkin viu que a substância tingia seda sem desbotar com lavagem ou luz e pediu a patente aos 18 anos. Com dinheiro do pai, abriu uma fábrica. Até então, todos os corantes de tecido eram naturais, e o roxo, cor de prestígio desde a Antiguidade, era caro e difícil de obter. Batizado de malva ("mauve", nome francês da flor), o tom virou febre entre 1859 e 1861, com a ajuda da rainha Vitória e da imperatriz Eugênia, que adotaram uma cor parecida, e das crinolinas, que gastavam muito pano. A revista satírica Punch fez piada com o "sarampo malva" que se espalhava. Em 1870, a malva já perdia espaço para cores sintéticas mais novas, de uma indústria que ela mesma tinha inaugurado.

fontes.trecho: It was discovered serendipitously by William Henry Perkin in 1856 while he was attempting to synthesise the phytochemical quinine for the treatment of malaria. [...] In 1856, William Henry Perkin, then age 18, was given a challenge by his professor, August Wilhelm von Hofmann, to synthesize quinine. In one attempt, Perkin oxidized aniline using potassium dichromate, whose toluidine impurities reacted with the aniline and yielded a black solid, suggesting a "failed" organic synthesis. Cleaning the flask with alcohol, Perkin noticed purple portions of the solution. [...] In 1859, it was named mauve in England via the French name for the mallow flower, and chemists later called it mauveine. Between 1859 and 1861, mauve became a fashion must have. [...] Punch magazine published cartoons poking fun at the huge popularity of the colour “The Mauve Measles are spreading to so serious an extent that it is high time to consider by what means [they] may be checked.” By 1870, demand succumbed to newer synthetic colours in the synthetic dye industry launched by mauveine.

Hofmann had published a hypothesis on how it might be possible to synthesise quinine, an expensive natural substance much in demand for the treatment of malaria. Having become one of Hofmann's assistants, Perkin embarked on a series of experiments to try to achieve this end. During the Easter vacation in 1856, Perkin performed some further experiments in the crude laboratory in his apartment on the top floor of his home on Cable Street in east London. [...] Their initial experiments indicated that it dyed silk in a way which was stable when washed or exposed to light. [...] Perkin filed for a patent in August 1856, when he was still only 18. At the time, all dyes used for colouring cloth were natural substances, many of which were expensive and labour-intensive to extract [...] The colour purple, which had been a mark of aristocracy and prestige since ancient times, was especially expensive and difficult to produce. [...] he persuaded his father to put up the capital, and his brothers to partner with him to build a factory [...] Public demand was increased when a similar colour was adopted by Queen Victoria in Britain and by Empress Eugénie, wife of Napoleon III, in France, and when the crinoline or hooped-skirt, whose manufacture used a large quantity of cloth, became fashionable.

gancho: Existe um tecido feito da "barba" de um molusco: a seda marinha, fiada com os filamentos que a nacra usa para se prender ao fundo do mar. Hoje, só umas poucas mulheres de uma ilha italiana mantêm a arte.
explicacao: A nacra (Pinna nobilis) produz um tufo de cerca de mil fibras, de até 20 centímetros, chamado bisso. Enxaguado no mar, lavado em água doce, seco, cardado e fiado à mão, ele rendia um tecido levíssimo e quente, de fios com espessura parecida com a da seda comum. A maior parte das peças era de tricô, sobretudo luvas, e um par levava o bisso de umas 150 conchas. As primeiras menções escritas são do século II. A peça mais antiga que sobrevive é um gorro de tricô do século XIV, achado num buraco de lixo perto de Paris. Em chinês, um dos nomes do tecido era "seda tricotada por sereias". Parte da fama é lenda: dizia-se que um par de luvas cabia em meia casca de noz, mas a escritora Helen Scales sugere que a história se confundiu com luvas de couro finíssimo vendidas em cascas de noz como truque de marketing. A nacra hoje está ameaçada de extinção, e desde 2016 um parasita causa mortandades em massa. Desde 1992, é proibido ferir ou colher nacras vivas, e a arte sobrevive com poucas mulheres em Sant'Antioco, na Sardenha.

fontes.trecho: Sea silk is an extremely rare fabric that is made from the long silky filaments, or byssus, secreted by a gland in the foot of pen shells (in particular Pinna nobilis). The byssus is used by the mussel to attach itself to the sea bed. [...] The cloth produced from byssus is extremely light and warm. It is also often described as being very thin, although it is similar in thickness to other fibers such as silk. Byssus was said to be so fine that a pair of women's gloves made from the fabric could fit into half a walnut shell and a pair of stockings in a snuffbox. However, Helen Scales has put forward the idea that this actually refers to Limerick gloves made from fine kid leather sold inside walnut shells as a marketing stunt, and that over time the walnut packaging and beliefs about byssus cloth were conflated. [...] Pinna nobilis produces a beard of about 1,000 fibers to attach itself to the sea floor, which are all attached to a central stem. They can be up to 20 centimetres (7.9 in) long. [...] First, it is rinsed in the sea to remove debris. It is then washed in fresh water and manually cleaned. [...] After drying, it is carded and then spun by hand. [...] While a few extant woven objects are known, most were knit, and many are gloves. A knitted pair of gloves probably took the byssus from around 150 shells to produce. [...] The first written mentions of sea silk date to the 2nd century AD [...] The oldest surviving sea silk object is a knit hat from the 14th century, which was found in a waste pit near Paris. [...] Chinese language names include "cloth from the west of the sea" and "silk knitted by mermaids". [...] Pinna nobilis has become threatened with extinction, due to overfishing, the decline in seagrass fields, and pollution. Since 2016, populations have also been attacked by a parasite called Haplosporidium pinnae, which has caused mass die-offs. [...] since 1992, it is illegal to harm or harvest living Pinna nobilis. The art is now preserved only by a few women in Sant'Antioco. [...] Also in the 1920s, Italo Diana began a school on the island of Sant'Antioco near Sardinia.

gancho: Uma capa dourada exibida no museu V&A, em Londres, em 2012, foi tecida com seda de mais de 1 milhão de aranhas de Madagascar. O dourado não é tinta: é a cor natural do fio.
explicacao: A capa e um xale feitos pela mesma dupla, o artista têxtil britânico Simon Peers e o empresário americano Nicholas Godley, são, segundo o V&A, os maiores tecidos de seda de aranha do mundo. Eles reviveram e adaptaram sistemas e ferramentas do século XIX para tirar a seda de cada aranha-de-teia-dourada viva. Só as fêmeas produzem o fio usado. Cada sessão de extração levava uns 25 minutos e rendia cerca de 30 metros de seda, e depois a aranha era solta. São precisas 23 mil aranhas para cerca de 28 gramas de seda; a capa consumiu 1,5 kg de fio, e os fios mais finos juntavam 24 filamentos. Depois de tecida, a capa ganhou 6 mil horas de bordado, num desenho com dezenas de aranhas tecendo teias entre flores. A ideia tinha precedentes. No fim do século XIX, um missionário jesuíta francês em Madagascar, Paul Camboué, montou um sistema para coletar essas aranhas, e autoridades coloniais fizeram com a seda um dossel de cama para a Exposição Universal de Paris de 1900, hoje perdido. Antes ainda, em 1709, o francês Bon de Saint-Hilaire juntou casulos de aranha e fez meias e luvas para a realeza europeia.

fontes.titulo: Golden spider silk (Victoria and Albert Museum)
fontes.trecho: This exquisitely brocaded, vibrantly coloured shawl and cape are the world’s largest pieces of cloth to be made from spider silk. The silk was painstakingly harvested from more than one million female golden orb-weaver spiders by a large team in the highlands of Madagascar. [...] The shawl and cape were on display at the V&A from January – June 2012.

fontes.titulo: High-fashion cape created using silk by the golden orb spider (Royal Ontario Museum)
fontes.trecho: They revived and adapted nineteenth-century systems and tools that allow the hundreds of yards of silk filaments to be safely extracted from individual female spiders, which are then released. It takes 23,000 spiders to produce around 28 grams of the silk

The textile is not dyed; the golden hue is created by light refraction, and is the natural colour of the spider silk. [...] In 1709, François-Xavier Bon de Saint-Hilaire began collecting spiders to gather cocoons and spin the fibers into threads. [...] Bon de Saint-Hilaire was able to produce some spider silk objects, including stockings and gloves, all given to assorted European royalty. [...] Later in the 19th century, French Jesuit missionary Father Paul Camboué, located in Madagascar, realized that by establishing a system for collecting golden orb spiders and harvesting their silk [...] Camboué's work inspired French colonial authorities, led by M. Nogué, to produce textiles on a larger scale than previously possible, culminating in a bed canopy, now lost, for the colonial exhibition at the 1900 Paris Exposition Universelle. In an effort to revive the history of harvesting threads from spiders, and to determine the possibility of creating a textile with these threads, Nicholas Godley, an American entrepreneur, and Simon Peers, a British textile artist and historian [...] Producing the cape required 1.5 kg (53 oz) of thread. The thinnest threads used for the production of the cape were made of 24 strands of spider silk [...] Only female golden orb spiders are capable of producing the thread used. Each spider produced about 100 feet (30 meters) of silk per extraction session, which took approximately twenty-five minutes each. [...] Once the base fabric for the cape was woven, a team of highly skilled embroiderers spent a total of 6,000 hours adding the embroidered patterns. Peers's design for the embroidery includes scores of spiders weaving webs and floral motifs to illustrate the spiders' natural habitat

gancho: O piolho-do-corpo vive nas roupas. Comparando o DNA dele com o do piolho da cabeça, cientistas estimaram que os humanos já se vestiam entre 83 mil e 170 mil anos atrás. A data ainda é discutida.
explicacao: Como as roupas antigas se decompõem, é difícil saber quando os humanos começaram a se vestir, e as estimativas de especialistas já foram de 40 mil a 3 milhões de anos. Pesquisadores do Instituto Max Planck de Antropologia Evolutiva tentaram um caminho indireto. O piolho-do-corpo põe a maioria dos ovos nas roupas e não vive fora delas, então ele só pode ter se separado do piolho da cabeça depois que as roupas surgiram. As mutações se acumulam a um ritmo conhecido; contando as diferenças entre as duas linhagens, estima-se quando elas se separaram. Os estudos deram datas de 40 mil a 170 mil anos: um de 2003 sugeriu 107 mil, e um de 2011 apontou 170 mil como a data mais provável. Achados no Marrocos, divulgados em 2021, indicam roupas feitas de 90 mil a 120 mil anos atrás, em linha com os piolhos. Ainda assim, nenhuma estimativa é amplamente aceita. E análises mais recentes dos genes em atividade nos dois piolhos põem o método em dúvida: eles seriam quase idênticos geneticamente, e o piolho-do-corpo talvez surja de mudanças na regulação dos genes disparadas pelo ambiente.

fontes.trecho: As early clothing was biodegradable, evidence of when humans started wearing clothes, and what these clothes were made of, has been difficult for scientists to determine. The earliest dates come from studies on the evolution of clothing lice, which suggest humans were wearing clothes sometime between 83,000 and 170,000 years ago. [...] Nonetheless, scientists have never agreed on when humans began wearing clothes and the estimates suggested by various experts have ranged greatly, from 40,000 to as many as 3 million years ago. Recent studies by Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser and Mark Stoneking [...] anthropologists at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology [...] have attempted to constrain the most recent date of the introduction of clothing with an indirect method relying on lice. The rationale for this method of dating stems from the fact that the human body louse (P. humanus corporus) cannot live outside of clothing [...] This strongly implies that the date of the body louse's speciation from its parent, the human louse (Pediculus humanus), can have taken place no earlier than the earliest human adoption of clothing. [...] Such mutations occur at a known rate and the date of last-common-ancestor for two species can therefore be estimated from the difference in number of their respective mutations. These studies have produced dates ranging from 40,000 to 170,000 years ago, with a 2003 study speculating a date of 107,000 years ago, and a 2011 study confirming the most likely time of 170,000 years ago. [...] Dating with direct archeological evidence produces dates consistent with those hinted at by lice. In September 2021, scientists reported evidence of clothes being made from 90,000 to 120,000 years ago based on findings in deposits in Morocco. However, despite these archaeological indications and genetic evidence, there is no single estimate that is widely accepted.

Body lice may lay eggs on the host's hairs and clothing, but clothing is where the majority of eggs are usually secured. [...] However, recent transcriptome analyses casts doubt on whether lice provide a means to date the origin of clothes since it has found that "body and head lice were almost genetically identical. Indeed, the phenotypic flexibility associated with the emergence of body lice, is probably a result of regulatory changes, perhaps epigenetic in origin, triggered by environmental signals."

gancho: No verão de 1858, o fedor do Tâmisa invadiu o Parlamento britânico, que aprovou às pressas uma rede de esgotos. A obra partiu de uma teoria errada sobre a cólera, mas acabou com as epidemias da doença em Londres.
explicacao: Os velhos esgotos de Londres despejavam tudo direto no rio. Com a chegada das privadas com descarga e uma população que saltou de pouco menos de um milhão para três milhões, a carga só cresceu. Em junho de 1858, o calor e a seca baixaram o nível do Tâmisa e deixaram os dejetos expostos nas margens. No Parlamento, as cortinas do lado do rio foram embebidas em cloreto de cal, sem sucesso, e chegou-se a discutir a mudança dos trabalhos para Oxford ou St Albans. Segundo o jornal The Times, os deputados foram quase obrigados a legislar "pela força do puro fedor", e a lei passou em 2 de agosto. O engenheiro Joseph Bazalgette ergueu 132 km de grandes coletores e cerca de 1.800 km de esgotos de rua, que levavam os dejetos para o leste, para longe da cidade. A premissa do projeto era a teoria do miasma, segundo a qual a cólera vinha do ar fétido. Estava errada: a doença se transmite pela água. Mas, ao afastar o esgoto da água que a população consumia, a obra eliminou a cólera nas áreas atendidas. Em 1866, um último surto se concentrou numa parte do East End ainda não ligada ao sistema, onde ocorreram 93% das mortes, e isso ajudou a convencer os médicos de que a cólera vinha da água.

fontes.trecho: The Great Stink was an event in Central London during July and August 1858 in which the hot weather exacerbated the smell of untreated human waste and industrial effluent that was present on the banks of the River Thames. The problem had been mounting for several years, with an ageing and inadequate sewer system that emptied directly into the Thames. [...] The authorities accepted a proposal from the civil engineer Joseph Bazalgette to move the effluent eastwards along a series of interconnecting sewers that sloped towards outfalls beyond the metropolitan area. [...] Bazalgette's work ensured that sewage was no longer dumped onto the shores of the Thames and brought an end to the cholera outbreaks [...] This, combined with the introduction of flushing toilets and the rising of the city's population from just under one million to three million, led to more water being flushed into the sewers, along with the associated effluent. [...] Combined with an extended spell of dry weather, the level of the Thames dropped and raw effluent from the sewers remained on the banks of the river. [...] By June the stench from the river had become so bad that business in Parliament was affected, and the curtains on the river side of the building were soaked in lime chloride to overcome the smell. The measure was not successful, and discussions were held about possibly moving the business of government to Oxford or St Albans. [...] The leading article in The Times observed that "Parliament was all but compelled to legislate upon the great London nuisance by the force of sheer stench". The bill was debated in late July and was passed into law on 2 August. [...] Bazalgette's plans for the 1,100 miles (1,800 km) of additional street sewers (collecting both effluent and rainwater), which would feed into 82 miles (132 km) of main interconnecting sewers [...] In 1866 there was a further cholera outbreak in London that claimed 5,596 lives, although it was confined to an area of the East End between Aldgate and Bow. At the time that was a part of London which had not been connected to Bazalgette's system, and 93 per cent of the fatalities occurred within the area. [...] The outbreak and the diagnosis of its causes led to the acceptance that cholera was water-borne, not transmitted by miasma. [...] It was the last outbreak of the disease in the capital.

Medical opinion at the time held that cholera was caused by foul air: a so-called "miasma". [...] The basic premise of this expensive project, that miasma spreads cholera infection, was wrong. However, the new sewer system's unintended consequence was removing the causal bacterium from the water supply, thereby eliminating cholera in areas served by the sewers.

gancho: O Fórum Romano, coração da Roma antiga, foi erguido sobre um pântano aterrado e drenado pela Cloaca Máxima, um dos esgotos mais antigos do mundo. Ela ainda escoa a água da chuva do centro de Roma.
explicacao: Segundo a tradição, a obra começou por volta de 600 a.C., por ordem do rei Tarquínio Prisco, com trabalhadores etruscos e plebeus. Antes, a baixada junto ao Fórum, um terreno alagado, foi aterrada com algo entre 10 mil e 20 mil metros cúbicos de terra, cascalho e entulho. No início, a drenagem era um canal a céu aberto. À medida que o espaço dentro da cidade ficava mais valioso, ela foi sendo coberta e ampliada, até se tornar o principal esgoto de Roma. Com o tempo, a água dos aquedutos que abasteciam a cidade passou a desaguar nela, depois de correr por termas, fontes e casas, e esse fluxo contínuo ajudava a manter os canais desobstruídos. Plínio, o Velho, a tratava como uma maravilha de engenharia por resistir durante séculos a enxurradas de água suja. Havia até um pequeno santuário a Vênus Cloacina, a "Vênus do Esgoto", no Fórum. A Cloaca continuou em uso depois da queda do Império, e no século XVII um cardeal criou um imposto para pagar sua manutenção. Hoje, os trechos que restam estão ligados à rede de drenagem moderna da cidade.

fontes.trecho: is one of the world's earliest sewage systems. [...] it was constructed in Ancient Rome in order to drain local marshes and remove waste from the city. [...] It began as an open air canal, but it developed into a much larger sewer over the course of time. [...] According to tradition, it may have initially been constructed around 600 BC under the orders of the king of Rome, Tarquinius Priscus. He ordered Etruscan workers and the plebeians to construct the drainage. Before constructing the Cloaca Maxima, Priscus, and his son Tarquinius Superbus, worked to transform the land by the Roman forum from a swamp into a solid building ground, thus reclaiming the Velabrum. In order to achieve this, they filled it up with 10-20,000 cubic meters of soil, gravel, and debris. [...] As building space within the city became more valuable, the drain was gradually built over. [...] covered up and expanded into also function as the main urban sewer system. [...] The eleven aqueducts which supplied water to Rome by the 1st century AD were finally channeled into this drainage system after having supplied many of the public baths [...] as well as the public fountains, imperial palaces and private houses. The continuous supply of running water helped to remove wastes and keep the drainage system clear of obstructions. [...] even today drains rainwater and debris from the center of town, below the ancient Forum, Velabrum, and the Forum Boarium. In more recent times, the remaining passages have been connected to the modern-day urban drainage system [...] After the fall of the Roman empire the Cloaca Maxima continued to be used. In the 1600s Cardinal Chamberlain imposed a tax on residents of Rome in order to pay for the upkeep of the drainage. [...] The writer Pliny the Elder describes the Cloaca Maxima as an engineering marvel due to its ability to withstand floods of filthy waters for centuries. [...] There was a small sanctuary dedicated to Venus Cloacina (Venus of the Drain) in the Forum Romanum.

gancho: Diz-se que Paris ganhou bulevares para o exército vencer as barricadas. Haussmann usou o argumento para tirar verba do Estado, mas escreveu que nunca pensou nisso. Na revolta seguinte, os bulevares quase não pesaram.
explicacao: Entre 1830 e 1848, o centro de Paris foi palco de vários levantes armados, em ruas estreitas que os moradores fechavam com pedras arrancadas do calçamento. A reforma encomendada por Napoleão III e dirigida pelo prefeito Georges-Eugène Haussmann, de 1853 a 1870, demoliu bairros medievais e abriu avenidas largas. Críticos, de Émile Zola ao americano Lewis Mumford, disseram que o objetivo real era militar: poucos cruzamentos amplos seriam fáceis de controlar com uma tropa pequena. Haussmann não negava o valor militar das ruas novas e admitiu ter usado essa justificativa no Parlamento, para que o Estado pagasse parte da conta em nome da defesa nacional. Mas escreveu que, ao acrescentar ao plano os trechos que ele mesmo propôs, nunca pensou no valor estratégico deles, embora nas mesmas memórias comemorasse ter rasgado com o Boulevard de Sébastopol o bairro dos motins e das barricadas. O historiador Patrice de Moncan lembra que boa parte da reforma (esgotos, aquedutos, parques, hospitais e escolas) não tinha valor militar. E os primeiros grandes eixos cortaram justamente os bairros onde a cólera tinha sido pior. O único levante depois disso, a Comuna de 1871, não confirmou a tese. O exército evitou os grandes bulevares, contornou as barricadas e as tomou por trás, e os rebeldes perderam por estarem em minoria de cinco para um, com menos armas, sem comando único e sem plano de defesa.

fontes.trecho: was a vast public works programme commissioned by French Emperor Napoleon III and directed by his prefect of Seine, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, between 1853 and 1870. It included the demolition of medieval neighbourhoods that were deemed overcrowded and unhealthy by officials at the time, the building of wide avenues [...] between 1830 and 1848, seven armed uprisings and revolts had broken out in the centre of Paris [...] The residents of these neighbourhoods had taken up pavement stones and blocked the narrow streets with barricades, which had to be dislodged by the army. [...] which cut through the centre of some of the most crowded neighbourhoods in Paris, where the cholera epidemic had been the worst [...] Some of Haussmann's critics said that the real purpose of Haussmann's boulevards was to make it easier for the army to manoeuver and suppress armed uprisings [...] These critics argued that a small number of large, open intersections allowed easy control by a small force. [...] Émile Zola repeated that argument in his early novel, La Curée [...] This argument was also popularized by the American architectural critic, Lewis Mumford. Haussmann himself did not deny the military value of the wider streets. [...] He admitted he sometimes used this argument with the Parliament to justify the high cost of his projects, arguing that they were for national defence and should be paid for, at least partially, by the state. He wrote: "But, as for me, I who was the promoter of these additions made to the original project, I declare that I never thought in the least, in adding them, of their greater or lesser strategic value." [...] There was only one armed uprising in Paris after Haussmann, the Paris Commune from March through May 1871, and the boulevards played no important role. [...] But when the newly organised army arrived at the end of May, it avoided the main boulevards, advanced slowly and methodically to avoid casualties, worked its way around the barricades, and took them from behind. The Communards were defeated in one week not because of Haussmann's boulevards, but because they were outnumbered by five to one [...] As Paris historian Patrice de Moncan observed, most of Haussmann's projects had little or no strategic or military value; the purpose of building new sewers, aqueducts, parks, hospitals, schools, city halls, theatres, churches, markets and other public buildings was, as Haussmann stated, to employ thousands of workers, and to make the city more healthy [...] In his memoirs, he wrote that his new Boulevard Sébastopol resulted in the "gutting of old Paris, of the quarter of riots and barricades". [...] they had fewer weapons and fewer people trained to use them, they had no hope of getting support from outside Paris, they had no plan for the defence of the city; they had very few experienced officers; there was no single commander

gancho: Estradas e trens mais rápidos costumam não poupar tempo de deslocamento: as pessoas passam a morar mais longe. Na média geral, o total fica perto de uma hora por dia, ida e volta, a chamada constante de Marchetti.
explicacao: O nome homenageia o físico italiano Cesare Marchetti, que atribuía a observação da "uma hora" ao engenheiro de transportes Yacov Zahavi. Zahavi falava num "orçamento de tempo de viagem": uma quantidade diária de tempo, bastante estável, que as pessoas se dispõem a gastar se deslocando. Para Marchetti, mesmo quando mudam o urbanismo e os meios de transporte, as pessoas vão ajustando a vida, inclusive a distância entre a casa e o trabalho, e o tempo médio de viagem fica mais ou menos o mesmo. A ideia é antiga. Em 1934, Lewis Mumford atribuiu a Bertrand Russell a percepção de que cada avanço na locomoção ampliava a área pela qual as pessoas precisam circular: quem levava meia hora a pé até o trabalho continuaria levando meia hora, agora vindo de um bairro mais distante. David Metz, que foi cientista-chefe do Departamento de Transportes do Reino Unido, encontrou apoio para isso nos dados da pesquisa nacional de viagens britânica: o tempo poupado tende a ser reinvestido em distância. A regularidade tem críticos.
