gancho: Em 1987, a Cidade Murada de Kowloon, em Hong Kong, abrigava cerca de 33 mil pessoas em 2,6 hectares, em prédios erguidos sem fiscalização. Dava para cruzá-la de ponta a ponta pelo alto, sem tocar o chão.
explicacao: O lugar começou como posto militar chinês e virou forte em 1847. Quando a Grã-Bretanha arrendou os Novos Territórios, em 1898, o acordo deixou o forte de fora, e ele virou um enclave quase sem governo: depois da Segunda Guerra, nem britânicos nem chineses queriam assumir o controle. Refugiados da guerra civil chinesa se instalaram ali, e a partir dos anos 1960 construtores empilharam prédios novos sobre os antigos, sem supervisão de arquitetos ou engenheiros. Um dos poucos limites vinha do aeroporto de Kai Tak, a 800 metros: por causa da rota dos aviões, os prédios não passavam de 14 andares. Os becos tinham de 1 a 2 metros de largura, a luz do sol raramente chegava aos níveis de baixo e algumas ruas eram iluminadas por lâmpadas fluorescentes. Uma rede de escadas e passagens nos andares superiores permitia atravessar a cidade de norte a sul. Entre os anos 1950 e 1970, tríades controlaram bordéis, jogo e ópio, mas a maioria dos moradores vivia em paz, com pequenas fábricas e muitos médicos e dentistas sem licença. A densidade, de cerca de 1,2 milhão de habitantes por km², estava entre as maiores do planeta. A cidade foi demolida em 1993 e 1994, e no lugar surgiu um parque.

fontes.trecho: was an ungoverned and densely populated de jure Chinese enclave within the boundaries of British Hong Kong. Originally the site of a military fort, it became an enclave after the New Territories were leased to Britain in 1898. The Walled City's population increased dramatically following World War II, and by 1987 it had an estimated 33,000 residents within its 2.6-hectare (6+1⁄2-acre) borders, making it one of the most densely populated places on Earth at approximately 1.2 million inhabitants per square kilometre (3 million per square mile). The city was demolished between 1993 and 1994; the Kowloon Walled City Park was built in its place [...] was converted into a coastal fort in 1847 [...] After World War II, with both Britain and China reluctant to assert control, the city's population swelled with refugees fleeing the Chinese Civil War. This near-ungoverned state allowed it to grow into a massive squatter settlement, with unregulated construction from the 1960s onward creating a labyrinth of interconnected high-rise buildings built without architectural or engineering oversight. From the 1950s to the 1970s, the Walled City was effectively controlled by local triads, becoming a haven for prostitution, gambling, and drug trafficking. [...] The city also underwent massive construction during the 1960s, with developers building new modular structures above older ones. [...] a height restriction of 13 to 14 stories had been imposed on the city due to the flight path of planes heading toward Kai Tak Airport. [...] A few of the streets were illuminated by fluorescent lights, as sunlight rarely reached the lower levels [...] the walled city was still known for its high number of unlicensed doctors and dentists [...] Although the walled city was for many years a hotbed of criminal activity, most residents were not involved in any crime and lived peacefully within its walls. Numerous small factories and businesses thrived inside the walled city [...] However, due to Kai Tak Airport's position 800 metres (0.50 mi) south of the city, buildings did not exceed 14 storeys. [...] The city's dozens of alleyways were often only 1–2 m (3–7 ft) wide, and had poor lighting and drainage. An informal network of staircases and passageways also formed on upper levels, which was so extensive that one could travel north to south through the entire city without ever touching solid ground.

gancho: Conta-se que, na Finlândia, planejadores visitam os parques logo após a primeira neve: as pegadas mostram os atalhos que as pessoas preferem, os "caminhos do desejo", e ajudam a decidir onde abrir trilhas novas.
explicacao: Caminho do desejo é a trilha que surge sem planejamento, gasta pelo pisoteio de pessoas ou animais. Quase sempre é o trajeto mais curto ou mais fácil, e aparece quando as calçadas oficiais dão voltas, têm falhas ou não existem. Basta pouco para criá-lo: estudos de pisoteio em áreas naturais indicam que umas 15 passagens já podem marcar uma trilha visível, e uma trilha visível atrai mais gente, porque seguir um caminho aberto é mais cômodo que abrir outro. Bloquear com cercas ou placas nem sempre resolve: num caso registrado, o uso de atalhos com placa de proibição quadruplicou nos meses seguintes. Por isso, há paisagistas que preferem pavimentar os atalhos, e planejadores que deixam uma área sem caminhos de propósito, esperam as trilhas aparecerem e só depois as calçam. A neve facilita o trabalho, porque esconde as trilhas antigas e deixa à mostra só as pegadas novas. O relato finlandês circula muito em textos de urbanismo, mas não há estudo que documente a prática. Alguns caminhos do desejo viram ruas: há urbanistas que acreditam que a Broadway, em Nova York, segue uma trilha dos indígenas Wecquaesgeek, anterior à colonização. E o conceito é usado no planejamento de transportes para mapear por onde as pessoas querem ir.

fontes.trecho: A desire path (also known as desire line in transportation planning and by many other names) is an unplanned small trail formed by erosion caused by human or animal traffic. The path usually represents the shortest or the most easily navigated route through a natural area or greenspace [...] Desire paths typically emerge as convenient shortcuts where more deliberately constructed roads and footpaths take a longer or more circuitous route, have gaps, or are non-existent. Once an improvised path has been trodden out through the natural vegetation, subsequent traffic tends to follow that visibly existing route (as it is more convenient than carving out a new path by oneself) [...] Desire paths may go on to become formal trails and even established thoroughfares, such as Broadway in New York City, which some urban planners believe to follow a convenient trail developed by the Wecquaesgeek people, predating American colonization. [...] Trampling studies have consistently documented that impacts on soil and vegetation occur rapidly with initial use of desire paths. As few as 15 passages over a site can be enough to create a distinct trail, the existence of which then attracts further use. [...] Signage posted at the entrances to desire paths does not completely curb usage, with more people returning to the path over time. Between directly after the signage was posted and several months after, the usage increased four times. [...] Landscapers sometimes accommodate desire paths by paving them, thereby integrating them into the official path network rather than blocking them. Sometimes, land planners have deliberately left land fully or partially unpathed, waiting to see what desire paths are created, and then paving those. In Finland, planners are known to visit parks immediately after the first snowfall, when the existing paths are not visible. The naturally chosen desire paths, marked by footprints, can then be used to guide the routing of new purpose-built paths. [...] In transportation planning and urban planning, desire lines are used to plan road networks and to analyze traffic patterns for a given mode of travel.

gancho: A grade de ruas de Manhattan, de 1811, foi riscada sobre morros, pântanos e fazendas. Proprietários arrancavam os marcos de mármore e soltavam cães na equipe, e o agrimensor-chefe chegou a ser detido pelo xerife.
explicacao: Sem conseguir decidir o traçado por causa da política local e da resistência dos donos de terras, a Câmara de Nova York pediu ajuda ao Legislativo do estado, que em 1807 nomeou uma comissão com amplos poderes. O plano saiu em 1811. A comissão dispensou círculos e ovais, como os de L'Enfant em Washington, e ficou com retângulos, porque casas de lados retos e ângulos retos seriam "as mais baratas de construir e as mais convenientes para morar". O resultado foram cerca de 2.000 quarteirões longos e estreitos, numa grade inclinada 29 graus em relação ao norte para acompanhar a ilha. O agrimensor-chefe, John Randel Jr., tinha 20 anos ao começar. Ele foi processado por invadir terrenos, cortar galhos e pisar em plantações, e escreveu que foi detido pelo xerife em várias dessas ações. Para fixar o traçado no chão, a equipe instalou 1.549 marcos de mármore e 98 pinos de ferro, presos com chumbo derretido em buracos abertos com pólvora nas rochas. Os mapas da época mostram casas no caminho das futuras ruas. Quando os proprietários arrancavam os marcos, Randel simplesmente os recolocava. O Central Park não estava no plano: só foi imaginado nos anos 1850.

fontes.trecho: The plan originated when the Common Council of New York City, seeking to provide for the orderly development and sale of the land of Manhattan between 14th Street and Washington Heights, but unable to do so itself for reasons of local politics and objections from property owners, asked the New York State Legislature to step in. The legislature appointed a commission with sweeping powers in 1807, and their plan was presented in 1811. [...] Their chief surveyor was John Randel Jr., who was 20 years old when he began the job. [...] Central Park [...] was not a part of the plan, as it was not envisioned until the 1850s. [...] In the end, the Commission decided on the gridiron as being the most practical and cost-effective, as "straight-sided and right-angled houses are the most cheap to build and the most convenient to live in." [...] the placement of natural features such as hills, rocks, swamps, marshes, streams, and ponds, as well as man-made features such as houses, barns, stables, fences, footpaths, cleared fields and gardens. [...] Randel wrote afterwards that in the course of his work he "was arrested by the Sheriff, on numerous suits instituted ... for trespass and damage by ... workmen, in passing over grounds, cutting off branches of trees. &c., to make surveys under instructions from the Commissioners." In August 1808, Randel was sued by a landowner for trespass and causing damage to the landowner's property, such as cutting down trees and trampling on crops [...] The grid had 12 primary 100 feet (30 m) wide north–south avenues and numerous cross streets arranged in a regular right-angled grid tilted 29 degrees east of true north to roughly replicate the angle of Manhattan island. The Commission chose not to use circles and ovals such as Pierre L'Enfant had used in his design of Washington D.C. [...] resulting in a grid of approximately 2,000 long, narrow blocks. [...] The maps are replete with houses that are directly in the way of where streets were scheduled to run [...] It is no wonder why people fought back against the Commissioners' Plan, or set their dogs on Randel and his men. [...] Where rocks prevented the use of the marble markers, they blasted a hole with gunpowder, inserted six-inch-long (15 cm) iron bolts that were one inch (2.5 cm) square, and embedded them with molten lead. In all, they positioned 1,549 marble markers and 98 iron bolts to define the pattern of the grid. As Randel's work proceeded, and landowners could see for themselves, on the ground and not on a map, where the planned streets would be, some of them took action to fight against the plan, not only destroying temporary measurement pegs, but also digging up the marble markers. Randel simply replaced the pegs and the markers

gancho: A região mais populosa do Distrito Federal, Ceilândia, tem nome de sigla: CEI, de Campanha de Erradicação das Invasões. Foi criada em 1971 para levar para longe do centro de Brasília os moradores de favelas.
explicacao: Pelos planos originais, Brasília seria uma cidade de autoridades e funcionários do governo, e o Plano Piloto foi pensado para cerca de 500 mil habitantes. Mas, já durante a construção, gente de todo o país migrou para as cidades-satélite atrás de emprego. Em 1969, com só nove anos de existência, o Distrito Federal tinha cerca de 79 mil pessoas em ocupações irregulares perto do centro, onde a maioria delas trabalhava. O governador Hélio Prates pediu a erradicação das invasões, criou-se uma campanha, presidida pela primeira-dama, e foram demarcados mais de 17 mil lotes ao norte de Taguatinga, em terras de uma antiga fazenda. Os lotes receberiam moradores de vilas e morros que somavam mais de 15 mil barracos e mais de 80 mil pessoas. Em 27 de março de 1971, as primeiras vinte famílias foram assentadas. O nome juntou a sigla CEI ao sufixo "-lândia", que estava na moda. O contraste ficou: o Plano Piloto nunca chegou aos 500 mil moradores previstos e tem pouco mais de 200 mil, enquanto Ceilândia sozinha tinha 350.347 em 2021.

fontes.trecho: Ceilândia é uma região administrativa do Distrito Federal brasileiro. Está localizada na porção oeste do DF, de cujo território é a subdivisão mais populosa, contando com 350.347 habitantes, de acordo a Pesquisa Distrital por Amostra de Domicílios (PDAD) divulgada, pela então Companhia de Planejamento do Distrito Federal (Codeplan), no ano de 2021. [...] Em 1969, com apenas nove anos de fundação, o Distrito Federal já tinha 79 128 habitantes em ocupações irregulares, que moravam em aglomerados próximos ao centro da capital, local de trabalho da maioria dessas pessoas [...] Reconhecendo a gravidade do problema e suas consequências, o governador Hélio Prates da Silveira solicitou a erradicação das invasões à Secretaria de Serviços Sociais [...] Foi criada, então, a "Campanha de Erradicação das Invasões" (CEI, donde "Ceilândia"), presidida pela então primeira-dama, dona Vera de Almeida Silveira. Em 1971, já estavam demarcados 17 619 lotes [...] Os lotes ficavam ao norte de Taguatinga, nas antigas terras da Fazenda Guariroba. [...] invasões com mais de 15 mil barracos e mais de 80 mil moradores. [...] Às 9 horas do mesmo dia, tinha início o processo de assentamento das vinte primeiras famílias da invasão do IAPI. Ceilândia foi fundada em 27 de março de 1971 [...] conferiu à nova localidade o nome de Ceilândia, inspirado na sigla "CEI" e na palavra inglesa "lândia" (o sufixo estava na moda).

The city of Brasília proper, the plano piloto was planned for about 500,000 inhabitants, a figure the plano piloto never surpassed, with a current population of only 214,529 [...] According to the original plans, Brasília would be a city for government authorities and staff. However, during its construction, Brazilians from all over the country migrated to the satellite cities of Brasília, seeking public and private employment.

gancho: A teoria das janelas quebradas tem um lado com apoio experimental: na Holanda, lixo e pichação levaram mais gente a furtar. Já a ideia de que reprimir pequenos delitos derrubou o crime em Nova York é contestada.
explicacao: A teoria foi lançada em 1982 pelos cientistas sociais James Q. Wilson e George Kelling: uma janela quebrada e não consertada é sinal de que ninguém se importa, e quebrar as outras passa a não custar nada. Um ambiente descuidado indicaria pouca vigilância e convidaria a delitos maiores. Nos anos 1990, William Bratton, chefe de polícia de Nova York, aplicou a ideia endurecendo contra calote no metrô, bebida e urina em público e pichação. Parte da teoria tem apoio em experimentos. Em 2007 e 2008, pesquisadores da Universidade de Groningen montaram locais urbanos com e sem desordem visível e observaram em segredo o comportamento das pessoas: a desordem levou a mais infrações, resultado publicado na revista Science. Em Lowell, nos EUA, limpar e consertar pontos críticos reduziu em 20% as chamadas à polícia, e o estudo concluiu que arrumar o ambiente funcionou melhor que prender por contravenções. Já a queda do crime em Nova York tem outras explicações possíveis: ela começou antes, sob o prefeito anterior, também ocorreu em cidades com políticas diferentes e coincidiu com uma forte queda do desemprego. E um estudo de 2017 viu que, quando a polícia da cidade reduziu a repressão a delitos menores, as queixas de alguns crimes graves caíram levemente.

fontes.trecho: In criminology, the broken windows theory states that visible signs of crime, antisocial behavior and civil disorder create an urban environment that encourages further crime and disorder, including serious crimes. [...] The theory was introduced in an article started in 1981 and published in 1982 by social scientists James Q. Wilson and George L. Kelling. [...] one un-repaired broken window is a signal that no one cares, and so breaking more windows costs nothing. [...] Conversely, a disordered environment, one that is not maintained (broken windows, graffiti, excessive litter), sends the signal that the area is not monitored and that criminal behavior has little risk of detection. [...] In particular, Bratton directed beat officers to more strictly enforce laws against petty offenses like subway fare evasion, public drinking, public urination, and graffiti. [...] However, other studies do not find a causal relationship between the adoption of such policies and decreases in crime. The decrease may have been part of a broader trend across the United States. The rates of most crimes, including all categories of violent crime, made consecutive declines from their peak in 1990, under Giuliani's predecessor, David Dinkins. Other cities also experienced less crime, even though they had different police policies. Other factors, such as the 39% drop in New York City's unemployment rate between 1992 and 1999, could also explain the decrease reported by Kelling and Sousa. A 2017 study found that when the NYPD stopped aggressively enforcing minor legal statutes in late 2014 and early 2015 that civilian complaints of the major crimes of burglary, felony assault, and grand larceny, decreased slightly with large error bars [...] In 2005, Harvard University and Suffolk University researchers worked with local police to identify 34 "crime hot spots" in Lowell, Massachusetts. [...] The areas that received additional attention experienced a 20% reduction in calls to the police. The study concluded that cleaning up the physical environment was more effective than misdemeanor arrests. [...] In 2007 and 2008, Kees Keizer and colleagues from the University of Groningen conducted a series of controlled experiments [...] The researchers then secretly monitored the locations to observe if people behaved differently when the environment was "disordered". Their observations supported the theory. The conclusion was published in the journal Science: "One example of disorder, like graffiti or littering, can indeed encourage another, like stealing."

gancho: A implosão do conjunto habitacional Pruitt-Igoe (EUA), em 1972, virou "o dia em que a arquitetura moderna morreu". Mas a culpa não foi só do projeto: a cidade perdeu 30% dos moradores e a manutenção vivia dos aluguéis.
explicacao: O conjunto, em St. Louis, recebeu os primeiros moradores em 1954: 33 prédios de 11 andares, 2.870 apartamentos e mais de 10 mil pessoas, com projeto do arquiteto Minoru Yamasaki. De início, foi visto como um avanço, e uma moradora chamou seu apartamento no 11º andar de "cobertura de pobre". Em quatro anos, porém, já havia elevadores quebrados e vandalismo, e as escadas viraram ponto de assaltos, em parte porque os elevadores só paravam em alguns andares. Em 1970, mais de dois terços do conjunto estavam vazios. Depois da demolição televisionada, o crítico Charles Jencks a tratou como a morte da arquitetura moderna. Só que muitas escolhas vieram do governo federal, que, para cortar custos, impôs a altura única de 11 andares no lugar da mistura de prédios proposta por Yamasaki, e o paisagismo saiu do plano. A lei obrigava a autoridade de habitação a pagar as despesas com o aluguel. E St. Louis, que esperava chegar a 1 milhão de habitantes, perdeu 30% da população para os subúrbios. Com menos inquilinos, a receita caiu, a manutenção foi cortada e o conjunto ficou ainda menos procurado. Para a revista The Architectural Review, o consenso atual é que o conjunto, sem verba suficiente, estava "condenado desde o início".

fontes.trecho: were joint urban housing projects first occupied in 1954 in St. Louis, Missouri, United States. The complex of 33 eleven-story high rises was designed in the modernist architectural style by Minoru Yamasaki. [...] and by 1970 more than two-thirds of the complex was vacant. Demolition of the complex began in 1972 with a televised implosion of several of the buildings. [...] Critic Charles Jencks described its demolition as "the day Modern architecture died". [...] The Architectural Review states in a summary of the modern consensus that the project was "doomed from the outset". [...] The complex totaled 2,870 apartments (1,736 in Pruitt and 1,132 in Igoe) housing more than 10,000 people at full occupancy. [...] "Skip-stop" elevators stopped only at the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth "anchor" floors in an attempt to lessen elevator congestion, forcing many residents to use the stairs. [...] His initial proposal, which included walk-up and mid-rise buildings as well as high-rises, was accepted by the St. Louis authorities, but exceeded the federal cost limits imposed by the Public Housing Administration; the agency intervened and imposed a uniform building height of 11 floors. [...] landscaping was omitted from the final plan and few trees were planted. [...] One early resident described her 11th floor apartment as a "poor man's penthouse". [...] By 1958, just four years after the opening of the project, deteriorating conditions were already evident. Elevator breakdowns and vandalism were cited as major problems [...] The stairwells and corridors attracted muggers, a situation exacerbated by the skip-stop elevators. [...] Increasing vacancy rates set off a feedback loop where the loss of revenue from rent forced the housing authority to curtail maintenance, further reducing the project's desirability. [...] The steep fall in St. Louis's population exacerbated the project's vacancy problem—instead of growing from 850,000 in the 1940s to 1 million in 1970 as projected, the city lost 30 percent of its residents in that timespan due to suburbanization and white flight [...] in particular the requirement of the Housing Act of 1949 that local housing authorities pay their expenses from rental income, which made them vulnerable to fiscal problems.

gancho: Na Roma antiga, morar no alto era coisa de pobre: nos prédios de aluguel, que chegavam a nove andares, os de cima eram os mais baratos, por causa das escadas e do risco de incêndio e desabamento.
explicacao: Esses prédios, as ínsulas, abrigavam a maior parte da população urbana de Roma, que no início do Império ficava entre 800 mil e 1 milhão de pessoas. O térreo era ocupado por lojas e oficinas, e as moradias ficavam acima. Os apartamentos maiores e mais caros estavam nos andares de baixo, e os menores, no alto. Muitos prédios eram erguidos com o mínimo de gasto, para especulação, em madeira, tijolo e mais tarde concreto, e o poeta satírico Juvenal descreveu como pegavam fogo e desabavam. Os donos costumavam ser romanos ricos, muitas vezes senadores, e um prédio podia ter vários donos: Cícero tinha um oitavo de uma ínsula. Para reduzir o perigo, o imperador Augusto limitou a altura a 70 pés romanos, cerca de 20,7 metros, e Trajano baixou o limite para 60 pés, cerca de 17,75 metros. Um catálogo do século IV registra entre 42 mil e 46 mil ínsulas na cidade, contra cerca de 1.790 casas unifamiliares da elite no fim do século III. A única ínsula que resta em Roma tem cinco andares e fica ao pé do monte Capitolino.

fontes.trecho: Insulae housed most of the urban citizen population of ancient Rome's massive population ranging from 800,000 to 1 million inhabitants in the early imperial period. [...] The ground-level floor of the insula was used for tabernae, shops and businesses, with living spaces above. [...] The owners of these buildings were typically wealthy Romans, often senators and those of similar rank. It was also possible for an insula to be owned by several people, such as Cicero, who owned a one-eighth share of an insula [...] but this type of housing was sometimes constructed at minimal expense for speculative purposes, resulting in insulae of poor construction. They were built in timber, brick, and later Roman concrete, and were prone to fire and collapse, as described by Juvenal, the Roman satirist. [...] Living quarters were typically the smallest in the building's uppermost floors, with the largest and most expensive apartments being located on the bottom floors. The insulae could be built up to nine storeys, before Augustus introduced a height limit of about 70 Roman feet (20.7 m). [...] The only surviving insula in Rome is the five-storey Insula dell'Ara Coeli dating from the 2nd century AD, which is found at the foot of the Capitoline Hill. Because of safety issues and extra flights of stairs, the uppermost floors of insulae were the least desirable, and thus the cheapest to rent. [...] Emperor Trajan reduced the height to 60 Roman feet (17.75 m). According to the 4th-century Regionary catalogues, there were about 42,000–46,000 insulae in the city, as compared to about 1,790 domus in the late 3rd century.

gancho: Depois do Grande Incêndio de 1666, Wren, Hooke e outros propuseram refazer Londres em grade. Nenhum plano vingou: redesenhar os lotes de cada dono era inviável, e a cidade voltou a crescer sobre o traçado medieval.
explicacao: O fogo de 1666 destruiu mais de 13 mil casas no centro de Londres, a City, que antes já era um amontoado de construções de madeira sem planejamento. O rei Carlos II incentivou projetos ousados de reconstrução, e além de Christopher Wren e do memorialista John Evelyn, Robert Hooke e outros apresentaram planos, todos baseados numa grade de ruas. O problema era a propriedade: o plano de Wren exigia redefinir os títulos de cada terreno. A Coroa e a cidade tentaram negociar indenizações para uma reforma tão grande, mas a ideia era irrealista e foi abandonada. Pedidos para que os donos levassem trabalhadores e medissem seus antigos lotes foram ignorados por quem lutava para sobreviver, e faltava mão de obra. Para agilizar, um Tribunal do Fogo decidia as disputas entre inquilinos e proprietários, em geral em um único dia. Londres foi refeita sobre o essencial do traçado medieval, que existe até hoje, mas com mudanças: ruas mais largas, cais livres ao longo do Tâmisa e prédios de tijolo e pedra, pois uma lei de 1666 proibiu a madeira nas fachadas. Um imposto sobre o carvão ajudou a pagar a obra.

fontes.trecho: Various schemes for rebuilding the city were proposed, some of them radical. After the fire, London was reconstructed on essentially the same medieval street plan, which still exists today. [...] called it a "wooden, northern, and inartificial congestion of Houses". By "inartificial", Evelyn meant unplanned and makeshift, the result of organic growth and unregulated urban sprawl. [...] The aim of the court, which was authorised by the Fire of London Disputes Act 1666 and the Rebuilding of London Act 1670, was to deal with disputes between tenants and landlords and decide who should rebuild, based on ability to pay. Cases were heard and a verdict usually given within a day [...] Radical rebuilding schemes poured in for the gutted City and were encouraged by Charles. Apart from Wren and Evelyn, it is known that Robert Hooke, Valentine Knight, and Richard Newcourt proposed rebuilding plans. All were based on a grid system [...] Wren's plan was particularly challenging to implement because of the need to redefine property titles. The Crown and the City authorities attempted to negotiate compensation for the large-scale remodelling that these plans entailed, but that unrealistic idea had to be abandoned. Exhortations to bring workmen and measure the plots on which the houses had stood were mostly ignored by people worried about day-to-day survival, as well as by those who had left the capital; for one thing, with the shortage of labour following the fire, it was impossible to secure workmen for the purpose. Instead, much of the old street plan was recreated in the new City. [...] The reconstruction saw improvements in hygiene and fire safety: wider streets, open and accessible wharves along the length of the Thames, with no houses obstructing access to the river, and, most importantly, buildings constructed of brick and stone, not wood. The Rebuilding of London Act 1666 banned wood from the exterior of buildings [...] A duty was imposed on coal to support civic rebuilding costs. [...] Approximately 9,000 new houses were built in the area in which over 13,000 had been destroyed

gancho: A diferença de temperatura entre a cidade e o campo em volta costuma ser maior à noite: o concreto guarda o calor do dia e o solta depois. E esse calor urbano pode fazer chover mais do lado para onde sopra o vento.
explicacao: O fenômeno se chama ilha de calor urbana, e a causa principal é a troca da vegetação e do solo por superfícies construídas. Durante o dia, sobretudo com céu limpo, ruas, telhados e paredes absorvem a radiação do sol e esquentam mais depressa que o campo. Por terem alta capacidade térmica, funcionam como um reservatório: o concreto pode guardar cerca de 2.000 vezes mais calor que o mesmo volume de ar. À noite, sem o sol, o ar sobre a cidade se estabiliza, pode se formar uma camada de inversão, e o ar junto ao chão continua sendo aquecido pelas superfícies ainda quentes. Prédios altos pioram o quadro, porque multiplicam as superfícies que absorvem luz e bloqueiam o vento que ajudaria a resfriar. Por isso a ilha de calor é mais perigosa nas ondas de calor: tira dos moradores o alívio noturno que o campo tem. O calor extra também empurra o ar para cima, o que pode provocar pancadas de chuva e tempestades, e, durante o dia, a baixa pressão criada sobre a cidade atrai ar úmido das áreas rurais. Em parte por isso, a chuva mensal costuma ser maior do lado para onde o vento leva o ar da cidade do que do lado de onde ele vem. Árvores, telhados verdes e superfícies claras ajudam a amenizar o efeito.

fontes.trecho: The temperature difference is usually larger at night than during the day [...] The main cause of the UHI effect is from the modification of land surfaces [...] Monthly rainfall is greater downwind of cities, partially due to the UHI. [...] Heat can be reduced by tree cover and green space [...] Other options include green roofs, passive daytime radiative cooling applications, ventilation corridors, the use of lighter-colored surfaces [...] Throughout the daytime, particularly when the skies are cloudless, urban surfaces are warmed by the absorption of solar radiation. Surfaces in the urban areas tend to warm faster than those of the surrounding rural areas. By virtue of their high heat capacities, urban surfaces act as a reservoir of heat energy. For example, concrete can hold roughly 2,000 times as much heat as an equivalent volume of air. [...] At night, the situation reverses. The absence of solar heating leads to the decrease of atmospheric convection and the stabilization of urban boundary layer. If enough stabilization occurs, an inversion layer is formed. This traps urban air near the surface, keeping surface air warm from the still-warm urban surfaces, resulting in warmer nighttime air temperatures within the UHI. [...] The tall buildings within many urban areas provide multiple surfaces for the reflection and absorption of sunlight, increasing the efficiency with which urban areas are heated. [...] Another effect of buildings is the blocking of wind, which also inhibits cooling by convection [...] The extra heat provided by the UHI leads to greater upward motion, which can induce additional shower and thunderstorm activity. In addition, the UHI creates during the day a local low pressure area where relatively moist air from its rural surroundings converges [...] The nighttime effect of UHIs can be particularly harmful during a heat wave, as it deprives urban residents of the cool relief found in rural areas during the night.

gancho: Os mercadores antigos não conheciam a "Rota da Seda": o nome foi popularizado em 1877 por um geógrafo alemão. E há historiadores que o acham enganoso, porque para Roma as especiarias do Índico pesavam mais que a seda.
explicacao: A rede de caminhos que ligava a China ao Ocidente funcionou do século II a.C. até meados do século XV e somava mais de 6.400 km só por terra. Durante quase toda essa história, ela não teve um nome próprio. A expressão vem do alemão Seidenstraße, que o barão Ferdinand von Richthofen, autor de sete expedições à China entre 1868 e 1872, tornou conhecida em 1877, embora o termo já aparecesse décadas antes. Mesmo assim, ele só pegou no século XX: o primeiro livro chamado "A Rota da Seda" saiu em 1938, escrito pelo sueco Sven Hedin, que tinha sido aluno de Richthofen. Não era uma estrada única. Nas rotas terrestres, predominava o comércio de revezamento, e as mercadorias mudavam de mão muitas vezes até o destino final. Por isso, parte dos historiadores prefere falar em "Rotas da Seda". O historiador Warwick Ball vai além e chama a ideia de "mito" da academia moderna: para a economia do Império Romano, o comércio marítimo de especiarias com a Índia e a Arábia teria importado muito mais que a seda chinesa. Ele lembra ainda que autores clássicos do comércio entre Oriente e Ocidente, como Marco Polo, nunca chamaram rota nenhuma de "da seda".

fontes.trecho: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. Spanning over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land [...] The name "Silk Road" was coined in the late 19th century, but some 20th- and 21st-century historians instead prefer the term Silk Routes [...] It derives from the German term Seidenstraße (literally "Silk Road") and was first popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen, who made seven expeditions to China from 1868 to 1872. However, the term itself had been in use in decades prior to that. [...] it did not gain widespread acceptance in academia or popularity among the public until the 20th century. The first book entitled The Silk Road was by Swedish geographer Sven Hedin in 1938. [...] Warwick Ball contends that the maritime spice trade with India and Arabia was far more consequential for the economy of the Roman Empire than the silk trade with China [...] Going as far as to call the whole thing a "myth" of modern academia [...] traditional authors discussing east–west trade such as Marco Polo and Edward Gibbon never labelled any route a "silk" one in particular. [...] Merchants along these routes were involved in "relay trade" in which goods changed "hands many times before reaching their final destinations". [...] Like the overland routes, the ancient maritime routes through Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean had no particular name for the majority of its very long history.
He is noted for coining the terms "Seidenstraße" and "Seidenstraßen" = "Silk Road(s)" or "Silk Route(s)" in 1877. [...] Among his most famous students was Sven Hedin, the Swedish explorer.

gancho: A Liga Hanseática, rede de cidades mercantes que saqueou Copenhague e enquadrou o rei da Dinamarca, nunca foi fundada nem dissolvida. A última reunião, em 1669, ninguém sabia que seria a última.
explicacao: "Hansa" era a palavra do alto-alemão antigo para bando ou tropa. A liga nasceu de associações de mercadores alemães e chegou a reunir um rol flexível de 70 a 170 cidades, que dominavam o comércio marítimo nos mares do Norte e Báltico. Mantinha entrepostos, os Kontore, em Londres, Bruges, Bergen e Novgorod, com grande autonomia jurídica; o de Londres, o Steelyard, virou um bairro murado com armazéns, igreja e casas. A liga também fazia guerra: entre 1361 e 1370, cidades aliadas lutaram contra a Dinamarca, saquearam Copenhague e Helsingborg e, pelo Tratado de Stralsund, arrancaram do rei dinamarquês isenções de impostos e influência sobre fortalezas do estreito de Øresund por 15 anos. Mesmo assim, nunca houve ato de fundação, e por isso a liga não tem data de nascimento. As assembleias eram irregulares, e muitas cidades nem mandavam representantes. O fim também veio sem anúncio. Em 1666, o Steelyard queimou no Grande Incêndio de Londres, e o pedido de ajuda para reconstruí-lo levou a uma Dieta Hanseática em 1669. Poucas cidades foram, quase ninguém quis pagar, e aquela foi a última reunião formal, sem que nenhum dos presentes soubesse disso. A liga nunca foi dissolvida oficialmente: simplesmente se desfez em silêncio.

fontes.trecho: During its time, the Hanseatic League dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas. It established a network of trading posts in numerous towns and cities, notably the Kontors in London (known as the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod, which became extraterritorial entities that enjoyed considerable legal autonomy. [...] Hansa is the Old High German word for a band or troop. [...] As the Hanseatic League was never formally founded, it lacks a date of foundation. [...] The network of alliances grew to include a flexible roster of 70 to 170 cities. [...] It grew into a walled community with its warehouses, weigh house, church, offices, and homes. [...] Assemblies of the Hanse towns met irregularly in Lübeck for a Hansetag (Hanseatic Diet) [...] Many towns chose not to attend nor to send repre [...] Between 1361 and 1370, League members fought against Denmark in the Danish-Hanseatic War. [...] sacked Copenhagen and Helsingborg, and forced Valdemar IV, King of Denmark, and his son-in-law Haakon VI, King of Norway, to grant tax exemptions and influence over Øresund fortresses for 15 years in the peace treaty of Stralsund in 1370. [...] In 1666, the Steelyard burned in the Great Fire of London. The Kontor-manager sent a letter to Lübeck appealing for immediate financial assistance for a reconstruction. Hamburg, Bremen, and Lübeck called for a Hanseatic Day in 1669. Only a few cities participated and those who came were reluctant to contribute financially to the reconstruction. It was the last formal meeting, unbeknownst to any of the parties. This date is often taken in retrospect as the effective end date of the Hansa, but the league never formally disbanded. It silently disintegrated.

gancho: Heródoto descreveu um comércio sem palavras: cartagineses deixavam mercadorias numa praia e voltavam aos navios; os nativos punham ouro ao lado e se afastavam, até os dois lados ficarem satisfeitos.
explicacao: O relato está no livro IV das Histórias, e Heródoto o atribui aos próprios cartagineses. Num lugar da Líbia, além das Colunas de Hércules, eles descarregavam a carga, a arrumavam em ordem na praia, voltavam a bordo e acendiam um fogo que fazia fumaça. Ao ver o sinal, os habitantes desciam ao mar, deixavam ouro como pagamento e se retiravam. Os cartagineses desembarcavam e avaliavam: se o ouro parecesse um preço justo, levavam-no e iam embora; se não, voltavam aos navios e esperavam que mais ouro fosse acrescentado. Segundo o relato, ninguém enganava ninguém: um lado não tocava no ouro antes de ele valer a carga, e o outro não tocava nas mercadorias antes de o ouro ser recolhido. A prática ganhou o nome de comércio silencioso ou escambo mudo. A ideia por trás dela é engenhosa: permitia negociar sem falar a mesma língua e talvez ajudasse a guardar o segredo de onde vinha o ouro.

fontes.titulo: Heródoto, Histórias 4.196 (trad. A. D. Godley, Perseus Digital Library)
fontes.trecho: Another story is told by the Carthaginians. There is a place in Libya, they say, where men live beyond the Pillars of Heracles; they come here and unload their cargo; then, having laid it in order along the beach, they go aboard their ships and light a smoking fire. The people of the country see the smoke, and, coming to the sea, they lay down gold to pay for the cargo, and withdraw from the wares. [2] Then the Carthaginians disembark and examine the gold; if it seems to them a fair price for their cargo, they take it and go away; but if not, they go back aboard and wait, and the people come back and add more gold until the sailors are satisfied. [3] In this transaction, it is said, neither party defrauds the other: the Carthaginians do not touch the gold until it equals the value of their cargo, nor do the people touch the cargo until the sailors have taken the gold.

Silent trade, also called silent barter, dumb barter ("dumb" here used in its old meaning of "mute"), or depot trade, is a method by which traders who cannot speak each other's language can trade without talking. [...] This system was used in many parts of ancient Africa. [...] In West Africa gold mined south of the Sahel was traded for salt mined in the desert. [...] The communication in this gold-for-salt was carried out using drums. Silent trade might be used because of an inability to speak the other traders' language, or to protect the secrets of where the valuable gold and salt came from.

gancho: No meio do Saara havia uma cidade de sal: as casas eram feitas de blocos de sal e cobertas com couro de camelo. Ibn Battuta achou o lugar imundo, mas viu muito ouro em pó mudar de mãos ali.
explicacao: Taghaza, hoje uma ruína no norte do Mali, foi até o fim do século XVI uma fonte importante de sal-gema para a África Ocidental e peça do comércio através do Saara. Por volta de 1275, o geógrafo al-Qazwini, com base no relato de um viajante, escreveu que as muralhas, as paredes e os telhados de lá eram de sal. O marroquino Ibn Battuta chegou em 1352, depois de 25 dias de viagem desde Sijilmasa. Não havia árvores, só areia e minas, e ali viviam apenas escravizados que cavavam o sal e se alimentavam de tâmaras, carne de camelo e milhete trazidos de longe. O sal era cortado em placas grossas, duas por camelo, e levado para o sul. Quem fazia o preço era sobretudo o transporte: segundo Ibn Battuta, o valor quadruplicava entre Oualata e a capital do Mali. Ele reclamou da água salobra e das moscas, mas anotou que, apesar da miséria, se negociavam ali quintais de ouro em pó. As minas eram tão cobiçadas que viraram pretexto de guerra. O sultão marroquino Ahmad al-Mansur exigiu do Império Songhai os impostos de Taghaza e, diante da recusa, mandou um exército de 4 mil mercenários atravessar o Saara. A derrota songhai em Tondibi, em 1591, levou ao colapso do império, e Taghaza foi abandonada.

fontes.trecho: Taghaza (Arabic: تاغزة) or Teghaza is an abandoned salt-mining centre located in a salt pan in the desert region of northern Mali. It was an important source of rock salt for West Africa up to the end of the 16th century [...] Salt from the Taghaza mines formed an important part of the long distance trans-Saharan trade. [...] The Taghaza mines are first mentioned by name (as Taghara) in around 1275 by the geographer al Qazwini who spent most of his life in Iraq but obtained information from a traveller who had visited the Sudan. He wrote that the town was situated south of the Maghreb near the ocean and that the ramparts, walls and roofs of the buildings were made of salt [...] In 1352, the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta arrived in Taghaza after a 25-day journey from Sijilmasa [...] According to Ibn Battuta, there were no trees, only sand and the salt mines. Nobody lived in the village other than the Musafa slaves who dug for the salt and lived on dates imported from Sijilmasa and the Dar'a valley, camel meat, and millet imported from the Sudan. The buildings were constructed from slabs of salt and roofed with camel skins. The salt was dug from the ground and cut into thick slabs, two of which were loaded onto each camel. The salt was taken south across the desert to Oualata and sold. The value of the salt was chiefly determined by the transport costs. Ibn Battuta mentions that the value increased fourfold when transported between Oualata and the Malian capital. In spite of the meanness of the village, it was awash in Malian gold. Ibn Battuta did not enjoy his visit; he found the water brackish and the village full of flies. He goes on to say, "For all its squalor, qintars of gold dust are traded in Taghaza." [...] On his succession in 1578 Ahmad al-Mansur asked for the tax revenues from Taghaza [...] a new demand by Ahmad al-Mansur in 1589–90 was met with defiance by Askiya Ishak II. This provided the pretext for Ahmad al-Mansur to send an army of 4,000 mercenaries across the Sahara led by the Spaniard Judar Pasha. The defeat of the Songhai in 1591 at the Battle of Tondibi led to the collapse of their empire. After the conquest Taghaza was abandoned

gancho: Por volta de 830, um navio árabe costurado com corda de coco, sem pregos, afundou na Indonésia com cerca de 60 mil peças chinesas. Parte delas trazia motivos persas e inscrições do Corão, pensadas para outros mercados.
explicacao: Pescadores acharam os restos em 1998, a 17 metros de profundidade, perto da ilha de Belitung. O navio, um dhow de cerca de 18 metros, tinha feito a ida da Arábia até a China e afundou na volta. É o primeiro navio árabe antigo encontrado e escavado, e as tábuas eram costuradas com uma corda fina de fibra de coco, e não presas com pinos ou pregos. Um texto chinês do fim da dinastia Tang já falava de navios de mercadores estrangeiros costurados com fibra de palmeira. A carga é a maior coleção de objetos da dinastia Tang encontrada fora da China. A maior parte das 60 mil peças eram tigelas de Changsha, embaladas em cilindros de palha ou em jarros. Uma delas tem a data de 826 escrita, confirmada pela datação por radiocarbono de anis-estrelado que estava a bordo. Os desenhos revelam vários mercados: lótus budistas, motivos da Ásia Central e da Pérsia, inscrições do Corão e tigelas salpicadas de verde que faziam sucesso no Irã. Havia também os mais antigos pratos azul e branco intactos de que se tem notícia. Arqueólogos criticaram a escavação como comercial e apressada demais, e o Smithsonian adiou em 2011 uma exposição do tesouro.

fontes.trecho: The Belitung shipwreck (also called the Tang shipwreck or Batu Hitam shipwreck) is the wreck of an Arabian dhow that sank around 830 AD. The ship completed its outward journey from Arabia to China but sank on the return voyage from China [...] the largest single collection of Tang dynasty artefacts found outside China [...] The wreck was discovered by local fishermen in 1998 in the Gelasa Strait, at a depth of 17 metres (56 ft). [...] The shipwrecked dhow was approximately 6.4 metres (21 ft) wide and 18 metres (58 ft) long and is notable for two reasons: it is the first ancient Arabian ship to be found and excavated, and its planks were sewn together using a thin rope made of coconut fibers, rather than the traditional pegs or nails used in Arabia in later centuries. [...] this text "describes the ships of foreign merchants as being stitched together with the fiber of coir-palms and having their seams caulked rather than using iron nails to secure their planks." [...] Changsha ware (produced in kilns in Tongguan), which made up the majority of the 60,000 items and was originally packed in either straw cylinders or "Dusun" storage jars; white ware, manufactured in the Ding kilns, which included the earliest known intact underglaze blue and white dishes [...] or 826 AD, a date later confirmed by radiocarbon dating of star anise found among the wreckage. The cargo showed a variety of influences and markets, featuring designs such as Buddhist lotus symbols, motifs from Central Asia and Persia, Koranic inscriptions, and green-splashed bowls popular in Iran. [...] on June 28, 2011, it was reported that the museum had postponed the exhibition. [...] Critics argued that the excavation was commercially motivated and conducted so rapidly that significant information about the crew and cargo may have been lost.

gancho: Um navio que afundou na Turquia por volta de 1320 a.C. levava cobre e estanho para fazer 11 toneladas de bronze. Análises mostraram que parte do estanho vinha de onde hoje ficam o Tajiquistão ou o Uzbequistão.
explicacao: O naufrágio de Uluburun foi encontrado em 1982 por um mergulhador que pescava esponjas, Mehmed Çakir, que descreveu ter visto "biscoitos de metal com orelhas": eram lingotes de cobre no formato de couro de boi. A escavação, de 1984 a 1994, somou 22.413 mergulhos. O barco, de uns 15 metros, levava mais de 20 toneladas de carga, com mercadorias de pelo menos sete regiões. Havia 354 lingotes de cobre, cerca de 10 toneladas, e cerca de 1 tonelada de estanho. Na proporção de 9 para 1, dariam 11 toneladas de bronze, o bastante para forjar quase 5 mil espadas. Que o cobre vinha de Chipre já se sabia. O estanho era um mistério até 2022, quando a sua composição química e isotópica foi comparada com a de jazidas das ilhas Britânicas à Ásia Central: cerca de 65% vinha de Kestel, nos montes Tauro, na Turquia, e cerca de 30% da jazida de Mušiston, no Tajiquistão, ou do leste do Uzbequistão, um estanho em geral de melhor qualidade. A bordo havia ainda lingotes de vidro azul-cobalto, que lembravam o lápis-lazúli, ébano da África Oriental, marfim e um escaravelho de ouro com o nome da rainha egípcia Nefertiti.

fontes.trecho: The sunken ship, approximately 15 meters long and carrying a cargo of over 20 tons [...] The shipwreck was discovered in the summer of 1982 by Mehmed Çakir, a local sponge diver from Yalıkavak [...] The shipwreck site was discovered in the summer of 1982 due to Mehmet Çakir's sketching of "the metal biscuits with ears" recognized as oxhide ingots. [...] Eleven consecutive campaigns of three to four months' duration took place from 1984 to 1994 totaling 22,413 dives [...] The most likely date of the sinking of the ship was rounded up to 1320±15 years. [...] "goods from at least seven different areas." [...] 354 ingots of copper (approximately 10 tons) [...] ingots of tin (approximately 1 ton), tin and copper being the constituents of bronze [...] With them, 11 tons of high quality bronze with a copper/tin ratio of 9 to 1 could be melted. This quantity would have been enough, for example, to forge almost 5,000 swords. The Cypriot origin of the copper has long been known (due to the isotopic composition of its lead, and from texts of the period), but that of the tin had remained a mystery. In 2022, its chemical composition (particularly its tellurium and lead content) and isotopic composition (tin and lead isotopes) were compared to those of all known tin sources from the British Isles to Central Asia. Approximately 65% of the tin originates from the Kestel archaeological site, located in the Taurus Mountains in present-day Turkey [...] Approximately 30% comes from the Mušiston deposit (Tajikistan) or eastern Uzbekistan, generally better quality tin, which explains why it traveled such a long distance. [...] the cobalt blue ingots are similar to those discovered at Tell el-Amarna in Egypt. They were prized in this country because their color is reminiscent of lapis lazuli [...] It is a product originating in East Africa [...] elephant ivory, hippopotamus teeth [...] a gold scarab (amulet) bearing the name of the Egyptian queen Nefertiti

gancho: Por 250 anos, galeões espanhóis cruzaram o Pacífico entre Manila e Acapulco levando seda e porcelana chinesas em troca de prata. A rota passava logo ao sul do Havaí, e não há registro de contato com os havaianos.
explicacao: A linha começou em 1565, quando o frade agostiniano e navegador Andrés de Urdaneta abriu o tornaviaje, o caminho de volta das Filipinas para o México, aproveitando a corrente de Kuroshio no Pacífico Norte. Os galeões saíam de Cavite, na baía de Manila, no fim de junho ou começo de julho, e a travessia até Acapulco levava pelo menos quatro meses. O motor do negócio era uma diferença de preço: a prata valia bem mais na Ásia que na América. Por isso, os navios iam abarrotados até nos conveses e cabines e, em casos extremos, rebocavam barcaças com mais carga. No México, o galeão era chamado de Nao de China, porque trazia sobretudo mercadorias chinesas. A tripulação era em grande parte filipina, muitas vezes recrutada à força, e filipinos que ficaram no México formaram a maioria dos asiáticos livres de lá. A rota durou até 1815, em meio à guerra de independência mexicana. Em centenas de travessias, a perna para o oeste passava logo ao sul do arquipélago havaiano, mas nenhum registro de contato chegou até nós. O historiador Henry Kamen atribui isso à falta de meios dos espanhóis para explorar direito o Pacífico. Há pontas soltas: uma carta náutica espanhola capturada pelos ingleses em 1743 mostra ilhas na latitude do Havaí, e tradições orais havaianas falam de estrangeiros chegados antes de Cook, mas os historiadores não as consideram provas confiáveis.

fontes.trecho: The Manila galleon trade route was a Spanish trade route linking the Philippines in the Spanish East Indies to Mexico (New Spain), across the Pacific Ocean, in use from 1565 to 1815. [...] The route was inaugurated in 1565 after the Augustinian friar and navigator Andrés de Urdaneta pioneered the tornaviaje or return route from the Philippines to Mexico. Urdaneta and Alonso de Arellano made the first successful round trips that year, by taking advantage of the Kuroshio Current. The galleons set sail from Cavite, in Manila Bay, at the end of June or the first week of July, sailing through the northern Pacific and reaching Acapulco in March to April of the next calendar year. [...] The trade using "Urdaneta's route" lasted until 1815, when the Mexican War of Independence broke out. [...] The vast majority of the galleon's crew consisted of Filipino natives; many of whom were farmers, street children, or vagrants press-ganged into service as sailors. [...] The galleons mostly carried cargoes of Chinese and other Asian luxury goods in exchange for New World silver. Silver prices in Asia were substantially higher than in America, leading to an arbitrage opportunity for the Manila galleon. Every space of the galleons was packed tightly with cargo, even spaces outside the holds like the decks, cabins, and magazines. In extreme cases, they towed barges filled with more goods. While this resulted in slow passage (which sometimes resulted in shipwrecks or turning back), the profit margins were so high that it was commonly practiced. These goods included Indian ivory and precious stones, Chinese silk and porcelain [...] comprising the majority of free Asian settlers ("chinos libres") in Mexico [...] The Manila galleons were also known colloquially in New Spain as La Nao de China ("The China Ship") because they carried mostly Chinese goods shipped from Manila. [...] It took at least four months to sail across the Pacific Ocean from Manila to Acapulco [...] Over 250 years, there were hundreds of Manila galleon crossings of the Pacific Ocean between present-day Mexico and the Philippines, with their route taking them just south of the Hawaiian Islands on the westward leg of their round trip. Despite this, there are no records of contact with the Hawaiians. British historian Henry Kamen maintains that the Spaniards did not have the ability to properly explore the Pacific Ocean and were not capable of finding the islands [...] A Spanish chart captured by the British in 1743 depicts islands in the latitude of Hawaii [...] he recorded several folk stories about foreigners who had visited Hawaii prior to first contact with Cook. [...] Scholars have dismissed these claims as lacking credibility.

gancho: Na China, a moeda de prata espanhola tinha nomes com "Buda": o rosto do rei lembrava o dele. Feita sobretudo com prata de Potosí, ela serviu de base ao yuan e ao iene e teve curso legal nos EUA até 1857.
explicacao: O real de a ocho, ou peça de oito, valia oito reales e era uma moeda de cerca de 38 mm, com 25,563 g de prata fina, cunhada depois de uma reforma monetária de 1497. A prata vinha sobretudo das jazidas de Potosí, na atual Bolívia, e as principais casas da moeda no Novo Mundo eram Potosí, Lima e Cidade do México. Como o padrão era uniforme, ela virou, já no século XVI, a primeira moeda mundial, usada na Europa, nas Américas e no Extremo Oriente. Pelos galeões de Manila, os pesos mexicanos chegavam à Ásia e eram trocados por mercadorias filipinas e chinesas. Lá, comerciantes conhecidos carimbavam nelas caracteres chineses para atestar que eram genuínas. Na China da dinastia Qing, alguns nomes da moeda levavam o caractere de Buda, pela semelhança do rei com as imagens dele, e outros o de "coluna", pelas duas colunas do brasão espanhol. O iene japonês e o yuan chinês se basearam de início nela. O dólar americano também nasceu dela, e a moeda espanhola teve curso legal nos Estados Unidos até a Lei da Moeda de 1857. A herança durou muito: a Bolsa de Nova York cotou ações em oitavos de dólar até 24 de junho de 1997 e só adotou preços decimais em 2001.

fontes.trecho: The Spanish dollar, originally known as the piece of eight (Spanish: real de a ocho, peso duro, peso fuerte or peso), and much later also dólar, is a silver coin of about 38 mm (1.5 in) diameter worth eight Spanish reales. It was minted in the Spanish Empire, following a monetary reform in 1497, with content 25.563 g (0.8219 ozt) fine silver. It was widely used as the first international currency because of its uniformity in standard and milling characteristics. [...] Because the Spanish dollar was widely used in Europe, the Americas, and the Far East, it became the first world currency by the 16th century. The Spanish dollar was the coin upon which the original United States dollar was based [...] and it remained legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857. Many other currencies around the world, such as the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan, were initially based on the Spanish dollar and other eight-real coins. [...] Thanks to the vast silver deposits that were found mainly in Potosí, in modern-day Bolivia [...] The main New World mints for Spanish dollars were at Potosí, Lima, and Mexico City [...] the Manila galleons that transported Mexican silver peso to Manila in the Manila–Acapulco Galleon Trade, where it would be exchanged for Philippine and Chinese goods [...] In Oriental trade, Spanish dollars were often stamped with Chinese characters known as chop marks, which indicated that a coin so marked had been assayed by a well-known merchant and determined to be genuine. [...] Contemporary names used for Spanish dollars in Qing dynasty China include [...] The "fó" element in those Chinese names referred to the King of Spain in those coins, as his face resembled that of images of the Buddha (佛 in Chinese); and the "zhù" part of those names referred to the two pillars in the Spanish coat [...] The pricing of equities on U.S. stock exchanges in 1⁄8-dollar denominations persisted until the New York Stock Exchange converted first to pricing in sixteenths of a dollar on 24 June 1997, and then in 2001 to decimal pricing.

gancho: Em 1833, um navio saiu de Boston com 180 toneladas de gelo cortado no inverno rumo a Calcutá, a quatro meses de viagem. Chegaram 100 toneladas, e a Índia virou o destino mais lucrativo do "Rei do Gelo".
explicacao: Frederic Tudor começou o comércio de gelo em 1806, mandando uma carga para a ilha da Martinica, no Caribe. Na época, os homens de negócios o viam como excêntrico, ou até tolo. Como não havia onde guardar o gelo, ele derreteu depressa. Endividado, Tudor passou partes de 1812 e 1813 na prisão por dívidas. Aprendeu com os erros: construiu um depósito de gelo em Havana e adotou o cortador puxado a cavalo inventado por Nathaniel Wyeth em 1825, que tirava blocos quadrados e baixou o custo da colheita de 30 para 10 centavos por tonelada. Os blocos iguais cabiam melhor no porão e derretiam menos, e eram socados em serragem, resíduo das serrarias da Nova Inglaterra que até então não tinha uso. Em 12 de maio de 1833, o brigue Tuscany partiu de Boston para Calcutá, a 26 mil km. Quando se aproximou do Ganges, em setembro, muita gente achava que a entrega era uma piada elaborada. A cidade virou o destino mais rentável de Tudor, com cerca de US$ 220 mil de lucro em 20 anos. Em 1834, ele mandou gelo e maçãs refrigeradas para o Rio de Janeiro, e os navios voltavam com açúcar e frutas. Só nos anos 1880 e 1890 fábricas de gelo começaram a substituir no Brasil o gelo importado.

fontes.trecho: Known as Boston's "Ice King", he was the founder of the Tudor Ice Company [...] he spent parts of 1812 and 1813 in debtor's prison. [...] In 1833, fellow Boston-based merchant Samuel Austin proposed a partnership for selling ice to India, then some 16,000 miles (26,000 km) and four months away from Massachusetts. On May 12, 1833, the brig Tuscany sailed from Boston for Calcutta, its hold filled with 180 tons of ice cut during the winter. When it approached the Ganges in September 1833, many believed the delivery was an elaborate joke, but the ship still had 100 tons of ice upon arrival. Over the next 20 years, Calcutta would become Tudor's most lucrative destination, yielding an estimated $220,000 in profits

The trade was started by the New England businessman Frederic Tudor in 1806. Tudor shipped ice to the Caribbean island of Martinique [...] At the time, Tudor was regarded by the business community at best as something of an eccentric, and at worst a fool. [...] Sales were hampered, however, by the lack of local storage facilities, both for Tudor's stock and any ice bought by domestic customers, and as a result the ice stocks quickly melted away. Learning from this experience, Tudor then built a functioning ice depot in Havana [...] Wyeth created a new form of horse-pulled ice-cutter in 1825 that cut square blocks of ice more efficiently than previous methods. [...] reducing the cost of harvesting ice from 30 cents ($7.30) a ton (901 kg) to only 10 cents ($2.40). [...] In 1834 Tudor sent shipments of ice to Brazil along with chilled apples, beginning the ice trade with Rio de Janeiro. These ships typically returned to North America carrying cargoes of sugar, fruit and, later, cotton. [...] ice plants began to be built in Brazil during the 1880s and 1890s, slowly coming to replace imported ice. [...] The uniform blocks that Wyeth's process produced also made it possible to pack more ice into the limited space of a ship's hold, and significantly reduced the losses from melting. The ice was typically packed up tightly with sawdust [...] This requirement for large quantities of sawdust coincided with the growth in the New England lumber industry in the 1830s; sawdust had no other use at the time

gancho: Entre 1500 e 1875, pelo menos 30 bilhões de búzios chegaram ao golfo do Benim como dinheiro. A moeda de Gana, o cedi, tem nome dessas conchas, e em chinês "riqueza" e "gastar" levam o desenho de um búzio.
explicacao: A concha mais usada como dinheiro no mundo foi a do búzio-moeda, Monetaria moneta, abundante no oceano Índico e colhida nas Maldivas, no Sri Lanka, na costa do Malabar e em outros lugares. Na África Ocidental, os búzios circulavam até em regiões longe do mar. Já no começo do século XVI, comerciantes europeus importavam milhares de quilos deles para trocar por tecidos, comida, cera, couro e também pessoas escravizadas. Esses fluxos ajudaram a erguer estados poderosos do litoral, como o Benim e Uidá. No golfo do Benim, os búzios chegaram a responder por 44% do valor total do comércio. Como valiam muito mais na África do que onde eram obtidos, o negócio rendia muito, com ganhos que teriam chegado a 500% em alguns casos. Mas, quanto mais conchas entravam, mais a inflação corroía as economias locais. Em partes da África Ocidental britânica, ainda se pagavam impostos com búzios no início do século XX, e o uso informal durou até os anos 1960. Do outro lado do mundo, na China antiga, eles foram tão importantes que muitos caracteres ligados a dinheiro e comércio incluem o caractere do búzio, como os de gastar e riqueza.

fontes.trecho: The shell most widely used worldwide as currency was the shell of Monetaria moneta, the money cowry. This species is most abundant in the Indian Ocean, and was collected in the Maldive Islands, in Sri Lanka, along the Malabar coast [...] In West Africa the cowrie shell was widely used, including regions far from the coast. By the early 16th century European traders were importing thousands of kilograms of cowries to trade for cloth, food, wax, hides, and other goods as well as slaves. These currency flows were instrumental in the development of the powerful states of Benin, Ouidah and others along the coast. Between 1500 and 1875 at least 30 billion cowries were imported to the Bight of Benin, accounting for 44% of the total value of trade. [...] As the value of the cowrie and the nzimbu was much greater in Africa than in the regions from which European traders obtained their supply, the trade was extremely lucrative. In some cases the gains are said to have been 500%. As these currency imports increased, however, inflation took hold and damaged the local economies. In parts of British West Africa, cowries remained accepted for tax payments until the early 20th centuries, and their use as currency in unregulated environments persisted until the 1960s. The national currency of Ghana introduced in 1965, the cedi, was named after cowrie shells. [...] In ancient China, cowries were so important that many characters relating to money or trade contain the character for cowry 貝 as a component (e.g. 價 "price", 費 "to spend", 買 "to buy", 財 "wealth"

gancho: No século IX, mercadores judeus chamados radhanitas, que falavam seis línguas, faziam rotas da França à China. Quase tudo o que se sabe deles vem de um livro escrito por um chefe de correios e de espionagem.
explicacao: O livro é o "Livro dos Caminhos e dos Reinos", escrito por volta de 870 por Ibn Khordadbeh, chefe dos correios, da polícia e da espionagem de uma província do Califado Abássida. Fora dele, os radhanitas praticamente não aparecem nas fontes, e até hoje não se sabe se o nome designava uma guilda, um clã ou os mercadores judeus em geral. A origem da palavra também é disputada: um distrito da Mesopotâmia, a cidade de Rey, no Irã, uma expressão persa para "quem conhece o caminho" ou o vale do rio Ródano. Segundo Ibn Khordadbeh, eles falavam árabe, persa, a língua dos "romanos", a dos francos, o espanhol e línguas eslavas, e usavam quatro rotas principais, todas começando no vale do Ródano e terminando na costa leste da China. Iam por mar e por terra, passando pelo Egito, por Bagdá ou pela terra dos cázaros. Para o Oriente levavam peles, espadas e escravizados; na volta traziam almíscar, cânfora e canela. O papel deles vinha de um impasse: na Alta Idade Média, reinos cristãos e estados muçulmanos muitas vezes proibiam a entrada dos mercadores uns dos outros, e os radhanitas funcionavam como intermediários neutros.

fontes.trecho: The Radhanites or Radanites [...] were early medieval Jewish merchants, active in the trade between Christendom and the Muslim world during roughly the 8th to the 10th centuries. [...] Only a limited number of primary sources use the term, and it remains unclear whether they referred to a specific guild, to a clan, or generically to Jewish merchants in the trans-Eurasian trade network. [...] believe it refers to a district in Mesopotamia called "the land of Radhan" in Arabic and Hebrew texts of the period. [...] Another hypothesis suggests that the name might be derived from the city of Ray (Rhages) in northern Iran. Still others think the name possibly derives from the Persian terms rah "way, path" and  dān "one who knows", meaning "one who knows the way". [...] have suggested a connection to the name of the Rhône River valley in France [...] The activities of the Radhanites are documented by Ibn Khordadbeh – the postmaster, chief of police (and spymaster) for the province of Jibal, under the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tamid – when he wrote Kitab al-Masalik wal-Mamalik (Book of Roads and Kingdoms), in about 870. The Radhanites are otherwise not attested. [...] He outlined four main trade routes used by the Radhanites in their journeys; all four began in the Rhone Valley in southern France and terminated on China's east coast. [...] These merchants speak Arabic, Persian, Roman, the Frank, Spanish, and Slav languages. They journey from West to East, from East to West, partly on land, partly by sea. They transport from the West eunuchs, female slaves, boys, brocade, castor, marten and other furs, and swords. [...] On their return from China they carry back musk, aloes, camphor, cinnamon, and other products of the Eastern countries [...] arrive at Khamlidj, the capital of the Khazars. [...] During the Early Middle Ages, Muslim polities of the Middle East and North Africa and Christian kingdoms of Europe often banned each other's merchants from entering their ports. [...] The Radhanites functioned as neutral go-betweens

gancho: No Egito romano, alguém ofereceu uma estátua de Buda num templo da deusa Ísis, a mais antiga já achada a oeste do Afeganistão. E uma estatueta de Buda feita no norte da Índia no século VI foi parar numa ilha da Suécia.
explicacao: A estátua egípcia foi achada em partes, em escavações recentes, no pátio de um templo de Ísis no antigo porto de Berenice, no mar Vermelho, que por quase 800 anos ligou esse mar ao mundo mediterrâneo. Mede 71 cm, é de mármore da ilha grega de Paros e deve ser do século II. Tem auréola com raios de sol e uma flor de lótus ao lado. No mesmo sítio apareceram uma inscrição em sânscrito datada do reinado do imperador Filipe, o Árabe, e moedas de uma dinastia indiana, indícios de mercadores budistas da Índia no Egito. Um dos pesquisadores resumiu a pergunta que fica: o que significa oferecer um Buda num templo romano de Ísis no Egito? A outra peça viajou ainda mais. Na ilha de Helgö, no lago Mälaren, no condado de Estocolmo, um entreposto que surgiu por volta do ano 200, escavações iniciadas em 1954 acharam uma pequena estatueta de Buda do norte da Índia e uma concha de batismo do Egito, ambas feitas no século VI. Acredita-se que o Buda só tenha chegado à ilha na Era Viking. O Buda de Helgö está hoje no Museu de História da Suécia, em Estocolmo.

fontes.trecho: The Berenike Buddha is a statue of the Buddha, parts of which were discovered in January 2018 and January 2022 in an archaeological excavation in the ancient harbour of Berenike, Egypt [...] The statue was discovered in the forecourt of an early Roman period temple dedicated to the Goddess Isis. The statue, dated around the second century CE, is the earliest statue of the Buddha to ever be found west of Afghanistan. [...] It was made from marble that was quarried from the Greek island of Paros [...] The statue has a halo around the head of the Buddha, decorated with the rays of the sun, and has a lotus flower by his side. It is 71 cm (28 in) tall. The excavations at Berenike also yielded other artifacts related to ancient India: an inscription in Sanskrit dated to the Roman Emperor, Philip the Arab (244 to 249 CE), as well as Satavahana coins dated to the 2nd century CE. [...] "What does it mean to make an offering of a Buddha statue in a Roman temple to Isis in Egypt? [...] The Berenike port site, which connects the Red Sea to the Mediterranean world, was an important trade nexus for almost 800 years

Helgö is an island in Ekerö Municipality in Stockholm County, Sweden. It is situated in Lake Mälaren. [...] The old trading town on Helgö began to emerge around the year 200 AD, 500 years before Birka at Björkö. The first archaeological dig in 1954 uncovered the remains of the early settlement [...] The most notable finds included a small Buddha statuette from North India and a christening scoop from Egypt, both dating from the 6th century. The Buddha statuette, the Irish crozier and the Egyptian Coptic scoop, which were found on Helgö, are presently on display in the Swedish History Museum in Stockholm.
the Berenike Buddha, suggesting the presence of Buddhist merchants from India in Egypt at that time.

The Helgö Buddha is a small Buddha figure of the 6th century Gupta Empire period, found during excavations at the site of a former trading post on the island of Helgö in Sweden. [...] It is believed to have come to Helgö during the Viking Age. It is North Indian

gancho: O maior tesouro de prata viking, achado na ilha sueca de Gotland em 1999, tinha 14.295 moedas, e 14.200 eram dirhams islâmicos. Havia tanta prata que as chapas de raio X do hospital local saíram em branco.
explicacao: A descoberta foi quase por acaso. Um arqueólogo e um professor de numismática tinham acabado de gravar para a TV uma reportagem sobre saques a sítios arqueológicos numa fazenda chamada Spilling. Vinte minutos depois que a equipe saiu, o detector de metais deu sinal; horas mais tarde, a três metros dali, o visor mostrou "sobrecarga" e desligou. Eram dois depósitos de prata, de 27 e 40 kg, guardados no século IX sob o assoalho de um galpão, e um terceiro, com mais de 20 kg de bronze. A prata daria para pagar ao rei da Suécia o imposto de toda Gotland por cinco anos. As moedas vieram de 69 casas da moeda, em 15 países atuais, e iam de uma persa de 539 a peças de 870; uma, cunhada pelos cázaros por volta de 800, diz "Moisés é o mensageiro de Deus". Uma das vias dessa prata era a rota do rio Volga, onde escravizados e peles eram vendidos a mercadores muçulmanos em troca de dirhams de prata e de seda. Até 2015, Gotland já tinha rendido mais de 1.000 kg de prata, em mais de 700 depósitos, com 168 mil moedas do mundo árabe, do norte da África e da Ásia Central.

fontes.trecho: The Spillings Hoard (Swedish: Spillingsskatten) is the world's largest Viking silver treasure, found on Friday 16 July 1999 in a field at the Spilling farm northwest of Slite, on northern Gotland, Sweden. [...] 14,295 coins most of which were Islamic from other countries. A third deposition containing over 20 kg (44 lb) of bronze scrap-metal was also found. The three caches had been hidden under the floorboards of a Viking outhouse sometime during the 9th century. [...] They chose to do a segment on the problem with looting of archaeological sites with archaeologist Jonas Ström acting as their guide along with Kenneth Jonsson, a professor of numismatics [...] Twenty minutes after the TV-crew had left, they heard a strong signal from their metal detector [...] A couple of hours later and only 3 metres (9.8 ft) from the first find, they received another signal from the detector: "The display blinked 'overload' and then it turned itself off." [...] The smaller weighed 27 kg (60 lb) and the larger one 40 kg (88 lb). An attempt to X-ray the finds at the local hospital failed because they contained so much silver that the X-ray plates remained blank. [...] The silver in the caches would have been enough to pay the tax to the Swedish king for all of Gotland for five years. [...] As of 2015, more than 1,000 kilograms (2,200 lb) of silver from over 700 caches deposited between the 9th and 12th centuries have been found on Gotland. This includes 168,000 silver coins from the Arab world, North Africa and Central Asia. [...] Of the 14,295 coins found, 14,200 were Islamic dirhams [...] The earliest, a Persian coin, dates from 539 and the latest from 870. [...] All in all, 69 different minting locations from 15 present-day countries were identified in the hoard. [...] One of the most noted coins in the hoard, dated to c. 800, is from the Khazar Kingdom and designated the "Moses Coin". [...] The coin is inscribed with "Moses is the messenger of God"
where Slavic slaves and furs were sold to Muslim merchants in exchange for Arab silver dirham and silk

gancho: Muziris, na Índia, foi um grande porto da pimenta para o mundo romano: um papiro registra uma só carga avaliada em cerca de 9 milhões de sestércios. Depois o porto sumiu dos mapas, e onde ele ficava ainda é debatido.
explicacao: Muziris ficava perto da foz do rio Periyar, na costa do Malabar, e aparece tanto em poemas tâmeis antigos quanto em autores greco-romanos, como Plínio, o Velho, e o Périplo do Mar Eritreu, sobretudo ligado ao comércio de especiarias. Um papiro grego do século II registra um contrato entre um importador de Alexandria e um financiador sobre cargas de pimenta e especiarias vindas de lá, com uma remessa de cerca de 9 milhões de sestércios trazida no navio Hermapollon. Um épico tâmil do século II descreve comerciantes gregos chegando de navio para trocar ouro por pimenta. A Tábua de Peutinger, cópia medieval de um mapa de estradas romano, marca ao lado de Muziris um "Templum Augusti", em geral lido como um templo do imperador Augusto; muitos romanos deviam passar meses ali, esperando ventos para voltar. Depois, Muziris desapareceu sem deixar rastro, provavelmente por causa de uma enchente do Periyar em 1341, que mudou a geografia da região e abriu o porto atual de Kochi. A localização exata é discutida há muito tempo: escavações feitas desde 2007 em Pattanam, em Kerala, levaram parte dos especialistas a apontar o lugar, mas a identificação gerou controvérsia entre historiadores.

fontes.trecho: It was located near the mouth of the Periyar River in the Chera country of Tamilakam. Muziris is celebrated in several ancient Tamil sources (the Sangam Literature or the early Tamil poems) and Graeco-Roman Classical texts, such as the Periplus and the writings of Pliny the Elder, especially for its importance in the Indian Ocean spice trade [...] presumably until the devastating "floods" of the Periyar River in 1341 CE. [...] The exact location of the ancient port has long been a matter of dispute among historians and archaeologists. [...] Excavations conducted since 2007 at Pattanam, near North Paravur (Ernakulam) in Kerala, have led some experts to favour that location. [...] This identification of Pattanam as Muziris also sparked controversy among historians. [...] This Greek papyrus of the 2nd century AD documents a contract involving an Alexandrian merchant importer and a financier concerning ship cargoes, especially of pepper and spices, from Muziris. The fragmentary record provides details about a cargo consignment valued at around 9 million sesterces brought back from Muziris on board a Roman merchant ship called the Hermapollon. [...] written by Ilango Adigal, a Jain poet-prince from Kodungallur during the 2nd century AD, describes Muziris as a place where Greek traders would arrive in ships to barter gold to buy pepper. [...] The Tabula Peutingeriana (Peutinger Map) is an odd-sized medieval copy of an ancient Roman road map [...] Beside the lake is an icon marked Templ(um) Augusti, widely taken to mean a temple of Augustus, a Roman emperor. Many Roman subjects must have spent months in this region awaiting favourable conditions for return sailings to Rome [...] Muziris disappeared from every known map of antiquity, and without a trace, presumably because of a cataclysmic event in 1341: flooding in the Periyar River that altered the region's geography. [...] which opened up the present harbour at Kochi
